entries.meaning: The right or ability to reach, enter, or use something.
examples: Only three people have access to the payroll system.
The new ramp gives access to the second floor.
Rural counties still lack reliable access to broadband.
Her lawyer was denied access to the case file for two weeks.
Interns get access to the archive but not to the vault.
Nothing in the settlement guarantees access to editing the original recordings.
entries.русский: доступ к — право или возможность войти, дойти, воспользоваться
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (access to funding, access to editing the master file) — never a to-infinitive (✗ access to edit the file, unless to edit is a purpose clause after a complete phrase) and never a that-clause
entries.pattern: have / gain / get / deny / grant access to [noun phrase] · access to [someone] · give [someone] access to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Access for names the beneficiary, not the thing reached: access to the building is what you can enter, access for wheelchair users is who gets in. The verb access takes a direct object and no preposition — she accessed the file, never ✗ she accessed to the file. Note also the adjective split: accessible to people (they can use it) against accessible by road (that is the route).
entries.see also: enter something, limit to/on, permission for, to

entries.meaning: Faithful, continued observance of a rule, a standard, or a course of treatment.
examples: Payment depends on strict adherence to the reporting schedule.
Only about half the patients showed good adherence to the six-month regimen.
The audit found no adherence to the written change-control policy at all.
Her adherence to the party line surprised people who had known her in law school.
Certification requires adherence to documenting every deviation, however small.
Adherence to the posted speed limit on that stretch is essentially voluntary.
entries.русский: приверженность чему-л., соблюдение чего-л. — верное следование правилу или режиму
entries.register: neutral to formal — policy, medicine, and compliance writing
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (adherence to logging every deviation) — never a to-infinitive (✗ adherence to log every deviation) and never a that-clause (✗ adherence that the rules be followed). The to here is a preposition, so a verb after it must end in -ing.
entries.pattern: adherence to [a rule / a standard / a schedule / a regimen] · strict / rigid / close / slavish adherence to [noun phrase] · in adherence to [noun phrase] (formal) · [someone's] adherence to [a party / a doctrine]
entries.contrast: Adherence is sticking to a rule; adhesion is sticking to a surface. Adherence to the protocol is following it; the adhesion of the coating to the steel is physical. In American medicine adherence to a drug regimen has largely displaced compliance with it, on the theory that patients cooperate rather than obey — compliance with survives in the regulatory sense. The verb is adhere to (✗ adhere with), and the adjective is adherent to. ✗ adherence of the rules and ✗ adherence with the policy are both errors.
entries.see also: compliance with, conformity with/to, deference to, comply with, in accordance with, to

entries.meaning: A benefit something gives you, or a way in which one thing beats another.
examples: The main advantage of leasing is that repairs aren't your problem.
Solar panels have a clear advantage over a diesel generator in the summer.
She had the advantage of having read the report the night before.
Don't let the contractor take advantage of your father.
The rule change works to the advantage of smaller schools.
Our only advantage over the incumbent is that we can move faster.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ədˈvænɪdʒ əv/ → /ədˈvænɪdʒ ə/; over has no weak form
entries.русский: преимущество: of — выгода от чего-л., over — превосходство над соперником
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (the advantage of arriving early) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the advantage to arrive early). over: a noun phrase naming a rival or a competing option, never a gerund (✗ an advantage over arriving early).
entries.pattern: the advantage of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an advantage over [competitor] · take advantage of [noun phrase] · have the advantage of [noun phrase] · to [someone's] advantage
entries.variants: the advantages to doing it this way — an accepted informal American variant of the advantage of, but of is the edited form
entries.contrast: The two prepositions are not interchangeable. The advantage of a hybrid is the good thing a hybrid gives you; an advantage over a hybrid is the way something beats a hybrid. Mixing them produces nonsense: ✗ the advantage over arriving early has no rival to compare with. Take advantage of is fixed and has a second, negative sense — exploiting a person — that take the advantage of does not carry. ✗ advantage on and ✗ advantage above are errors.
entries.see also: benefit of/to, disadvantage of, comparison with/to, of, over

entries.meaning: A recommendation about what someone should do.
examples: I need advice on whether to refinance now or wait.
She gave me some good advice about handling difficult clients.
The website has advice on choosing a health plan.
His only advice to new teachers was to learn every name in the first week.
Take my advice and get it in writing.
That's the worst piece of advice I've heard all year.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ədˈvaɪs ən/; about clips to /ˈbaʊt/ in fast speech
entries.русский: совет по поводу чего-л. — в русском исчисляемо, в английском нет (✗ an advice)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (advice on choosing a plan), or a wh-clause (advice on what to do, advice on how to file) — never a that-clause (✗ advice that you should wait; write advice to wait). Advice to + infinitive is possible and names the content of the advice: his advice to sell was wrong.
entries.pattern: advice on / about [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · advice to [person] · advice to [verb] · give / take / follow / ignore advice · a piece of advice
entries.variants: advice on — the default for a domain or procedure · advice about — slightly more conversational and more usual with a specific worry
entries.contrast: Advice is uncountable in American English: ✗ an advice, ✗ some advices, ✗ many advices. Count it with a piece of advice, two pieces of advice, or some advice. Do not confuse the noun advice /ədˈvaɪs/ with the verb advise /ədˈvaɪz/ — the c form is the noun. The verb takes a person as a direct object with no preposition (she advised me, ✗ she advised to me) and takes on for the topic (she advised us on the merger).
entries.see also: information about/on, opinion on/of/about, knowledge of/about, on, about

entries.meaning: A settlement between parties, or the state of holding the same view.
examples: The company signed a five-year agreement with the pilots' union.
We never reached agreement on who would pay the deductible.
There's broad agreement about the diagnosis and none at all about the treatment.
They came to an agreement that neither side would talk to reporters.
I'm in agreement with you on almost everything except the timeline.
The agreement between the two districts expires in June.
entries.русский: соглашение с кем-л. / о чём-л.; также согласие с кем-л.
entries.complement: with: a person, party, or institution. on / about: a topic — noun phrase, gerund (agreement on postponing the vote), or wh-clause (no agreement on who pays). Agreement also takes a bare that-clause with no preposition (an agreement that he would leave) and a to-infinitive (an agreement to split the costs).
entries.pattern: an agreement with [party] · an agreement on / about [issue] · an agreement to [verb] · an agreement that [clause] · reach / sign / break an agreement · in agreement with [someone]
entries.variants: agreement on — an issue settled · agreement about — looser and more conversational · agreement between [two parties] — from the outside, naming both sides
entries.contrast: Three frames with three jobs: an agreement with the union names the other side, an agreement on wages names the subject, and an agreement between the city and the union names both sides from outside. The related verb splits the same way and is a classic error zone: agree with someone (share their view), agree to a proposal (accept it), agree on a date (settle it jointly), agree that... — and ✗ agree something is not American English, though British writers use agree a deal.
entries.see also: disagreement with/about, opposition to, difference between/in, with, agree with, agree to, agree on, on

entries.meaning: Something you can choose or use instead of something else.
examples: Biking is a serious alternative to driving in a town this flat.
We're looking for an alternative to the current supplier.
Is there any alternative to filing an appeal?
Community college was the only affordable alternative to a four-year school.
She had no alternative but to resign.
The board rejected all three alternatives to the merger.
entries.русский: альтернатива чему-л. — то, что можно выбрать вместо
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (an alternative to driving) — never a to-infinitive. ✗ an alternative to drive downtown is the single commonest error with this word, because the to looks like an infinitive marker and is not. Test it: a noun fits the slot (an alternative to the car), so to is a preposition and the verb takes -ing.
entries.pattern: an alternative to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · have no alternative but to [verb] · the only alternative is to [verb] · offer / propose / seek an alternative to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Alternative to names what you would be replacing; there is no ✗ alternative for, ✗ alternative of, or ✗ alternative from. Two other frames use a different to: in no alternative but to wait and the only alternative is to wait, the to really is an infinitive marker, which is why the bare verb is right there and wrong after an alternative to. Purists once insisted alternative could apply to exactly two options; American usage abandoned that long ago and three alternatives is unremarkable.
entries.see also: substitute for, objection to, preference for, solution to, to

entries.meaning: A formal change proposed or made to a document already in force.
examples: The committee attached an amendment to the highway bill at two in the morning.
We signed a one-page amendment to the lease so the dog could stay.
She offered an amendment to strike the residency requirement.
The amendment to the bylaws needed a two-thirds vote of the full membership.
The Twenty-Sixth Amendment to the Constitution lowered the voting age to eighteen.
Every amendment to the settlement has to be filed with the court within ten days.
entries.русский: поправка к — официальное изменение уже действующего документа
entries.register: neutral to formal — legislatures, contracts, bylaws, court filings
entries.complement: either a noun phrase naming the document amended (an amendment to the lease) or a bare infinitive naming what the amendment would do (an amendment to strike the residency requirement) — the two to's are different words and both are standard. Never a gerund (✗ an amendment to striking the requirement) and never a that-clause (✗ an amendment that the fee be capped; write an amendment capping the fee).
entries.pattern: an amendment to [a bill / a contract / the constitution] · an amendment to [verb] · propose / offer / attach / adopt / defeat an amendment · an amendment banning [noun phrase] · the First / Fifth / Fourteenth Amendment (usually cited bare)
entries.contrast: The two to's are the whole difficulty. An amendment to the lease attaches to a document, and a noun follows; an amendment to cap the fee says what it does, and a bare verb follows — put a plain noun in the slot to tell them apart. Amendment of is the act of amending and is stiffer and rarer: amendment of the bylaws requires a two-thirds vote, but the sheet of paper is an amendment to the bylaws. ✗ an amendment on the bill is an error. A numbered constitutional amendment is normally cited bare (the Fourth Amendment), with to the Constitution added only in full formal citation.
entries.see also: appendix to, exhibit to/schedule to/annex to, waiver of, notice of/to, change in/of, to

entries.meaning: A likeness drawn between two things in order to explain or argue from one to the other.
examples: He drew an analogy to the way a fever burns off an infection.
The analogy with the 1970s only goes so far, and it stops at the oil price.
There's a rough analogy between a watershed and a circuit board.
By analogy to the earlier case, the court found no duty of disclosure.
The analogy to a household budget is the one every politician reaches for, and it is wrong.
Her analogy with chess made the whole strategy suddenly obvious.
entries.русский: аналогия с — сходство, проводимое ради объяснения или довода
entries.register: neutral to formal; heaviest in law, philosophy, and science writing
entries.complement: to / with: a noun phrase or gerund (an analogy to boiling a frog slowly). between: two things joined by and. Never a to-infinitive (✗ an analogy to boil a frog) and never a that-clause (✗ an analogy that the market is a machine).
entries.pattern: an analogy to / with [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an analogy between X and Y · draw / make / press an analogy · by analogy to / with [noun phrase] · the analogy breaks down
entries.variants: analogy to and analogy with are both standard American English — to is commoner in legal and mathematical writing, with in general prose. Analogy between is not a third alternative but a different frame: it needs two named terms.
entries.the adjective takes only one preposition: analogous to, and ✗ analogous with is not the edited form even though it is heard. Against similarity to/between: a similarity is a fact about two things, an analogy is an argument you build out of one — which is why an analogy can be good, strained, or false, and a similarity cannot. Watch the stress, which moves across the family: analogy /əˈnælədʒi/, analogous /əˈnæləɡəs/, but analog /ˈænəlɔɡ/ and analogical /ænəˈlɑdʒɪkəl/.
entries.see also: comparison with/to, similarity to/between, contrast to/with, comparable to, similar to

entries.meaning: A response to a question, or the solution to a problem.
examples: Nobody could give me a straight answer to a simple question.
The answer to the housing shortage isn't going to be one policy.
I never got an answer to my email.
In answer to your question, yes, the lease renews automatically.
The answer to number twelve was on the back of the page.
She answers to the board, not to the CEO.
entries.русский: ответ на (вопрос), решение (задачи) — рус. «на», не «к» и не «о»
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund — usually a question, problem, or letter (the answer to my email), but a gerund is normal when the complement names a task rather than a question (the answer to reducing traffic is not more lanes, the answer to getting kids to read). That gerund is the proof that the to is a preposition, so it is never a to-infinitive: ✗ the answer to reduce traffic. The noun also takes an appositive that-clause naming its content, with no preposition: the answer, that nobody had checked the valve, took a week to surface.
entries.pattern: the answer to [question / problem / letter] · an answer to [someone] · in answer to [noun phrase] · have / know / give the answer to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The classic noun-versus-verb shift. The verb answer takes a direct object and no preposition — answer the question, answer the phone, answer my letter, never ✗ answer to the question. The noun requires to: the answer to the question, never ✗ the answer of the question. The one place answer to is a verb is the unrelated sense "report to, be accountable to": she answers to the regional director, he'll answer for this. Compare reply to, where the to survives in both the noun and the verb — which is exactly why answer trips people.
entries.see also: reply to, response to, solution to, answer something, to

entries.meaning: An expression of regret for something you did.
examples: The airline sent a form apology for the four-hour delay.
You owe your sister an apology for what you said at dinner.
He offered an apology to the family but never admitted fault.
I make no apology for holding the vote in public.
Her apology for missing the funeral came three months too late.
The mayor's apology to the neighborhood was read aloud at the meeting.
entries.русский: извинение за — выражение сожаления о содеянном
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (an apology for being late) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an apology to be late). Apology to takes the person owed: an apology to the family. Both can appear at once: an apology to the family for the delay.
entries.pattern: an apology for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an apology to [person] · an apology to [person] for [noun phrase] · owe / offer / demand / accept an apology · make no apology for [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Two prepositions, two roles: for names the offense, to names the person wronged. Swapping them is ungrammatical, not just odd: ✗ an apology for the family. The verb follows the same split — apologize to her for the delay — and takes no direct object at all: ✗ I apologized her, ✗ I apologized the delay. Note the American spelling apologize, and that apologia is a different word meaning a formal defense, not a regret.
entries.see also: excuse for, complaint about, responsibility for, for, apologize to, apologize for, to

entries.meaning: A section of supporting material attached at the end of a longer document.
examples: The full data set is in the appendix to the final report.
She published the letters as an appendix to the second edition.
Appendix C to the grant application lists every subcontractor by name.
The methodology is buried in an appendix to a 1978 study nobody reads.
Nothing in the appendix to the contract changes the payment terms.
Reviewers rarely read past the first appendix to a submission this long.
entries.русский: приложение к — раздел с дополнительным материалом в конце документа
entries.register: formal — academic writing, agency reports, and legal instruments
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the document the appendix hangs off — never a gerund, never an infinitive (✗ an appendix to show the raw data, unless to show is a purpose clause), and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an appendix to [a report / a book / an agreement] · Appendix A / Appendix 3 (cited bare, no preposition) · set out / attached / reproduced in the appendix · see the appendix to [document]
entries.variants: the plural is appendices /əˈpɛndəsiz/ for documents in scholarly and legal prose and appendixes for the organ; American general writing uses appendixes for both without anyone objecting
entries.contrast: In contract drafting the attached documents are exhibits, schedules, and annexes, not appendices — see exhibit to/schedule to/annex to. An addendum to adds material that did not exist before; an appendix to parks supporting material that did. ✗ an appendix of the report is wrong for the attachment sense, though an appendix of tables (what it contains) is fine. The organ takes no preposition at all: ✗ an appendix to the colon.
entries.see also: exhibit to/schedule to/annex to, amendment to, citation to, reference to, to

entries.meaning: Whether and how far a rule, standard, or principle reaches a particular case.
examples: The brief spends four pages on the statute's applicability to out-of-state sellers.
Counsel conceded the rule's applicability to the 2019 transactions.
Section 1 sets out the code's applicability to existing buildings.
Nobody disputed the standard's applicability to leased equipment.
The agency limited the guidance's applicability to federally funded projects.
Its applicability to volunteer fire departments is still unsettled in this circuit.
entries.русский: применимость к — насколько правило распространяется на данный случай
entries.register: formal — regulatory analyses, court opinions, and standards documents; an American meets it as the heading "Applicability" at the front of a federal rule, a building code, or an insurance policy
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (its applicability to franchising the brand) — never a to-infinitive (✗ applicability to cover franchises) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: the applicability of X to Y · [possessive] applicability to [a case / a class of persons / a transaction] · question / dispute / concede / limit the applicability of [rule] to [facts]
entries.contrast: The frame has two halves and needs both. Standard is the applicability of the exemption to small carriers; the of phrase may shrink to a possessive (its applicability to small carriers, the statute's applicability to small carriers) but it cannot simply vanish. The adjective is applicable to, and ✗ applicable for is an error. Do not confuse it with application to, which is an everyday word for a form you file: her application to the program is paperwork, the rule's applicability to the program is a question of law. ✗ applicability for and ✗ applicability on are errors.
entries.see also: relevance to, compliance with, exemption from, subject to, pursuant to

entries.meaning: A scheduled meeting with a professional or an official, or the act of placing someone in an office.
examples: I've got an appointment with the orthodontist at eight-fifteen.
She made an appointment with the county assessor to contest the valuation.
Can you move my appointment with Dr. Reyes to Thursday afternoon?
His appointment to the appeals court took fourteen months and two hearings.
The clinic is by appointment only after four.
He missed a third appointment with the probation officer and a warrant issued.
entries.русский: приём у кого-л., назначенная встреча с; отдельно — назначение на должность
entries.complement: with: a person, an office, or a business — never a gerund (✗ an appointment with seeing the dentist) and never a clause. for: the purpose or the day (an appointment for a cleaning, an appointment for Tuesday). at: the place or the clock time (an appointment at the clinic, an appointment at four). to: an office or a body, in the wholly different sense of the word (her appointment to the bench).
entries.pattern: an appointment with [person] · an appointment for [purpose / day] · an appointment at [place / time] · make / keep / miss / cancel / reschedule an appointment · [someone's] appointment to [a position] · by appointment only
entries.contrast: With names the other party, for the reason, at the place, and to the job. ✗ an appointment to the dentist is an error in the meeting sense, though his appointment to the FCC is correct in the office sense — one spelling, two nouns. American English keeps appointment for professional slots and reservation for tables, rooms, and seats: you have an appointment with the dentist and a reservation at the restaurant, where British English would say booking for both.
entries.see also: conversation with, interview with, encounter with, visit to, with

entries.meaning: A way of dealing with something, or the final stretch leading to a place.
examples: Her approach to classroom discipline is quieter than mine.
We need a completely different approach to funding rural clinics.
The company took a cautious approach to the acquisition.
Traffic backs up on the approach to the tunnel every weekday.
There's no single right approach to teaching a child to read.
His approach to negotiating is to say nothing for the first ten minutes.
entries.русский: подход к — способ решения; также приближение к месту
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (an approach to teaching writing) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an approach to teach writing). In the physical sense the complement is a place: the approach to the bridge. A wh-clause does not follow it (✗ an approach to how we hire; write an approach to hiring).
entries.pattern: an approach to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · take an approach to [noun phrase] · a [adjective] approach to [noun phrase] · the approach to [place]
entries.contrast: The verb takes no preposition at all. The plane approached the runway, he approached me after class — never ✗ approached to the runway. The noun requires to, and ✗ an approach of, ✗ an approach on, and ✗ an approach for are all wrong. Keep the -ing rule in view: because a noun fits the slot, the to is a preposition, so an approach to solving it, not ✗ an approach to solve it. The plural approaches is also the aviation term for the final descent path.
entries.see also: attitude to/toward, solution to, way of/to, approach something, to

entries.meaning: A quarrel, or a reasoned case for a position.
examples: I had a stupid argument with my brother about a parking space.
The argument over the property line has been going on since 1998.
Her argument for raising the minimum wage runs eighty pages.
There's a strong argument against rebuilding on the same site.
They got into an argument about who forgot to lock the shed.
The argument that the tax is regressive has never been answered.
entries.русский: спор с кем-л. / о чём-л.; отдельно — довод, аргумент в пользу позиции
entries.complement: with: a person. about / over: the subject — noun phrase, gerund (an argument about paying the deposit), or wh-clause (an argument about who was driving). for / against: a position, and here a that-clause is possible after the noun (the argument that the tax is regressive). ✗ an argument to do something.
entries.pattern: an argument with [person] · an argument about / over [issue] · an argument for / against [position] · an argument that [clause] · have / start / win / lose an argument · get into an argument with [person]
entries.variants: argument about — neutral · argument over — the same, with more heat and usually a scarce resource (an argument over the last seat)
entries.contrast: Four prepositions, four jobs. With is the opponent, about/over is the topic, for/against is the side taken — an argument for raising the cap is a reasoned case, while an argument about raising the cap is a quarrel. Because argument means both "quarrel" and "line of reasoning," the preposition is what tells the reader which one you mean. ✗ an argument to the manager and ✗ an argument on the topic are both wrong; use with and about. The verb keeps the same set: argue with someone about something, argue for a position, argue that.
entries.see also: disagreement with/about, discussion about/of, opposition to, with, argue with, argue about, argue over, about

entries.meaning: A tie between a person and a group, or an observed pattern linking two variables.
examples: He cut every association with the group the week after the indictment.
The study reports an association between night shifts and elevated blood pressure.
The exhibit was mounted in association with the state historical society.
Her only association with the case was one memo written in 2011.
Researchers found no association between the vaccine and the reported symptoms.
Guilt by association cost him the nomination before a single vote was counted.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˌsoʊsiˈeɪʃən wəθ/, /əˌsoʊʃiˈeɪʃən bəˈtwin/ · both /-siˈeɪ-/ and /-ʃiˈeɪ-/ are standard American
entries.русский: связь с / между — принадлежность к кругу либо статистическая связь величин
entries.register: neutral; the between frame is technical
entries.complement: with: a person, group, or thing, or a gerund (his association with running the fund). between: two items joined by and. Never a to-infinitive (✗ an association to reduce risk) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: an association with [person / organization] · an association between X and Y · in association with [partner] · guilt by association · break off / sever / deny an association with [noun phrase] · a trade / homeowners' / alumni association (no preposition)
entries.contrast: With for affiliation, between for statistics. His association with the firm is who he worked for; an association between lead exposure and reading scores is a pattern in a data set — and a researcher will insist that an association between claims far less than a cause of. ✗ an association to is an error in both senses. Against correlation with/between: a correlation is a measured coefficient, an association need only be a tendency, which is why epidemiologists reach for the looser word first.
entries.see also: connection with/to/between, correlation with/between, link between/to, relationship with/between, in association with, with

entries.meaning: An act of violence, or a hostile public criticism.
examples: The attack on the substation knocked out power to nine counties.
His column was a sustained attack on the mayor's housing record.
The clinic has been under attack from state legislators all spring.
She had an attack of vertigo halfway up the stairs.
Two of the attacks on the pipeline were never claimed.
The senator called the ruling an attack on the First Amendment.
entries.русский: нападение на, атака на — также резкая публичная критика кого-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun — a target, whether physical (an attack on the depot) or reputational (an attack on her record). It does not take a gerund or a clause: ✗ an attack on raising taxes; write an attack on the tax increase. Attack of takes an illness or a fit: an attack of nerves.
entries.pattern: an attack on [target] · an attack against [target] · an attack by [attacker] · an attack of [illness / emotion] · come / be under attack · launch an attack on [target]
entries.variants: an attack upon — formal and chiefly written · an attack against — normal with abstract or institutional targets (an attack against press freedom), less usual with physical ones
entries.contrast: Three different of / on / by jobs: on names the target, by names the attacker, of names an ailment or a fit — an attack of the flu, an attack of conscience, a heart attack. The verb takes a direct object and no preposition: they attacked the depot, never ✗ they attacked on the depot or ✗ attacked against the depot. Compare threat to, where the preposition names who is endangered rather than what is struck.
entries.see also: threat to, complaint about, opposition to, on, against

entries.meaning: A try at doing or producing something.
examples: His attempt at an apology made everything worse.
This is our third attempt at getting the permit approved.
She made no attempt to hide her irritation.
The bread was a first attempt at sourdough and it showed.
There was an attempt on the governor's life in 1974.
He passed the exam at the second attempt.
entries.русский: попытка чего-л. — рус. родительный, английское at предлогом не переводится
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (an attempt at reconciliation, an attempt at fixing the leak) — never a bare infinitive after at (✗ an attempt at fix the leak). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition at all: an attempt to fix the leak. Both are correct; see the contrast.
entries.pattern: an attempt at [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an attempt to [verb] · make an attempt at / to · an attempt on [someone's life / a record] · at the first attempt
entries.variants: an attempt at doing it and an attempt to do it — both standard; at + -ing stresses the trying, to + infinitive stresses the goal
entries.contrast: At and to divide the labor. An attempt at humor is a try at producing a thing; an attempt to be funny is a try at performing an act, so the gerund frame is normal with result nouns (an attempt at a soufflé) and the infinitive frame with action verbs (an attempt to reach him). A third preposition changes the meaning entirely: an attempt on his life is an attempted murder, and an attempt on the record is a try at breaking it. ✗ an attempt for and ✗ an attempt of are errors. The verb attempt takes a direct object or an infinitive and no preposition: she attempted the climb, she attempted to climb it, never ✗ attempted at the climb.
entries.see also: willingness to, chance of, success in/at, at, to

entries.meaning: Notice, care, or concentration directed at something.
examples: The renovation shows real attention to detail.
Pay attention to the fine print on page nine.
The report drew attention to three unreported spills.
She gives more attention to her houseplants than to her email.
Very little attention has been paid to rural transit funding.
May I have your attention for one minute.
entries.русский: внимание к — сосредоточенность и забота, направленные на что-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (attention to getting the details right) — never a to-infinitive (✗ attention to get the details right) and never a that-clause (✗ attention that the details were wrong). A wh-clause is fine, chiefly in the pay attention to frame: pay attention to what he says, little attention to how the work was funded.
entries.pattern: attention to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · pay attention to [noun phrase / wh-clause] · draw / call / bring attention to [noun phrase] · attention to detail · the attention of [person]
entries.contrast: The preposition never changes, but the near-synonyms do. Attention to is the only frame — ✗ attention on, ✗ attention about, ✗ attention for — yet the closely related focus takes on (focus on the details), which is where the mixing starts. The verb attend splits by sense: attend the meeting takes no preposition and means "be present at," while attend to the patient means "take care of." A speaker saying ✗ I attended to the conference has produced a different sentence from the one they meant.
entries.see also: focus on, emphasis on/stress on, interest in, respect for, to

entries.meaning: A settled way of thinking or feeling about something.
examples: Her attitude toward deadlines has improved since the reorganization.
Public attitudes to nuclear power shifted sharply after 2011.
I don't like his attitude about being asked to show ID.
The whole department has a casual attitude toward recordkeeping.
There's been a real change in attitude among younger farmers.
You'll get further with a better attitude toward being coached.
entries.русский: отношение к — устойчивый взгляд или чувство по поводу чего-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (her attitude toward working weekends) — never a to-infinitive (✗ his attitude to work weekends). No clause: ✗ an attitude that we should wait means something different (attitude + that-clause exists only in the rare "stance" sense).
entries.pattern: an attitude to / toward [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an attitude about [noun phrase] · someone's attitude · have / take an attitude toward [noun phrase] · a change in attitude
entries.variants: toward — the American default, with no -s · towards — British · to — standard everywhere but distinctly more British in feel · about — colloquial American, common in speech (his attitude about money)
entries.contrast: Toward is the American form, and the -s on towards buys no formality — it just reads as British. All three of toward, to, and about are grammatical; ✗ attitude against, ✗ attitude on, and ✗ attitude for are not. Note that bare attitude with no complement has become an American noun in its own right meaning insolence (don't give me that attitude, she's got attitude), which is why he has an attitude and he has an attitude toward authority say almost opposite things about the speaker's judgment.
entries.see also: approach to, opinion on/of/about, view on/of, reaction to, toward

entries.meaning: An expert on a subject, or power exercised over people or resources.
examples: She's the leading authority on nineteenth-century Shaker furniture.
The commission has no authority over privately owned wells.
He exceeded his authority when he signed the settlement.
The department has authority to issue permits but not to revoke them.
I have that on the authority of the county clerk herself.
Two authorities in the field reviewed the manuscript.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /əˈθɔrəti ən/; over has no weak form
entries.русский: on — авторитет, специалист по чему-л.; over — власть над кем-л.
entries.complement: on / in: a field of knowledge — noun phrase only (✗ an authority on how bridges fail; write an authority on bridge failures). over: a person, territory, or budget. The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: the authority to sign checks — and there the to is an infinitive marker, so ✗ the authority to signing checks.
entries.pattern: an authority on / in [field] · authority over [person / area / budget] · the authority to [verb] · on the authority of [source] · have / exercise / exceed one's authority
entries.variants: an authority on — the usual for a subject · an authority in — a field or discipline (an authority in pediatric oncology), slightly more institutional
entries.contrast: Two nouns wearing one spelling. An authority on medieval coins is an expert — countable, and you can be one of several. Authority over the budget is power — uncountable, and there is only so much of it. The prepositions keep them apart, so ✗ an authority over medieval coins claims a strange dominion and ✗ authority on the budget claims expertise where you meant control. A third frame, the authority to approve it, is a granted right, and it takes the infinitive, not a preposition.
entries.see also: expert on/in, control over/of, influence on/over, responsibility for, over

entries.meaning: Knowledge or perception that something exists or is the case.
examples: There's a growing awareness of how much water the plant actually uses.
The campaign raised awareness of early stroke symptoms.
She had a vague awareness of being followed down the block.
Public awareness of the recall was almost nonexistent.
An awareness that the fund would be exhausted by June changed the vote.
Safety awareness among the night crew has improved since the training.
entries.русский: осведомлённость о чём-л., осознание чего-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (awareness of being watched), or a wh-clause (an awareness of what the job actually pays) — never a to-infinitive. Unusually for a noun in this file, it also takes a bare that-clause with no preposition: an awareness that the money would run out.
entries.pattern: awareness of [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · awareness that [clause] · raise / increase awareness of [noun phrase] · a growing awareness of [noun phrase] · awareness among [group]
entries.variants: awareness about — increasingly common in public-health and campaign writing (awareness about the symptoms), but of remains the edited form
entries.contrast: Of is the preposition; about is a marketing habit. Both are heard, but of is what edited American prose uses, and ✗ awareness on, ✗ awareness to, and ✗ awareness for are simply wrong. Watch the two frames after the noun: awareness of the risk takes a noun, awareness that there was a risk takes a clause with no preposition at all. Dropping the of before a clause (✗ awareness of that there was a risk) is the error that follows from mixing them. The adjective aware takes the same two: aware of the risk, aware that there was a risk.
entries.see also: knowledge of/about, understanding of, insight into, belief in, aware of, of

entries.meaning: The evidence, principle, or foundation that something rests on or could be built on.
examples: There's no basis for the claim that the well was tested in June.
The affidavit gave the judge a basis for issuing the warrant.
His whole case rests on the basis of one unsigned memo.
Attendance is not a basis for dismissal under this contract.
She had no basis for believing the transfer had cleared.
The board meets on a quarterly basis, which is to say four times a year.
entries.русский: основание для — то, на чём что-л. держится или может быть построено
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a basis for believing him) — the edited frame. A that-clause is fine after the noun (no basis for the claim that the fund was solvent). A to-infinitive after basis is common in legal and journalistic prose (no basis to conclude that) but is still the marked choice; for + -ing is the form no editor will touch.
entries.pattern: a basis for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · the basis of [something] · on the basis of [evidence] · have / provide / lay / lack a basis for [noun phrase] · on a first-come basis, on a monthly basis (adverbial, no complement)
entries.variants: the basis of and the basis for split by direction: the basis of his argument is what the argument rests on, a basis for an argument is material you could build one out of. Both are standard; they are not interchangeable in every sentence.
entries.contrast: The plural is bases /ˈbeɪsiz/, spelled like the plural of base /ˈbeɪsɪz/ and pronounced differently — a written trap in on these two bases. ✗ a basis to the claim is an error. Note the frozen adverbial on a ... basis, which takes no preposition of its own and which editors compress on sight: on a weekly basis is usually just weekly.
entries.see also: grounds for, evidence of/for, justification for, rationale for, on the basis of, based on

entries.meaning: Relevance — the quality of having something to do with the matter at hand.
examples: His military record has no bearing on the zoning question.
What the neighbors saw has a direct bearing on the timeline.
The rate cut will have some bearing on next quarter's numbers.
Whether she liked him has no bearing on whether he was negligent.
The witness's memory has a real bearing on deciding which account to credit.
Anything with a bearing on the merger goes to outside counsel first.
entries.русский: отношение к делу — have a bearing on = иметь значение для чего-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal; common in courtrooms, editorials, and committee reports
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (no bearing on choosing a successor) — never a to-infinitive (✗ no bearing to choose a successor) and never a that-clause. The noun almost always appears inside have a bearing on or have no bearing on; a bare the bearing on is not idiomatic.
entries.pattern: have a bearing on [noun phrase] · have no bearing on [noun phrase] · a direct / material / significant bearing on [noun phrase] · bear on [noun phrase] (the verb) · get / find one's bearings (a different noun)
entries.contrast: Two unrelated nouns share the spelling. A bearing on something is relevance; one's bearings are orientation (get your bearings), and a bearing in a machine is a part — only the first takes on. ✗ a bearing to the case and ✗ a bearing with the case are errors. Against relevance to: the two say the same thing with different prepositions, and swapping the prepositions is the standard slip — ✗ no relevance on the case, ✗ no bearing to the case. The verb keeps on: the memo bears on the timeline.
entries.see also: relevance to, effect on, impact on, influence on/over, relevant to, on

entries.meaning: Confidence that something exists, works, or is worth holding to.
examples: Her belief in the program survived two rounds of budget cuts.
He lost his belief in the possibility of a negotiated settlement.
A belief in rewarding effort rather than results runs through the whole handbook.
The belief that housing prices only go up died in 2008.
They pressed on in the belief that the weather would clear.
Contrary to popular belief, the bridge was never named after him.
entries.русский: вера в — убеждённость, что нечто существует, работает или стоит того
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (a belief in taking the long view) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a belief in take the long view, ✗ a belief to take the long view). Like awareness, it also takes a bare that-clause with no preposition: a belief that the market will correct.
entries.pattern: a belief in [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a belief that [clause] · in the belief that [clause] · beliefs about [topic] · contrary to popular belief
entries.variants: beliefs about — the plural, for opinions on a topic (beliefs about diet), where singular belief in is about faith or confidence
entries.contrast: In for faith, that for content, and no preposition before the clause. A belief in vaccines is confidence in them; a belief that vaccines work is a specific proposition held — and ✗ a belief in that vaccines work mashes the two together. ✗ belief on and ✗ belief to are errors. The verb splits the same way and produces the file's most useful minimal pair: I believe you (I accept what you just said) against I believe in you (I have confidence in your ability), and ✗ I believe in that you can do it is wrong for the same reason.
entries.see also: confidence in, faith in, dependence on/reliance on, doubt about, believe in, in

entries.meaning: The person or entity legally entitled to receive something, or anyone who gains from an event.
examples: She is the sole beneficiary of her aunt's estate.
Every beneficiary under the policy must be notified within thirty days.
The contractor was the unexpected beneficiary of a drafting error in section 9.
He named his daughter as the primary beneficiary and his brother as contingent.
Farmers in three counties were the real beneficiaries of the rate freeze.
A beneficiary under the trust cannot also serve as its sole trustee here.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌbɛnəˈfɪʃieri əv/ → /ˌbɛnəˈfɪʃieri ə/; under has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. выгодоприобретатель, бенефициар — по завещанию, полису, договору
entries.register: of is neutral; under is legal drafting — a will, a trust instrument, a life-insurance form, an ERISA plan document. An American meets beneficiary under on the day a parent's estate is probated, or on the form the HR office hands out in the first week of a job.
entries.complement: of: a noun phrase naming the instrument, the person, or the windfall (the beneficiary of the trust, the beneficiary of a clerical error). under: a noun phrase naming the legal instrument only — a will, a policy, a plan, a section (a beneficiary under the policy). Never a gerund after under, and never an infinitive or a clause after either.
entries.pattern: the beneficiary of [an instrument / an act / a mistake] · a beneficiary under [a will / a policy / a plan] · name / designate [someone] as beneficiary · the primary / contingent beneficiary · a third-party beneficiary of [a contract]
entries.variants: beneficiary under the will and beneficiary of the will are both correct in a probate file; under is the drafter's form because it matches the other under phrases in the instrument (rights under, obligations under, hereunder)
entries.contrast: Of works everywhere; under only where there is a document. You may be the beneficiary of a lucky mistake, but ✗ a beneficiary under a lucky mistake is nonsense — under needs an instrument to sit beneath. Do not confuse the noun with benefit of/to: the benefit of the doubt is an advantage, the beneficiary of the estate is a person. In American insurance the fixed phrases are primary beneficiary and contingent beneficiary, both without a preposition.
entries.see also: benefit of/to, entitlement to, party to, signatory to, title to, hereunder

entries.meaning: An advantage gained, or the person or group that gains it.
examples: The main benefit of the new schedule is that nobody drives home in the dark.
The tax credit is of real benefit to first-time buyers.
She had the benefit of eight years' experience in the same building.
I'll give him the benefit of the doubt one more time.
The concert was a benefit for the county food bank.
There's no obvious benefit to switching carriers midyear.
entries.русский: of — польза от чего-л.; to — выгода для кого-л.
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (the benefit of starting early) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the benefit of to start early). to: a person or group who gains. A to-infinitive does attach directly to the noun in the informal the benefits to doing it this way, which is standard American speech but avoided in edited prose.
entries.pattern: the benefit of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a benefit to [person / group] · of benefit to [person] · for the benefit of [person] · give [someone] the benefit of the doubt · a benefit for [cause]
entries.variants: the benefits to doing X — accepted informal American variant of the benefits of doing X
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three meanings. The benefit of insulation is the advantage insulation gives; a benefit to homeowners is who receives it; and a benefit for the animal shelter is a fundraising event, an entirely separate noun. The verb takes yet another preposition: benefit from — homeowners benefit from the rebate, never ✗ benefit of the rebate, and this verb-to-noun shift (from → of) is one of the commonest in the file.
entries.see also: advantage of/over, disadvantage of, importance of/to, price of/for, of

entries.meaning: The violation of a duty, an agreement, a standard, or a barrier.
examples: Missing two deliveries is a breach of the supply agreement.
The suit alleges a breach of fiduciary duty by three former officers.
Reading her mail was a plain breach of trust.
The company disclosed the data breach eleven months after it happened.
Showing up in shorts was a breach of etiquette, not of the dress code.
He was arrested for breach of the peace outside the arena.
entries.русский: нарушение чего-л. — договора, обязанности, стандарта; юр.
entries.register: neutral to formal; the core term of American contract and fiduciary law, and an everyday word for a security failure
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the duty, agreement, or standard broken — never a gerund (✗ a breach of failing to disclose; write a breach of the duty to disclose), never an infinitive, and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: a breach of [contract / duty / trust / the peace / etiquette] · in breach of [an agreement] · a material / minor / anticipatory breach · sue for breach of contract · a data breach (compound, no preposition)
entries.contrast: Breach and breech are homophones and neither one is the other. A breach is a break; a breech is the back end of a gun or a baby delivered feet first, and breeches are trousers. ✗ a breech of contract is the commonest spelling error in small-claims filings. Note that breach of contract takes no article inside the fixed phrase — sued for breach of contract, not ✗ for a breach of the contract, unless a particular breach is meant. The verb takes a bare object: they breached the agreement, ✗ they breached of the agreement. In American practice a material breach excuses the other side's performance; a minor one only supports damages.
entries.see also: compliance with, default on/under, damages for, liability for/to, obligation to/under, remedy for/against, in violation of

entries.meaning: The argument in favor of or opposed to a course of action — and, separately, a legal action or a single instance.
examples: Nobody has made a serious case for keeping the old boiler another winter.
The case against expanding the runway is mostly noise and mostly persuasive.
She built the case for consolidating the two departments over six months.
The state's case against him rested on a single unreliable witness.
There's a strong case for waiting until the audit closes.
It was a case of mistaken identity, and it cost him two nights in county.
entries.русский: доводы за / против; отдельно — судебное дело и отдельный случай
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the case for raising rates) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the case to raise rates). A that-clause attaches to the verb frame instead: she made the case that rates should rise. The legal noun takes different prepositions: a case against a defendant, a case for the plaintiff, the case of Ruiz v. Kemper.
entries.pattern: the case for / against [noun phrase / verb-ing] · make / build / press / state the case for [noun phrase] · a case against [a person] (legal) · in case of [emergency] · a case of [flu / wine / mistaken identity]
entries.contrast: For and against are the argument; of is the instance. The case for a bond issue is the argument in favor; a case of the flu is one occurrence; a case against Ruiz is a prosecution. ✗ the case of raising rates means nothing. Note that in case of (a fixed compound preposition — see in case of) and in the case of (= "as for") are different phrases doing different jobs. ✗ a case to raise rates is the infinitive error, and it is common in memos.
entries.see also: argument with/about, grounds for, justification for, rationale for, in case of, against

entries.meaning: The thing that makes something happen.
examples: Investigators never determined the cause of the fire.
Heart disease is still the leading cause of death in the county.
The cause of the outage turned out to be a squirrel.
The lab results are no cause for alarm.
Falling enrollment is the cause of the budget gap, not the result of it.
There's cause for cautious optimism in the third-quarter numbers.
entries.русский: причина чего-л. — рус. родительный падеж, не «для»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the cause of the flooding, the cause of so many people leaving) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the cause of to flood) and never a that-clause (✗ the cause that the pipe burst; write the cause of the burst pipe).
entries.pattern: the cause of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a cause for [concern / alarm / celebration] · the cause of [death / the fire / the delay] · a lost cause · the leading cause of [outcome]
entries.contrast: Cause of against cause for, and the difference is total. The cause of names what produced a result — the cause of the fire was faulty wiring. Cause for appears only in a short fixed list of abstract nouns — cause for concern, cause for alarm, cause for celebration, cause for complaint — and means "grounds, justification." ✗ the cause for the fire is an error; a cause of concern is not wrong but says something different (what caused the concern, not what justifies it). Note also the unrelated third noun in a good cause, a lost cause, meaning a movement or aim.
entries.see also: reason for, result of, consequence of, effect on, of

entries.meaning: The likelihood that something will happen, or an opportunity to do something.
examples: There's a sixty percent chance of thunderstorms after four.
She has a real chance of making the Olympic team.
Give me a chance to explain before you decide.
What are the chances of the ferry running on a day like this?
We met entirely by chance at a gas station in Nebraska.
He never got the chance to say goodbye.
entries.русский: вероятность чего-л. (of + -ing); ср. chance to — возможность что-л. сделать
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (a chance of rain, a chance of winning) — never a to-infinitive after of (✗ a chance of to win, ✗ a chance of win). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: a chance to speak. Both are correct and they do not mean the same thing.
entries.pattern: a chance of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a chance to [verb] · the chances are that [clause] · stand / have a chance of [verb-ing] · by chance · give [someone] a chance to [verb]
entries.contrast: Chance of is probability; chance to is opportunity. There's a chance of speaking to her means it might happen; there's a chance to speak to her means the opening exists and you could take it. Weather forecasts and odds always use of (a forty percent chance of rain, ✗ a chance to rain), and offers always use to (give me a chance to explain, ✗ a chance of explaining in that sense). ✗ chance for doing is an error, though a chance for the kids (an opportunity for a person) is fine. Compare possibility of, which has only the of frame; opportunity behaves like chance but prefers the infinitive (an opportunity to speak) and takes for rather than of with a noun (an opportunity for growth).
entries.see also: possibility of, risk of, danger of/to, hope for/of, of

entries.meaning: An alteration, a replacement, or an edit.
examples: There's been a change in the weather since Thursday.
You'd better pack a change of clothes.
I've made two small changes to the contract — see the redline.
The most striking change in the neighborhood is the number of children.
We're looking at a change from fee-for-service to a flat rate.
Let's eat outside for a change.
entries.русский: in — изменение в чём-л.; of — смена, замена одного другим
entries.complement: in: a noun naming what is being altered (a change in the weather, a change in how we bill). of: a noun naming what is being swapped out (a change of address, a change of clothes). to: the modification made to a document or plan (a change to the schedule). Gerunds follow in freely (a change in staffing); no to-infinitive and no that-clause.
entries.pattern: a change in [thing that alters] · a change of [thing replaced] · a change to [document / plan] · a change from X to Y · make a change to [noun phrase] · for a change
entries.variants: a change of — swap · a change in — internal alteration · a change to — an edit · changes for — never; use changes to
entries.contrast: Three prepositions and three different events. A change in the schedule means the schedule itself is now different; a change of schedule means one schedule has replaced another; a change to the schedule is a specific edit made to it. Errors cluster around of: ✗ a change of the weather (the weather alters, it is not swapped) and ✗ a change in address (an address is swapped, not internally altered). Change from X to Y names both endpoints. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition — change the tire, ✗ change to the tire — except in change into (transform) and change from X to Y.
entries.see also: difference between/in, improvement in/on, increase in/decrease in, effect on, in

entries.meaning: A pointer to a source in a text, or an official notice of an offense or a commendation.
examples: The brief has forty pages of argument and one citation to the record.
He got a citation for an expired tag on the way to the hearing.
Every citation to an unpublished opinion has to be flagged.
Her citation for valor is framed in the hallway outside the chief's office.
The footnote gives a citation to the 1976 committee report.
Two paragraphs in, the memo drops a citation to a statute that was repealed.
entries.русский: ссылка на источник; отдельно — уведомление о нарушении (штраф) или благодарность
entries.register: to is legal and academic — briefs, law-review footnotes, style manuals; for is everyday American in two unrelated senses, a traffic ticket and a military commendation
entries.complement: to: a noun phrase naming a source — a case, a statute, a page, an authority. for: a noun phrase or gerund naming the offense or the deed (a citation for speeding, a citation for running the light, a citation for valor). of: what is quoted (the citation of three district-court opinions). Never an infinitive or a clause after any of them.
entries.pattern: a citation to [a case / a statute / page 14] · a citation for [an offense / an act of bravery] · the citation of [authorities] · issue / write / fight a citation · a pin citation
entries.contrast: To points at a source, for at a reason. A citation to Miranda sends the reader to a case; a citation for speeding is a ticket a Michigan trooper hands you; a citation for valor is a medal. ✗ a citation of Miranda is not wrong but means the act of citing rather than the reference itself. The verb splits the same way: cite to the record is legal usage, cite the record is general usage, and cite someone for a violation is the ticket. Do not confuse it with sight or site.
entries.see also: reference to, appendix to, penalty for, refer to, to

entries.respell: klaym uh-GENST, klaym for, klaym too
entries.meaning: An assertion of a right, a demand for payment, or a right asserted in something.
examples: Three contractors filed a claim against the estate before the deadline.
Her claim for lost wages was denied twice before it was paid.
The family still has a claim to forty acres along the river.
Grandchildren have no claim on his time and he tells them so.
The insurer disputes the claim for water damage but not the one for wind.
He laid claim to the discovery in a letter nobody kept.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kleɪm fɚ/, /kleɪm tə/; against has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. претензия к кому-л., требование о чём-л., притязание на что-л.
entries.register: neutral to formal; the against and to frames are legal and insurance usage, met on a proof-of-claim form in probate or a homeowner's policy
entries.complement: against: the party or fund you are proceeding against. for: what you want — damages, benefits, a refund. to: the thing you assert a right in — a title, a throne, an inheritance. on: a demand on a resource (a claim on her time). The noun also takes a bare that-clause (the claim that the meter was broken) but never a to-infinitive (✗ a claim to be paid, in the entitlement sense — that reading is only the verb, he claims to be paid).
entries.pattern: a claim against [a person / an estate / an insurer] · a claim for [damages / benefits] · a claim to [property / a title] · a claim on [resources / attention] · file / press / settle / deny a claim · lay claim to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Four prepositions and four different sentences. A claim against the estate is who owes; a claim for $40,000 is what is owed; a claim to the mineral rights is what you say is yours; a claim on my afternoon is a demand for time. Swap them and the meaning breaks: ✗ a claim to the estate for the mineral rights is word salad. Note the to trap: a claim to the land takes a noun, and a claim to own the land is not the entitlement noun at all. The verb claim takes a bare object (she claimed the deduction) and a that-clause (he claims that he paid), never ✗ claim for the deduction in American English.
entries.see also: damages for, entitlement to, liability for/to, right to/of/over, title to, against

entries.meaning: A spoken or written remark about something.
examples: The professor left three comments on my second paragraph.
Her comment about the parking situation got a bigger laugh than it deserved.
The agency declined to comment on the pending lawsuit.
His comment that the numbers were "directionally fine" did not reassure anyone.
The report was released without comment.
A single comment to the wrong reporter cost him the job.
entries.русский: комментарий к чему-л., замечание по поводу чего-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (a comment on being passed over), or a wh-clause (no comment on what was said) — never a to-infinitive. The noun takes a bare that-clause as its content: his comment that the numbers were soft.
entries.pattern: a comment on / about [noun phrase] · a comment to [person / the press] · a comment that [clause] · make a comment on [noun phrase] · no comment · without comment
entries.variants: comment on — the default, and the only form in no comment on · comment about — conversational, common in speech
entries.contrast: On for the subject, to for the audience. A comment on the draft is what the comment is about; a comment to reporters is who heard it. ✗ a comment for the draft and ✗ a comment of the draft are errors. The verb keeps on and cannot take a direct object: she commented on the delay, never ✗ she commented the delay — a frequent error because the parallel verb criticize does take a bare object (criticized the delay). Commentary on behaves identically to the noun.
entries.see also: opinion on/of/about, complaint about, view on/of, reference to, comment on, on

entries.meaning: A promise to do something, or a settled devotion to a person or a cause.
examples: The city made a public commitment to cutting emissions in half by 2035.
Her commitment to the students never wavered, even in the worst years.
We need a firm commitment from the vendor before anyone signs.
I have a prior commitment on Thursday, so count me out.
Nothing in the current draft is a commitment to hiring locally.
He broke every commitment he had made to the union that spring.
entries.русский: обязательство, приверженность чему-л. — обещание или преданность делу
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (a commitment to the plan, a commitment to reducing emissions) — a noun fits the slot, so that to is a preposition and the verb after it takes -ing. The same noun also licenses a to-infinitive in the undertaking sense (a commitment to reduce emissions by half, a commitment to appear at the hearing), where to is the infinitive marker; both frames are standard American English. A that-clause is possible in formal use (a commitment that no jobs would be cut). ✗ a commitment of reducing and ✗ a commitment for reducing are errors.
entries.pattern: a commitment to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · make / honor / break / renew a commitment · a commitment from [party] · a prior commitment · commitment to [a person or a cause]
entries.variants: a commitment toward — occasional and slightly off; to is the edited form · a commitment on — bureaucratic, as in a commitment on funding levels
entries.contrast: The noun forgives what the adjective does not. A commitment to reducing emissions and a commitment to reduce emissions are both good English, because commitment licenses a prepositional complement and an infinitive alike. The adjective allows only the gerund: committed to raising standards, ✗ committed to raise standards — see committed to. A writer moving from the noun to the adjective therefore has to switch from "either" to "-ing only," and that is where the mistake gets made. ✗ a commitment for and ✗ a commitment with are errors: the party who gave the promise takes from (a commitment from the vendor), while commitment to plus a person names devotion rather than a promise (her commitment to the students).
entries.see also: contribution to, objection to, responsibility for, dependence on/reliance on, to

entries.meaning: The act of setting two things side by side, or the relation that results.
examples: The report makes a careful comparison with three neighboring districts.
Any comparison to the 1970s energy crisis is going to be inexact.
There's simply no comparison between the two engines.
In comparison with last winter, this one has been mild.
The second draft is, by comparison, a model of clarity.
A side-by-side comparison of the two policies is on page four.
entries.русский: сравнение с чем-л., сопоставление — рус. «с», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (no comparison with running a marathon) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a comparison to run a marathon) and never a clause. Comparison between takes two items joined by and: a comparison between the two designs.
entries.pattern: a comparison with / to [noun phrase] · a comparison between X and Y · a comparison of X with / to Y · in comparison with / to [noun phrase] · by comparison · there's no comparison
entries.variants: comparison with — the analytical default, and the usual form in academic prose · comparison to — commoner in speech and in the figurative sense · both are standard American English
entries.contrast: The verb splits where the noun does not. Compare X with Y means measure them against each other point by point; compare X to Y means liken them, assert a resemblance — he compared the mayor to Nero is an insult, he compared the mayor with Nero is a study. The noun tolerates either preposition for both jobs, which is why the distinction survives mainly in careful writing. ✗ comparison than is an error (than belongs with the adjective different, see difference between/in), and by comparison takes no object at all — ✗ by comparison with the others, by comparison is a doubling.
entries.see also: contrast to/with, difference between/in, similarity to/between, relationship with/between, with

entries.meaning: An expression of dissatisfaction, formal or otherwise.
examples: We've had four complaints about the noise from the loading dock.
She filed a formal complaint against her supervisor.
A complaint to the state board takes about ninety days to process.
His only complaint about the apartment was the water pressure.
The patient came in complaining of numbness in her left hand.
There were complaints about being asked to work through lunch.
entries.русский: жалоба на — рус. «на», не «о» (✗ жалоба о качестве)
entries.complement: about: noun phrase, gerund (a complaint about being kept waiting), or wh-clause (complaints about how the tests are graded) — never a to-infinitive. against: a person or institution, in the formal sense of a filed grievance. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: a complaint that the heat was never turned on.
entries.pattern: a complaint about [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a complaint against [person / company] · a complaint to [authority] · a complaint that [clause] · file / lodge / make a complaint · a complaint of [symptom]
entries.variants: complain about — the everyday verb · complain of — used for symptoms and formal grievances (he complained of chest pain)
entries.contrast: Four prepositions, four roles: about is the subject, against is the party accused, to is the authority receiving it, and of is reserved for symptoms and legal pleading — she complained of dizziness. Choosing against for a subject produces ✗ a complaint against the noise, which reads as though the noise had been sued. The verb takes no direct object: ✗ he complained the delay, ✗ I complained the manager; it must be complained about the delay, complained to the manager.
entries.see also: objection to, doubt about, problem with, argument with/about, complain to, complain about, about

entries.meaning: The act or state of doing what a rule, order, or standard requires.
examples: The plant was cited for failure of compliance with the emissions limit.
We are in compliance with every condition of the permit as of Friday.
Compliance with the subpoena took four paralegals and a weekend.
Voluntary compliance with the guideline has been about sixty percent.
Bringing the stairwell into compliance with the code cost more than the roof.
She runs compliance for a mid-sized bank in Columbus.
entries.русский: соблюдение чего-л., выполнение требований — рус. родительный, не «с»
entries.register: neutral to formal — regulatory, corporate, and clinical writing; in American companies Compliance is also the name of a department
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a rule, order, standard, or request — never a gerund (✗ compliance with filing on time; write compliance with the filing deadline), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: compliance with [a rule / an order / a standard / a subpoena] · in compliance with [noun phrase] · full / substantial / voluntary compliance · bring [something] into compliance with [noun phrase] · a compliance officer (compound)
entries.contrast: ✗ Compliance to is the error, and it is everywhere — in vendor emails, in ISO paperwork, in job listings. The noun takes with and only with, matching the verb comply with and the adjective compliant with. Against adherence to, which takes to and only to: the two nouns mean nearly the same thing and take opposite prepositions, which is exactly why each attracts the other's. American medicine has largely swapped patient compliance with a regimen for adherence to it. Note that in compliance with (the complex preposition) is stiffer than the plain noun and belongs in filings, not in email.
entries.see also: adherence to, conformity with/to, breach of, exemption from, comply with, in compliance with

entries.meaning: Worry about something, care for someone, or the subject someone is occupied with.
examples: There's growing concern about the condition of the levee.
Her concern for the older residents kept the shelter open another week.
The book's central concern with labor history is clear from the first chapter.
The board raised concerns over the auditor's independence.
Water quality is of real concern to everyone downstream.
Concern that the vote had been miscounted led to a manual recount.
entries.русский: about — беспокойство из-за чего-л.; for — забота о ком-л.
entries.complement: about / over: what worries you — noun phrase, gerund (concern about losing the contract), or wh-clause. for: a person or a thing whose welfare is at stake. with: what someone is occupied with, an entirely different sense. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: concern that the levee would not hold. Never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: concern about / over [issue] · concern for [person / welfare] · concern with [subject matter] · concern that [clause] · of concern to [person] · express / raise / voice concern about [issue]
entries.variants: concern about — neutral · concern over — the same, slightly more journalistic · concerns regarding — bureaucratic
entries.contrast: The three-way split is the whole entry. Concern about the bridge is worry that something is wrong with it; concern for the residents is care about their welfare; concern with the bridge is having the bridge as your subject or business — the report's concern with rural roads. Saying ✗ concern for the delay misfires, because delays do not have welfare. ✗ concern on is wrong. Note the third life of this word: the modern adjective concerning meaning "worrying" (a concerning trend) is separate from the preposition concerning meaning "about," for which see concerning.
entries.see also: worry about, doubt about, interest in, sympathy for/with, concerned about, for

entries.meaning: Trust that someone or something will perform.
examples: I have complete confidence in the surgeon who did my mother's knee.
The board's confidence in the CEO has visibly eroded.
She lacked the confidence to speak up in the first three meetings.
Investors lost confidence in the currency within a week.
He told me in confidence, so I can't repeat it.
There's little confidence that the deadline will hold.
entries.русский: уверенность в ком-л./чём-л., доверие к чьим-л. способностям
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (confidence in getting it done on time) — never a to-infinitive after in (✗ confidence in to finish). The noun separately takes a to-infinitive with no preposition, meaning self-assurance: the confidence to ask for a raise. It also takes a bare that-clause: confidence that the funding will come through.
entries.pattern: confidence in [person / thing] · the confidence to [verb] · confidence that [clause] · have / lose / restore confidence in [noun phrase] · a vote of confidence in [person] · in confidence
entries.variants: confidence about — heard in speech about a future outcome (confident about the exam), but in is the noun's fixed preposition
entries.contrast: In is the only preposition for the object of your trust: ✗ confidence on the team, ✗ confidence to the team, ✗ confidence of the team — that last one means the team's own confidence, not yours in them. Distinguish the two frames: confidence in speaking is trust placed in the activity, while the confidence to speak is the nerve to do it. Note also in confidence (privately) and a confidence (a secret told), both unrelated senses. The adjective is confident in a person and confident about an outcome.
entries.see also: belief in, faith in, dependence on/reliance on, doubt about, confident of, in

entries.meaning: Agreement with a standard, rule, or model, or the act of matching one.
examples: The inspector certified conformity with the 2021 electrical code.
Each casting is checked for conformity to the drawing before it ships.
The order was entered in conformity with the parties' stipulation.
Nothing in the design is in conformity with what the client approved.
Conformity to type is what breeders are paid to judge.
The whole essay is about conformity and none of it is about conforming.
entries.русский: соответствие чему-л. — согласованность со стандартом или образцом
entries.register: formal — specifications, audits, court opinions, and theology; the social sense (conformity without a complement) is neutral
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the standard, rule, or model — never a gerund (✗ conformity with reporting quarterly) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: conformity with / to [a standard / a rule / a type] · in conformity with [noun phrase] · bring [something] into conformity with [noun phrase] · a certificate of conformity · conformity (bare, the social pressure sense)
entries.variants: conformity with and conformity to are both standard American English and interchangeable in most sentences; with is commoner in legal and regulatory prose, to in engineering and in the sense "matching a model." Manufacturing also uses conformance to, a narrower technical variant.
entries.contrast: Against compliance with: compliance is obedience to something binding, conformity is resemblance to a pattern — which is why goods conform to a specification but a firm complies with an order. ✗ conformity of the rules is an error for conformity with. The verb keeps both (conform to the spec, conform with the requirements), and the adjective is conformable to, now rare. Note the bare social noun, which takes no preposition at all: the pressure toward conformity in a high school.
entries.see also: compliance with, adherence to, consistent with, in accordance with, with

entries.meaning: A link, relationship, or association between things or people.
examples: Police questioned two men in connection with the break-in.
There's no proven connection between the additive and the symptoms.
The house still has a connection to the old well.
She has a family connection with the shipyard going back four generations.
I missed my connection in Denver by nine minutes.
Investigators see a connection between the two fires.
entries.русский: связь с чем-л. / между чем-л. — соединение или отношение
entries.complement: with / to: a single noun phrase. between: two or more items joined by and (a connection between the leak and the bad valve). Gerunds are possible (no connection with smuggling arms); never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause (✗ a connection that the two are related).
entries.pattern: a connection with / to [noun phrase] · a connection between X and Y · in connection with [noun phrase] · make / see / deny a connection · a connection to [network / flight]
entries.variants: connection with — association, involvement · connection to — a physical or network link, and increasingly the general form in American speech
entries.contrast: Between needs two things and the others need one. ✗ a connection between the fire is incomplete; ✗ a connection with the fire and the wiring should be between. Connection to is the everyday choice for a physical or digital link (a connection to the water main, a connection to the airport) and for a personal tie (she has a connection to the family), while connection with carries the sense of involvement, which is why questioned in connection with the robbery means suspected of it. The fixed phrase is in connection with, not ✗ in connection to.
entries.see also: link between/to, relationship with/between, reference to, similarity to/between, with

entries.meaning: General agreement within a group, or the position that group holds.
examples: There's no consensus on whether to rebuild the pier or remove it.
The committee reached a consensus about the timeline in one afternoon.
Consensus among the county's engineers has shifted twice since March.
The scientific consensus that the warming is human-caused is not in serious dispute.
They never got to a consensus on funding the second position.
