The board decided by consensus rather than by a recorded vote.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kənˈsɛnsəs ən/; about clips to /ˈbaʊt/ in fast speech
entries.русский: консенсус по чему-л., общее согласие в группе
entries.complement: on / about: a noun phrase or gerund (consensus on raising the levy) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a consensus to raise the levy). among / within: the group that holds it. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: the consensus that the levee will hold.
entries.pattern: a consensus on / about [topic] · consensus among [a group] · the consensus that [clause] · reach / build / break a consensus · by consensus · the scientific consensus
entries.contrast: Two usage fights ride on this word. Consensus of opinion is criticized as redundant, since a consensus is already an agreement of opinion, and general consensus draws the same complaint; both are old, both are common, and both are worth cutting in edited prose. ✗ concensus is a misspelling that survives spellcheck in nobody's favor. ✗ a consensus to postpone is the infinitive error — write a consensus on postponing or an agreement to postpone, since agreement with/on does take the infinitive and consensus does not.
entries.see also: agreement with/on, disagreement with/about, opinion on/of/about, view on/of, on

entries.meaning: Something that follows from an earlier action, usually an unwelcome one.
examples: Higher premiums are a direct consequence of two bad fire seasons.
As a consequence of the recount, certification slipped by a week.
Nobody modeled the consequences for small landlords.
The consequence of ignoring the warning light was a $2,000 repair.
He's old enough to face the consequences of his own decisions.
The typo was, fortunately, of no consequence.
entries.русский: следствие, последствие чего-л. — обычно нежелательное
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the consequence of ignoring the warning) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. In the separate sense "importance," it takes to: a matter of no consequence to us.
entries.pattern: a consequence of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · as a consequence of [noun phrase] · the consequences for [person / group] · of no consequence to [person] · face / suffer the consequences
entries.contrast: Of names the cause; for names who bears it. The consequences of the flood are what the flood produced; the consequences for homeowners are what homeowners now face. Both can appear together: the consequences of the flood for homeowners. ✗ a consequence to the flood is an error, though of no consequence to me is correct in the unrelated "importance" sense. Compare result of, which is neutral, where consequence usually implies something unwelcome, and note the fixed connector as a consequence of, treated in full at as a consequence of.
entries.see also: result of, effect on, cause of, impact on, of

entries.meaning: A courtesy shown to others, the weighing of a candidate, or — in contract law — the price paid for a promise.
examples: Out of consideration for the neighbors, they moved the band inside at ten.
He shows no consideration for anyone who has to drive behind him.
Her name is under consideration for the deputy's job.
Submitting after Friday means no consideration for this year's fellowship.
The court found no consideration for the modification and refused to enforce it.
A promise to do what you already owe is not consideration for anything.

senses.head: Thoughtfulness toward other people
body: Regard for someone else's comfort or feelings. The complement is a person or a group, and the phrase often appears as out of consideration for.
examples: Out of consideration for the neighbors, they moved the band inside at ten.
He shows no consideration for anyone who has to drive behind him.

senses.head: Being weighed as a candidate
body: The complement is a position, an award, or a slot, and the noun almost always follows for.
examples: Her name is under consideration for the deputy's job.
Submitting after Friday means no consideration for this year's fellowship.

senses.head: In contract law, the thing of value exchanged for a promise
body: Without it a promise is a gift and unenforceable. American drafters open with the formula in consideration of the mutual covenants herein, and the amount can be nominal — the classic recital is ten dollars and other good and valuable consideration.
examples: The court found no consideration for the modification and refused to enforce it.
A promise to do what you already owe is not consideration for anything.

entries.русский: внимание, уважение к кому-л.; юр. встречное предоставление по договору
entries.register: senses 1 and 2 neutral; sense 3 is legal — the word that decides whether a promise is enforceable, met on the first page of almost every American contract and in the first month of law school
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (consideration for agreeing not to compete) — never a to-infinitive (✗ consideration for be promoted, ✗ consideration to promote her) and never a clause. In the courtesy sense the complement is a person or their interests; in the contract sense it is the promise being paid for.
entries.pattern: consideration for [a person / a position / a promise] · out of consideration for [someone] · under consideration (no complement) · take [something] into consideration · in consideration of [a promise] (the contract formula) · good and valuable consideration
entries.contrast: Three unrelated nouns, one spelling. Consideration for the neighbors is courtesy; consideration for the job is being weighed as a candidate; consideration for the promise is the dollar or the peppercorn that makes a contract binding. Only the first two are interchangeable in tone; the third is a term of art, and in a contract in consideration of is a fixed formula — see in consideration of. ✗ consideration to the neighbors is an error, and considerate of is the adjective (considerate of her neighbors, not ✗ considerate for). Note under consideration, which takes no complement at all.
entries.see also: concern about/for, respect for, eligibility for, in consideration of, for

entries.meaning: A striking difference, or the act of setting differences side by side.
examples: In contrast to last year's turnout, this election was quiet.
There's a sharp contrast between the two neighborhoods on either side of the highway.
Her calm stood in stark contrast to the panic in the hallway.
The southern route, by contrast, adds four hours and no scenery.
The essay draws a contrast between what the law says and what the clerks do.
In contrast with the federal rule, the state standard has no exemption.
entries.русский: контраст с чем-л., противопоставление — рус. «с», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (in contrast to spending a fortune on consultants) — never a to-infinitive (✗ in contrast to spend) and never a clause (✗ in contrast to that he left; write in contrast to his departure). A contrast between takes two items joined by and.
entries.pattern: in contrast to / with [noun phrase] · a contrast between X and Y · by contrast (no object) · a contrast to [noun phrase] · stand in stark contrast to [noun phrase]
entries.variants: in contrast to and in contrast with — both standard American English; to is commoner and slightly lighter
entries.contrast: Watch the -ing rule in in contrast to. The to is a preposition, so in contrast to hiring outside counsel, never ✗ in contrast to hire outside counsel — the same trap as alternative to and objection to. ✗ in contrast of is an error. By contrast takes no object at all and is a sentence adverb: By contrast, the second quarter was flat — ✗ by contrast to the second quarter is a blend of two constructions. Against comparison with/to, which looks for likeness, contrast insists on difference. The verb stresses differently from the noun: CON-trast the noun, con-TRAST the verb.
entries.see also: comparison with/to, difference between/in, similarity to/between, opposition to, with

entries.meaning: Something given to help a cause, or a part played in a result.
examples: Her contribution to the field was mostly methodological.
The company makes a monthly contribution to each employee's retirement account.
Poor drainage made a real contribution to the flooding.
We're asking for a small contribution toward the cost of the bus.
His biggest contribution to getting the bill passed was staying quiet.
Contributions from alumni were down eleven percent.
entries.русский: вклад в — рус. «в», не «к» (вклад в науку)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a contribution to reducing emissions) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a contribution to reduce emissions). This is one of the highest-frequency -ing traps in the file, because the sentence reads perfectly well as an infinitive and is wrong.
entries.pattern: a contribution to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a contribution toward [goal / cost] · a contribution of [amount / item] · make a contribution to [noun phrase] · contributions from [donors]
entries.variants: contribution toward — a partial payment against a total (a contribution toward the deductible) · contribution to — everything else
entries.contrast: The to is a preposition, so the verb after it takes -ing: a contribution to solving the shortage, never ✗ a contribution to solve the shortage. Test it with a noun — a contribution to the solution — and the trap is obvious. ✗ a contribution for the fund is wrong in the donation sense (use to), though a contribution for the holiday party names a purpose and is fine. The verb keeps the same preposition and takes no direct object: she contributed to the fund, ✗ she contributed the fund, though contribute money to the fund is correct.
entries.see also: supply of, commitment to, share in/of, responsibility for, attention to, contribute to, to

entries.meaning: Power to direct something, or possession of it.
examples: The trustees have no control over how the money is spent day to day.
She lost control of the car on black ice near the county line.
The family retained control of the newspaper until 1997.
The fire was out of control within twenty minutes.
New controls on short-term rentals take effect in January.
He's not in control of his own calendar anymore.
entries.pronunciation note: weak over has no weak form; of → /əv/ → /ə/
entries.русский: контроль над, власть над чем-л.; также владение чем-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun. A gerund is possible but rare (control over what gets published is the natural form, using a wh-clause). Never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. Controls on takes a noun naming what is being restricted: controls on spending.
entries.pattern: control over / of [noun phrase] · in control of [noun phrase] · under the control of [person] · out of control · lose / take / regain control of [noun phrase] · controls on [activity]
entries.variants: control over — power to direct, especially over people and processes · control of — possession of the thing itself, and the usual form in take control of, lose control of
entries.contrast: The plural is a different word. Control over the budget is authority; controls on the budget are the rules restricting it, and ✗ control on the budget is an error in the authority sense. Of and over overlap heavily — control of the company and control over the company are both fine — but only of works in the fixed phrases in control of, out of control, lose control of the car. ✗ control to and ✗ control for are wrong, though control for is a real technical verb in statistics (controlled for income).
entries.see also: authority on/over, influence on/over, limit to/on, responsibility for, over

entries.meaning: An exchange of talk between people, and what it is about.
examples: I had a long conversation with the county clerk about the easement.
Her conversation with the loan officer lasted four minutes.
He overheard a conversation between two of the contractors in the stairwell.
That's a conversation for after the audit, not before it.
We should have a conversation about who covers weekends.
She is in conversation with two publishers and will not say which.
entries.русский: разговор, беседа с кем-л. — тема вводится через about
entries.complement: with: a person or group — never a gerund (✗ a conversation with explaining it) and never a clause. about / on: the topic, as a noun phrase or gerund (a conversation about selling the house). Never a to-infinitive after either (✗ a conversation to sell the house, unless to sell is a purpose clause).
entries.pattern: a conversation with [person] · a conversation about / on [topic] · have / start / end / overhear a conversation · in conversation with [person] · make conversation (small talk) · a conversation between [two people]
entries.contrast: With names the other party and never to: ✗ a conversation to my landlord is an error, even though the verb talk allows both talk to and talk with — see talk to, talk with, talk about. A conversation between us views the two speakers from outside; a conversation with you views it from my side. American usage note: since about 2010 a conversation about has become office-speak for a difficult topic (we need to have a conversation about attendance), which is a euphemism, not a new grammar.
entries.see also: appointment with, interview with, discussion about/of, argument with/about, talk to, talk with, talk about, with

entries.meaning: A measured tendency for two variables to move together.
examples: There's a strong correlation between household income and third-grade reading scores.
Sales show almost no correlation with the weather in this market.
The correlation between the two indexes broke down in 2020.
Any correlation with the treatment disappears once you control for age.
She warned the board that a correlation between the two lines proves nothing.
The reported correlation between screen time and sleep is weaker than the headline.
entries.русский: корреляция с / между — согласованное изменение двух величин
entries.register: neutral to formal; a technical term in statistics and a loose one in journalism
entries.complement: between: two variables joined by and. with: a single second variable. Both take noun phrases; a gerund is possible but stiff (a correlation with starting school later). Never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: a correlation between X and Y · a correlation with [variable] · a strong / weak / positive / negative / spurious correlation · correlate with [variable] (the verb) · the correlation coefficient
entries.contrast: ✗ Correlation to is the error that gets past most editors; the noun takes between or with, and so does the verb — X correlates with Y, never ✗ correlates to Y. Between needs two named terms: ✗ a correlation between income is incomplete. And the sentence every statistics course exists to teach: correlation is not causation — a correlation between ice cream sales and drownings is real and explains nothing, which is why cause of claims more than association with/between, and association claims more than a mere correlation coefficient.
entries.see also: association with/between, link between/to, relationship with/between, ratio of ... to, cause of, between

entries.meaning: A standard or test by which something is judged or selected.
examples: Cost is only one criterion for awarding the contract.
The criteria for admission changed the year after she applied.
Two applicants met every criterion for the fellowship and one got it.
What criteria are you using to rank these?
Residency is not a criterion for jury service in this county.
The single criterion for replacement is whether the part has cracked.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /kraɪˈtɪriən fɚ/; the plural is /kraɪˈtɪriə/ · kry-TEER-ee-uh
entries.русский: критерий чего-л. — мерило отбора или оценки (мн. ч. criteria)
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (a criterion for awarding the contract) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the criteria to award the contract) and never a that-clause. The frame the criterion by which + clause is the formal alternative.
entries.pattern: a criterion for [selection / eligibility / admission] · the criteria for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · meet / satisfy / fail the criteria · the criterion by which [clause] · on what criteria [clause]
entries.contrast: The countability rule is the trap. Criterion is singular and criteria is plural: ✗ a criteria, ✗ this criteria is, ✗ criterias. Write one criterion, three criteria, these criteria are. The error is now so common in job listings and grant guidelines that it is drifting toward acceptance, but it is still marked in edited prose. Against grounds for: a criterion is a test you apply in advance, grounds are reasons you already have. ✗ criterion of eligibility is not wrong but is stiffer than for.
entries.see also: grounds for, basis for, eligibility for, threshold for, rule against/for, for

entries.meaning: A remedy that ends a disease or a persistent problem.
examples: There's still no cure for the common cold.
Everyone in the family has a different cure for hiccups.
The trial is testing a possible cure for sickle cell disease.
Sunlight is not a cure for a badly designed office.
The drug cured him of the infection but wrecked his hearing.
By then the rot was beyond cure.
entries.русский: лекарство от, средство от — рус. «от», не «для»
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a disease or a problem (a cure for hiccups). A gerund is unusual but possible (a cure for waking up at three a.m.). Never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a cure for [disease / problem] · find / seek a cure for [noun phrase] · beyond cure · the cure is worse than the disease
entries.contrast: For names the ailment; of belongs to the verb and names the patient's affliction. A cure for insomnia is the remedy; cure someone of insomnia is what a doctor does — ✗ cure someone for insomnia and ✗ a cure of insomnia are both wrong. ✗ cure to and ✗ cure against are errors; the near-synonyms diverge, with remedy for, treatment for, vaccine against or for, and antidote to or for. Note the unrelated culinary and industrial verb (cured ham, cured concrete), which takes no preposition at all.
entries.see also: solution to, protection from/against, damage to, danger of/to, for

entries.meaning: The right or duty of keeping and caring for someone or something.
examples: She has legal custody of both children and he has alternate weekends.
The suspect has been in the custody of the marshals since Tuesday.
Custody of the original tapes passed to the university in 1998.
The defense attacked the chain of custody of the blood sample.
Two deputies took him into custody outside the courthouse.
The clerk has custody of every filing in the case.
entries.русский: опека над кем-л., попечение; хранение чего-л.; юр. также содержание под стражей
entries.register: neutral to formal — family court, criminal procedure, records management; an ordinary American word because of divorce and arrest
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming a person, a thing, or a record — never a gerund (✗ custody of keeping the files), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: custody of [a child / the records / the evidence] · in the custody of [an authority] · take [someone] into custody · have / share / lose custody · joint / sole / physical / legal custody · the chain of custody
entries.is the only preposition the noun takes: ✗ custody over the children and ✗ custody on the evidence are errors, even though jurisdiction and control do take over — see jurisdiction over and control over/of. Two senses live side by side and neither uses a different preposition: custody of a child is a parental right, and in custody alone means under arrest. In American family law legal custody is decision-making and physical custody is where the child sleeps; in criminal cases the chain of custody is the paper trail on a piece of evidence, and breaking it can lose the case.
entries.contrast: Of
entries.see also: possession of, control over/of, jurisdiction over, responsibility for, title to, of

entries.meaning: Physical or reputational harm done to something.
examples: There's serious water damage to the subfloor under the sink.
Damage to the levee will take two seasons to repair.
The leak did more damage to the building's reputation than to the building.
Most of the damage from the storm was in the eastern half of the county.
By the time anyone noticed, the damage was done.
The jury awarded damages of $1.2 million.
entries.русский: ущерб, вред, повреждение чему-л. — рус. дательный падеж
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming the thing harmed (damage to the roof, damage to her reputation). Never a gerund, never a to-infinitive, never a clause. Damage from names the cause: damage from the storm.
entries.pattern: damage to [thing harmed] · damage from / by [cause] · do / cause damage to [noun phrase] · the damage was done · damages (plural) for [loss]
entries.contrast: To for the victim, from for the cause — damage to the siding from hail. ✗ damage of the roof is an error, and so is ✗ damage on the roof. The plural is a legal term, not a plural: damages means money awarded by a court, so he sued for damages is compensation and he inspected the damage is the harm itself — ✗ the damages to my car were extensive is a common and conspicuous slip. The verb takes a direct object and no preposition: the hail damaged the siding, ✗ damaged to the siding.
entries.see also: threat to, responsibility for, effect on, protection from/against, to

entries.meaning: Money awarded by a court to compensate for a loss or wrong.
examples: She sued for damages for lost wages and emotional distress.
The jury awarded damages of $1.2 million against the hospital.
Damages for breach of contract are limited to what the parties could foresee.
Punitive damages are rare in this state and capped when they happen.
The clause fixes liquidated damages for each day the work runs late.
He recovered nothing in damages for the delay because he could not prove it.
entries.русский: юр. убытки, возмещение за — присуждённая судом компенсация, всегда мн. ч.
entries.register: legal — complaints, jury instructions, settlement letters; an American meets it in a demand letter or on a small-claims form
entries.complement: for: the wrong or loss being compensated, as a noun phrase or gerund (damages for failing to warn). of: an amount (damages of $2.4 million). against: the party ordered to pay. Never a to-infinitive (✗ damages to compensate her as a complement of the noun) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: damages for [breach / injury / lost wages] · damages of [an amount] · damages against [a defendant] · sue / recover / award damages · compensatory / punitive / liquidated / nominal damages · treble damages
entries.contrast: Damage is harm and takes to; damages is money and takes for. Damage to the roof is the hole; damages for the damage to the roof is the check. ✗ damages to the roof is one of the commonest errors in insurance correspondence, and it converts a physical fact into a legal claim. The plural has no singular in this sense: ✗ a damage of $500. Note the stacking, exactly as with tax on: damages of $40,000 for lost profits against the general contractor.
entries.see also: damage to, claim against/for/to, liability for/to, remedy for/against, judgment against/for, penalty for

entries.meaning: Exposure to harm, or the harmful outcome itself.
examples: There's a real danger of the ceiling coming down.
Loose gravel on that curve is a danger to cyclists.
Two of the buildings are in danger of collapsing.
She was out of danger by Tuesday morning.
The danger of signing before an inspection is that you own the problem.
Untreated, the infection poses a danger to the whole ward.
entries.русский: of — опасность чего-л. (самого исхода); to — угроза для кого-л.
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund naming the bad outcome (the danger of infection, in danger of losing the house) — never a to-infinitive (✗ in danger to lose the house). to: a person or thing at risk. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: the danger that the fund runs dry.
entries.pattern: the danger of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a danger to [person / thing at risk] · in danger of [verb-ing] · out of danger · the danger that [clause]
entries.contrast: Of is what might happen; to is who it happens to. The danger of fire is the outcome feared; a danger to firefighters is who is exposed. Swapping them gives ✗ the danger to fire. In danger of is a fixed frame that requires -ing: in danger of collapsing, ✗ in danger to collapse — the single commonest error with this word. ✗ danger for is wrong in American English, though it is a natural transfer from French and Spanish. Compare risk of, which behaves identically and is commoner in technical prose.
entries.see also: risk of, threat to, chance of, protection from/against, of

entries.meaning: A failure to meet an obligation when it comes due.
examples: Two missed payments put him in default on the second mortgage.
Any transfer of the shares is an event of default under section 8.
The country's default on its dollar bonds was the first since 2001.
The tenant cured the default within the ten-day window.
She won the seat by default when no one else filed.
A default under the lease also triggers a default on the equipment loan.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /dɪˈfɔlt ən/; under has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. неисполнение обязательства, дефолт по кредиту — просрочка в срок платежа
entries.register: on is financial and neutral — mortgages, student loans, sovereign debt; under is legal drafting, met in the "Events of Default" section of a loan agreement or a commercial lease
entries.complement: on: the obligation not met — a loan, a payment, a bond. under: the instrument the default arises beneath — an agreement, a lease, a section number. Never a gerund (✗ default on paying the note; write default on the note), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a default on [a loan / a payment] · a default under [an agreement / section 8] · in default of [something owed] (formal) · by default · cure a default · an event of default · a default judgment
entries.variants: in default of survives in formal and legal prose meaning "for want of" (in default of any other bidder); it is a different frame from default on and is not interchangeable with it
entries.contrast: On points at the debt, under at the paper. You default on the note and are in default under the credit agreement — the same event described from the borrower's side and the drafter's side. ✗ default of the loan is an error in American usage. Keep the litigation sense separate: a default judgment is entered because a party failed to appear, and win by default means the other side did not show up. In computing the noun means a preset value and takes to on the verb (it defaults to Eastern time), a fourth sense with a fourth preposition.
entries.see also: breach of, liability for/to, obligation to/under, lien on/against, judgment against/for, hereunder

entries.meaning: Respectful submission to another's judgment, authority, or wishes.
examples: Out of deference to his widow, the department held the announcement a week.
The panel showed unusual deference to the trial judge's findings.
Courts owe some deference to an agency's reading of its own rule.
Her deference to the older partners was strategic and did not last.
In deference to the family, no photographs were taken inside the church.
The report criticizes the board's deference to management on every close question.
entries.русский: книжн. почтительное подчинение чьему-л. мнению или власти
entries.register: formal; a term of art in American administrative law, where courts owe agencies varying degrees of it, and an ordinary courtesy word in out of deference to
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the person, body, or judgment yielded to — never a gerund (✗ deference to reading it his way), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: deference to [a person / a court / an agency / someone's judgment] · in / out of deference to [noun phrase] · show / owe / accord deference to [noun phrase] · undue / excessive deference · with all due deference (a hedge before disagreeing)
entries.contrast: Three near neighbors, three different words. Deference is yielding to someone's judgment; deferment and deferral are postponements (a student-loan deferment); difference is another word entirely, and the near-rhyme catches typists. ✗ deference of and ✗ deference toward are errors. The verb splits by sense and preposition: defer to the chair is yielding, defer the payment is postponing — one takes a preposition and one takes a bare object. In American law, deference to an agency is measured (Chevron deference, Skidmore deference) and with all due deference is the formula that introduces a refusal to defer.
entries.see also: adherence to, respect for, attitude to/toward, authority on/over, to

entries.meaning: An academic qualification, named by the subject it was earned in — and, separately, an extent or a unit of measure.
examples: She has a degree in environmental engineering from a state school.
He finished a master's degree in library science at night.
A degree in philosophy is not a bad way into law school.
There's always some degree of guessing in a first estimate.
The thermostat was set to seventy-two degrees and nobody believed it.
I agree with him to a degree, and the degree is small.
entries.русский: диплом, учёная степень по специальности; отдельно — степень, градус
entries.complement: in: the field of study, as a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ a degree in nursing patients, though a degree in nursing is a field and fine) and never a clause. from: the institution. of: an amount or extent, in the wholly different sense (a degree of certainty), where a gerund is possible (some degree of guessing).
entries.pattern: a degree in [field] · a degree from [institution] · a bachelor's / master's / law degree in [field] · a degree of [certainty / difficulty] · to a degree · by degrees · ninety degrees
entries.contrast: In for the subject, from for the school, and never the reverse: ✗ a degree of economics and ✗ a degree in Michigan are both errors, though a degree from Michigan in economics stacks correctly. The measurement sense takes no preposition at all (it's ninety degrees), and to a degree means "somewhat" with no complement. American usage note: the possessive is a bachelor's degree and a master's degree, with the apostrophe, but an associate degree usually without one, and a doctorate replaces a doctor's degree entirely.
entries.see also: experience of/in/with, expert on/in, knowledge of/about, success in/at, in, from

entries.meaning: A holdup, and the length of one.
examples: A delay in processing the claims pushed everything into the next quarter.
There was a delay of almost four hours at the border.
Any delay in seeking treatment makes the outcome worse.
The bridge work is causing delays to the northbound lanes.
Report the loss without delay.
The delay in notifying the families became the center of the inquiry.
entries.русский: задержка с чем-л., промедление — рус. чаще «с», а не «в»
entries.complement: in: a gerund or a noun of process (a delay in processing, a delay in the delivery) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a delay to process the claims). of: a length of time (a delay of two hours). to: what is being held up, chiefly in transport and construction writing (delays to the northbound lanes).
entries.pattern: a delay in [verb-ing / noun of process] · a delay of [time span] · delays to [service / project] · without delay · there was a delay before [clause]
entries.variants: delays to — normal in British transport English and in American engineering prose, less usual in general American writing, where delays in or delays on is commoner
entries.contrast: In for the activity held up, of for how long. A delay in shipping is the holdup itself; a delay of three days is its size; ✗ a delay of shipping mixes them. The gerund is obligatory after in — ✗ a delay in to notify the family, ✗ a delay in notify the family. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition (the storm delayed the flight, ✗ delayed to the flight) and a gerund when it is the subject's own action (he delayed telling her, ✗ he delayed to tell her).
entries.see also: difficulty with/in, problem with, limit to/on, progress in/on, in

entries.meaning: The wish or need for something, or an insistent request.
examples: Demand for one-bedroom apartments has outrun supply for six years.
There's growing demand for bilingual paralegals.
The union's demand for a cost-of-living clause held up the whole contract.
She made a formal demand to inspect the books.
Welders are very much in demand right now.
The demands of the job finally got to him.
entries.русский: спрос на что-л.; настойчивое требование чего-л. — рус. «на», не «для»
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what is wanted (demand for housing). A gerund is unusual after the economic sense; the "insistent request" sense takes a to-infinitive with no preposition (a demand to see the warrant) and a that-clause with the subjunctive (a demand that he resign, not ✗ that he resigns).
entries.pattern: demand for [goods / services] · a demand to [verb] · a demand that [clause with subjunctive] · in demand · meet / satisfy the demand for [noun phrase] · the demands of [job / role]
entries.contrast: Two nouns, two grammars. The economic noun is uncountable and takes for: demand for rentals is up. The "insistent request" noun is countable and takes an infinitive or a subjunctive clause: a demand to see the manager, a demand that the fee be waived. A third pattern, the demands of the job, means the requirements it imposes — ✗ the demands for the job means something else entirely. ✗ demand of housing is an error. Note that the American subjunctive after demand that keeps the bare verb: that he resign, not that he resigns.
entries.see also: need for, supply of, request for, order for, for

entries.meaning: A leaving, or a break with an established practice.
examples: The ruling is a sharp departure from thirty years of precedent.
Departure from the north terminal is now through Gate 44.
Her cover of the song is a real departure from the original.
Any departure from the written protocol has to be logged.
Departure for the base camp is at four in the morning.
The chairman's abrupt departure from the board surprised everybody.
entries.русский: отъезд, отправление из; также отход от заведённой практики
entries.complement: from: a place left, or a norm broken (a departure from tradition, a departure from the airport). A gerund is possible in the abstract sense (a departure from doing it by hand). for: the destination (departure for Lisbon). Never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a departure from [place / norm] · departure for [destination] · departure time · a radical / sharp departure from [precedent] · on / upon departure
entries.contrast: From is where you left; for is where you are headed — departure from Newark for Lisbon. ✗ departure to Lisbon is a widespread error, and arrival runs the other way (arrival in Lisbon from Newark, ✗ arrival to Lisbon). The abstract sense is the commoner one in writing: a departure from precedent means a break with it, and ✗ a departure of precedent is wrong. The verb takes from likewise (depart from the script) and is transitive only in travel announcements (flights departing Gate 14).
entries.see also: escape from, change in/of, exception to, difference between/in, from

entries.meaning: The state of needing something or someone in order to function.
examples: The plan is meant to reduce our dependence on imported fertilizer.
Her whole argument rests on the town's reliance on a single employer.
Dependence on borrowing to cover payroll is what sank the company.
The bank acted in reliance on the appraisal it was given.
There's a documented dependence of crop yield on soil temperature.
Long-term reliance on the medication carries its own risks.
entries.русский: зависимость от чего-л., опора на что-л. — рус. «от», хотя англ. on
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (dependence on borrowing, reliance on being bailed out) — never a to-infinitive (✗ reliance on be bailed out) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: dependence / reliance on [noun phrase / verb-ing] · dependence of X on Y · reduce / end dependence on [noun phrase] · in reliance on [noun phrase] · dependent on [noun phrase]
entries.variants: dependence upon / reliance upon — identical in meaning, more formal and commoner in legal and academic writing · dependency on — the same noun in bureaucratic and clinical registers (chemical dependency)
entries.contrast: On is fixed and there is no alternative: ✗ dependence of foreign oil, ✗ dependence to foreign oil, ✗ reliance in the report. The one place of is right is the two-place technical frame the dependence of yield on temperature, where of names the variable and on still names what it depends on. The related adjective and verb keep on as well — dependent on the weather, it depends on the weather — and ✗ depend of, ✗ depend from are the classic transfer errors from French and Italian. Bare It depends. with no complement is fine; ✗ It depends of. is not.
entries.see also: confidence in, faith in, need for, control over/of, dependent on, on

entries.meaning: A wish or longing for something.
examples: There's a widespread desire for some kind of independent review.
His desire for privacy is not the same as having something to hide.
The changes came out of a desire to simplify the paperwork.
She has no desire to relive any of it.
The survey found a strong desire for more frequent bus service.
A desire for approval runs through every page of the memoir.
entries.русский: желание чего-л., стремление к чему-л.
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase naming what is wanted (a desire for privacy). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: a desire to be left alone. Never of in modern American English (✗ a desire of privacy), and no gerund after for in edited prose (a desire for privacy, not a desire for being private).
entries.pattern: a desire for [noun phrase] · a desire to [verb] · a desire that [clause with subjunctive] · express / feel a desire for [noun phrase] · out of a desire to [verb]
entries.contrast: For takes a thing; to takes an act. A desire for change names the object wanted; a desire to change names the action wanted — and mixing them yields ✗ a desire for change the schedule. The word is markedly more formal than wish for or want, which is why out of a desire to help reads well in a report and stiffly in conversation. The verb is likewise formal and takes an object or an infinitive with no preposition: she desired an explanation, she desired to know, ✗ she desired for an explanation.
entries.see also: wish for, need for, hope for/of, preference for, for

entries.meaning: A departure from a standard, plan, or expected course.
examples: Any deviation from the written protocol has to be logged and initialed.
The audit found three deviations from the approved change process.
A small deviation from course put them twelve miles off by morning.
There's a noticeable deviation in the readings after the sensor was moved.
The standard deviation of the sample is larger than the effect they claim.
His answer was a polite deviation from the truth.
entries.русский: отклонение от — отступление от нормы, плана или ожидаемого хода
entries.register: neutral to formal — engineering, statistics, auditing, and aviation
entries.complement: from: the norm, plan, standard, or course departed from, as a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ a deviation from following the plan), never an infinitive, and never a clause. in: where the deviation shows up (a deviation in the readings). The statistical compound takes of: the standard deviation of the sample.
entries.pattern: a deviation from [the norm / the plan / the standard / course] · a deviation in [a measurement] · the standard deviation of [a data set] · any deviation from [protocol] · two standard deviations above the mean
entries.contrast: ✗ Deviation of the norm is the error — the noun takes from, exactly as the verb does (deviate from the script, never ✗ deviate of). Careful with the one compound that flips it: the standard deviation of the sample takes of, because there deviation is a measured quantity and not a departure. Against departure from, which is the everyday synonym: a deviation implies a rule that was supposed to be followed, a departure need only imply a previous practice.
entries.see also: departure from, discrepancy between, disparity between/in, difference between/in, conformity with/to, from

entries.meaning: The way in which two things are not the same.
examples: The difference between the two engines is mostly noise, not power.
There's a real difference in tone between her first book and this one.
Can you tell the difference between margarine and butter in a cookie?
One good sous chef makes all the difference to a small kitchen.
We had a difference of opinion about how to handle it.
The difference between buying and leasing comes down to how long you keep the car.
entries.русский: различие между чем-л. / разница в чём-л.
entries.complement: between: two or more items joined by and, or a plural (the difference between the two engines, differences between states). in: the respect in which they differ (a difference in tone). Gerunds follow both (the difference between buying and leasing). Never a to-infinitive; a wh-clause follows only the between frame indirectly (the difference between what he said and what he did).
entries.pattern: the difference between X and Y · a difference in [respect] · make a difference to / in [noun phrase] · tell the difference between X and Y · a difference of [amount / opinion]
entries.variants: make a difference to and make a difference in — both American; to is commoner with people (it made a difference to her), in with situations (it made a difference in the outcome)
entries.contrast: Between needs two things. The difference between the two engines and the older model is fine because both sides are named, but ✗ the difference between the engine is incomplete, and ✗ the difference of the two engines is wrong. Do not carry the adjective's preposition over to the noun: the adjective is different from (American standard), and ✗ the difference from the two is an error — though a difference from last year is correct when you are naming a single baseline. On different than: American English accepts it before a clause (different than I expected) and prefers different from before a noun; different to is British. A difference of opinion and a difference of four points are fixed quantity frames.
entries.see also: similarity to/between, comparison with/to, contrast to/with, change in/of, different from, between

entries.meaning: Trouble doing something, or the thing that causes it.
examples: He's having difficulty with the new billing software.
She had no difficulty finding parking at that hour.
The difficulty in proving intent is what makes these cases rare.
Patients report difficulty swallowing in the first week.
The team ran into difficulties with the foundation almost immediately.
He got up the stairs, but with obvious difficulty.
entries.русский: трудность с чем-л., затруднение в чём-л.
entries.complement: with: a noun phrase naming the troublesome thing (difficulty with the software). in + gerund, or a bare gerund with the preposition dropped (difficulty in finding a job, difficulty finding a job) — never a to-infinitive (✗ difficulty to find a job). ✗ difficulty with to find is likewise impossible.
entries.pattern: difficulty with [noun phrase] · difficulty (in) [verb-ing] · have difficulty [verb-ing] · with difficulty · the difficulty of [verb-ing / noun phrase] · run into difficulties
entries.variants: difficulty in doing and difficulty doing — both standard American English; dropping in is commoner in speech and increasingly in writing
entries.contrast: The infinitive is the error, and it is everywhere: ✗ she has difficulty to concentrate, ✗ no difficulty to understand him. Write difficulty concentrating, no difficulty understanding him. With takes a thing, in takes an activity, and of takes the activity when difficulty is the head of a definite description (the difficulty of proving intent). ✗ difficulty for is wrong. The same -ing rule governs the near-synonyms trouble and a hard time: trouble sleeping, a hard time sleeping, never ✗ trouble to sleep.
entries.see also: trouble with, problem with, delay in, success in/at, with

entries.meaning: A drawback, or a position of relative weakness.
examples: The main disadvantage of the older model is that parts are hard to find.
There's one real disadvantage of living this close to the tracks.
Smaller districts are at a serious disadvantage when they bid for grants.
The rule change works to the disadvantage of first-time applicants.
The disadvantage of paying cash is that you have no record of it.
Arriving late put her at a disadvantage for the rest of the interview.
entries.русский: недостаток, минус чего-л.; также невыгодное положение
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the disadvantage of living downtown) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the disadvantage to live downtown). In at a disadvantage, the complement is dropped entirely or introduced by to/compared with.
entries.pattern: the disadvantage of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · at a disadvantage · put [someone] at a disadvantage · to [someone's] disadvantage · the disadvantages for [group]
entries.variants: the disadvantages to doing it that way — an accepted informal American variant, parallel to the advantages to
entries.contrast: Mirror image of advantage of/over, but with one frame missing: there is no ✗ disadvantage over. Where an advantage over a rival is idiomatic, the negative version is at a disadvantage compared with a rival or simply at a disadvantage. A disadvantage for the students is not wrong but names who suffers rather than what the drawback is; keep of for the drawback itself. The adjective disadvantaged is a social term (disadvantaged neighborhoods) and takes no preposition.
entries.see also: advantage of/over, benefit of/to, problem with, limit to/on, of

entries.meaning: A difference of opinion, and the people or issues involved.
examples: I had a sharp disagreement with my accountant about the deduction.
The disagreement over the property line has been to court twice.
There's honest disagreement about what the data show.
A disagreement between the two departments delayed the report by a month.
She's in open disagreement with the rest of the committee.
The disagreement about who signs off on refunds is still unresolved.
entries.русский: разногласие с кем-л. / по поводу чего-л.
entries.complement: with: a person or party. about / over / on: the issue — noun phrase, gerund (disagreement about hiring outside counsel), or wh-clause (disagreement about who should sign). The noun also takes a bare that-clause. Never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: a disagreement with [person] · a disagreement about / over / on [issue] · a disagreement between X and Y · in disagreement with [person] · a sharp disagreement as to whether [clause]
entries.variants: disagreement over — implies more heat · disagreement on — an issue formally at stake · disagreement about — the neutral default
entries.contrast: Same three-way frame as agreement with/on: with the person, about/over/on the issue, between both sides named from outside. ✗ a disagreement to the proposal is an error — for opposition to a specific proposal use objection to. The verb takes the same set (disagree with her about the timeline) and, unlike its British cousin, ✗ disagree something is never American English. Note the mild-to-strong scale: disagreement is milder than argument with/about, which in turn is milder than dispute.
entries.see also: agreement with/on, argument with/about, objection to, opposition to, with

entries.meaning: A mismatch between two accounts, figures, or records that ought to agree.
examples: There's a $4,000 discrepancy between the invoice and the purchase order.
Nobody could explain the discrepancy between the two witnesses' timelines.
Auditors flagged three discrepancies in the payroll ledger.
The discrepancy between what he told the bank and what he told the IRS is the case.
A small discrepancy between the counts turned into a two-week recount.
She reconciled every discrepancy before the quarter closed.
entries.русский: расхождение между — несовпадение данных, которые должны были сойтись
entries.register: neutral to formal — accounting, auditing, and reporting
entries.complement: between: two things joined by and, or a plural (a discrepancy between the two counts, discrepancies between the invoices). in: where the mismatch shows up (a discrepancy in the ledger). Never a gerund, never an infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: a discrepancy between X and Y · a discrepancy in [a record / an account] · account for / explain / reconcile a discrepancy · a minor / material / unexplained discrepancy
entries.needs one location: ✗ a discrepancy between the ledger is incomplete, and ✗ a discrepancy of the two counts is an error. Against difference between/in: a difference is neutral, a discrepancy implies that the two figures were supposed to match and did not — which is why an auditor writes discrepancy and a shopper writes difference. Against disparity between/in: a disparity is a gap that raises a question of fairness, not of arithmetic.
entries.contrast: Between needs two terms and in
entries.see also: difference between/in, disparity between/in, deviation from, distinction between, between

entries.meaning: A conversation in which a subject is talked through.
examples: We had a long discussion about whether to close the Elm Street branch.
Chapter six is a careful discussion of the evidence for the early date.
There was a panel discussion on water rights at the county fair.
I had a useful discussion with the inspector about the setback rules.
Three proposals are still under discussion.
The discussion about how to pay for it lasted longer than the vote.
entries.русский: обсуждение чего-л. — рус. родительный (а глагол discuss идёт без предлога)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (a discussion about closing the branch), or wh-clause (a discussion about what to do next) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a discussion to close the branch) and never a that-clause (✗ a discussion that we should close it).
entries.pattern: a discussion about / of / on [topic] · a discussion with [person] · a discussion between X and Y · under discussion · have / open / close a discussion · in discussion with [party]
entries.variants: discussion about — conversational and the American default · discussion of — more formal, and the usual choice when the noun heads a definite description (a thorough discussion of the evidence) · discussion on — a scheduled or published treatment (a panel discussion on water rights)
entries.contrast: The flagship noun-versus-verb shift, and the source of the single most persistent error in advanced English: the verb discuss takes a direct object and no preposition — we discussed the budget — so ✗ we discussed about the budget is wrong, while the noun cannot attach anything without one — a discussion about the budget, ✗ a discussion the budget. Both halves have to be learned together, because dropping the preposition on the noun and adding it to the verb are two faces of the same confusion. ✗ a discussion for the budget is likewise an error; with names the other party, between names both from outside.
entries.see also: argument with/about, comment on, agreement with/on, discuss something, discuss, about

entries.meaning: A wide and usually troubling gap between groups or measures.
examples: The report documents a persistent disparity between rural and urban response times.
Disparities in maternal mortality have widened in three of the five counties.
There's a real disparity in pay between the two campuses for the same job.
Sentencing disparities among the district's judges drew the appeal.
The disparity between what was budgeted and what was spent is the whole story.
Nothing in the plan addresses the disparity in broadband access.
entries.русский: неравенство между, разрыв в — большой и обычно тревожный разрыв
entries.register: formal — policy writing, public health, civil-rights litigation, and journalism about them
entries.complement: between: two groups or figures joined by and. in: the dimension along which the gap runs (a disparity in pay, disparities in outcomes). among: three or more groups. Never a gerund, never an infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: a disparity between X and Y · a disparity in [pay / sentencing / access] · disparities among [groups] · a wide / growing / persistent / racial disparity · the disparity between [rich and poor]
entries.contrast: Between names the parties, in names the measure, and the two stack: a disparity in sentencing between federal and state courts. ✗ a disparity of pay is an error, and ✗ a disparity with is another. Against difference between/in: every disparity is a difference, but the word carries a charge — it says the gap is large and probably unjust, which is why pay disparity and pay difference are not the same claim. Against discrepancy between: a discrepancy is a bookkeeping mismatch, a disparity is a social gap.
entries.see also: difference between/in, discrepancy between, distinction between, ratio of ... to, in proportion to, between

entries.meaning: A difference someone deliberately marks between two things — and, separately, an honor.
examples: The opinion turns on a fine distinction between possession and control.
He draws no distinction between a friend and a client, which is a problem.
The distinction between weather and climate is the one every argument ignores.
That's a distinction without a difference and the judge said so.
She has the distinction of being the first woman elected from the district.
The old rules applied to everyone without distinction.
entries.русский: различие между — сознательно проводимое; отдельно — почётное отличие
entries.complement: between: two things joined by and. of: an honor, in the other sense (the distinction of being the oldest bank in the state), where a gerund is required — of + -ing, never ✗ the distinction to be the oldest. Never a that-clause after between.
entries.pattern: a distinction between X and Y · draw / make / blur a distinction between X and Y · without distinction · a distinction without a difference · the distinction of [verb-ing] · with distinction (an honor)
entries.contrast: A difference is a fact; a distinction is drawn. The difference between copper and aluminum wire exists whether or not anyone notices; the distinction between negligence and recklessness is one the law draws on purpose — which is why you can accuse someone of making a distinction without a difference and cannot make the same complaint about a difference. ✗ a distinction of X and Y is an error in this sense. The second noun, the honor, takes of plus a gerund and has nothing to do with the first: she graduated with distinction.
entries.see also: difference between/in, contrast to/with, discrepancy between, comparison with/to, as distinct from, between

entries.meaning: Uncertainty about whether something is true or will happen.
examples: I have serious doubts about the contractor's estimate.
There's some doubt about whether the roof will last another winter.
The new testimony casts doubt on the timeline.
There's no doubt that she knew before the meeting.
The outcome was in doubt until the last precinct reported.
Her doubts about signing anything without a lawyer were well founded.
entries.русский: сомнение в чём-л., сомнения насчёт — рус. «в», не «о»
entries.complement: about / as to: noun phrase, gerund (doubts about signing anything), or wh-clause (doubt about whether it will hold). The noun also takes a bare that-clause, almost always under a negative (no doubt that he meant it). Never a to-infinitive (✗ doubt to sign).
entries.pattern: doubt about / as to [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · no doubt that [clause] · in doubt · beyond a reasonable doubt · cast doubt on [noun phrase] · have one's doubts about [noun phrase]
entries.variants: doubt about — the everyday form · doubt as to — formal and legal · doubt over — journalistic (doubts over the funding) · doubt of — archaic outside the fixed no doubt of it
entries.contrast: Three frames that look alike and are not. Doubts about the plan is uncertainty; cast doubt on the plan is the fixed collocation for undermining it — ✗ cast doubt about is wrong; and no doubt that he meant it takes a clause with no preposition — ✗ no doubt about that he meant it. The verb behaves differently again: I doubt it, I doubt that he'll come, I doubt whether it will hold — all with no preposition, so ✗ I doubt about his story is an error where I have doubts about his story is correct.
entries.see also: confidence in, belief in, concern about/for, worry about, about

entries.meaning: An obligation attached to a role or a relationship — and, separately, a tax on imported goods.
examples: A landlord has a duty to warn tenants about a known hazard.
Directors owe a duty of loyalty to the corporation, not to the majority holder.
He was off duty and two blocks away when the call came in.
Jury duty pays fourteen dollars a day in this county.
The duty on imported olive oil went up in the spring.
She bought the perfume duty-free in Detroit on the way back.

senses.head: What a person or office is bound to do
body: The to frame names either the party owed or the act required; the of frame names the kind of duty. In American law the recurring pairs are duty of care, duty of loyalty, duty to warn, and duty to mitigate.
examples: A landlord has a duty to warn tenants about a known hazard.
Directors owe a duty of loyalty to the corporation, not to the majority holder.
He was off duty and two blocks away when the call came in.
Jury duty pays fourteen dollars a day in this county.

senses.head: A government charge on imported goods
body: This noun takes on, is countable, and sits beside tariff and levy. The compound duty-free is fixed.
examples: The duty on imported olive oil went up in the spring.
She bought the perfume duty-free in Detroit on the way back.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈduti tə/, /ˈduti əv/ → /ˈduti ə/ · American /ˈduti/ or /ˈdjuti/; the flapped /d/ makes duty and doody homophones for most speakers
entries.русский: обязанность перед кем-л., долг; отдельно — пошлина на ввозимый товар
entries.register: sense 1 neutral to formal, and a term of art in tort and corporate law; sense 2 is trade and customs usage
entries.complement: to: either a person or body owed the duty (a duty to his clients) or a bare infinitive naming the act required (a duty to disclose) — the two to's are different words, and both are standard. Never a gerund after to (✗ a duty to disclosing). of: the kind of duty, as a noun (a duty of care, a duty of loyalty), or the person who bears it (the duty of every officer). on: what a customs duty falls on.
entries.pattern: a duty to [person] · a duty to [verb] · a duty of [care / loyalty / candor] · the duty of [a person] to [verb] · on / off duty · do one's duty · a duty on [imported goods] · duty-free
entries.contrast: Put a plain noun in the to slot to see which word it is. A duty to the shareholders takes a noun; a duty to disclose takes a bare verb; ✗ a duty to disclosing is impossible either way. Against obligation to/under: the two behave alike, but obligations come from agreements and duties from roles — a director has a duty of loyalty and an obligation under the credit agreement. And keep the second noun clear of the first: the duty on imported steel is a tax and belongs with tariff on/duty on/levy on, not with anything you owe your employer.
entries.see also: obligation to/under, responsibility for, liability for/to, onus on, right to/of/over, tariff on/duty on/levy on

entries.meaning: A legal right to use a strip of someone else's land for a limited purpose.
examples: The deed reserves a ten-foot easement over the north edge of the lot.
There's a utility easement across the back of every parcel on this street.
They bought the cabin without noticing the logging easement over the access road.
The county holds a drainage easement across both fields.
An easement for ingress and egress runs with the land and binds the next owner.
Her neighbor sued to extinguish the easement over the driveway.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈizmənt əˈkrɔs/; over has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. сервитут — право ограниченного пользования чужим участком
entries.register: legal — deeds, title reports, surveys, and zoning disputes. An American meets the word exactly once, at a real-estate closing, when the title company lists the utility easement running along the back of the lot.
entries.complement: over / across / on: the burdened land, as a noun phrase. for: the purpose (an easement for ingress and egress, an easement for a sewer line), where a gerund is possible (an easement for maintaining the line). Never a to-infinitive (✗ an easement to cross the field, as a complement of the noun) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an easement over / across [land] · an easement for [a purpose] · grant / reserve / extinguish an easement · an easement appurtenant / in gross · a utility / drainage / access easement · the dominant and servient estates
entries.variants: easement over, easement across, and easement on are all used of the same right; over is the drafter's default, across is picked when the strip physically crosses the parcel, and on is commoner in surveys
entries.contrast: The land is the object, not the beneficiary: an easement over the Harmons' pasture burdens the Harmons and benefits somebody else, so ✗ an easement over the power company is nonsense. Note the near neighbors: a right of way is the commonest kind of easement, a license is revocable where an easement is not, and a covenant restricts what you may do rather than letting someone else in. ✗ an easement of the pasture is an error.
entries.see also: title to, right to/of/over, lien on/against, jurisdiction over, access to, over

entries.meaning: The change produced in something by something else.
examples: The tariff had almost no effect on retail prices.
Nobody studied the effect of the closure on the surrounding businesses.
Two cups of coffee have a noticeable effect on my sleep.
The rule takes effect on the first of the month.
Side effects of the medication include dizziness and dry mouth.
Her testimony had a visible effect on the jury.
entries.русский: воздействие на, влияние на — рус. «на», не «в»
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund naming what is affected (an effect on morale, an effect on recruiting new staff) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an effect to lower morale) and never a that-clause (✗ an effect that morale dropped). A wh-clause follows on freely (an effect on how the crew is scheduled). The full frame names both sides: the effect of X on Y.
entries.pattern: an effect on [thing affected] · the effect of X on Y · have / produce an effect on [noun phrase] · in effect · take effect · side effects of [drug]
entries.variants: an effect upon — formal, identical in meaning · an impact on — the journalistic near-synonym; see impact on
entries.the homophone problem is the real one he: effect is the noun (the effect on sales) and affect is the verb (it affected sales), so ✗ the affect on sales and ✗ it effected sales are the two directions of the same mistake — with the rare exception of the verb effect meaning "bring about" (effect a change) and the psychological noun affect meaning observable emotion (flat affect). And note that affect the verb takes no preposition: ✗ it affects on sales.
entries.contrast: Of names the cause, on names the target: the effect of the drug on blood pressure. Reversing them is nonsense. ✗ an effect to morale and ✗ an effect for morale are errors.
entries.see also: impact on, influence on/over, result of, consequence of, on

entries.meaning: Qualification to receive something or to take part.
examples: Her eligibility for the subsidy ended when the second job started.
The clerk verifies eligibility to vote against the county roll.
A felony conviction does not affect eligibility for federal student aid the way it used to.
He has one year of eligibility left and a bad knee.
Eligibility for enrolling mid-year depends on why the family moved.
The form asks nine questions and settles eligibility for none of them.
entries.русский: право на что-л., соответствие условиям для получения или участия
entries.register: neutral to formal — benefits administration, college admissions, insurance, athletics
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase or gerund (eligibility for enrolling mid-year). to: a bare infinitive (eligibility to vote, eligibility to receive benefits). Both are standard, and the two to's test cleanly: after for a noun fits, after to only a verb does. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: eligibility for [benefits / a program / a scholarship] · eligibility to [verb] · determine / verify / establish / lose eligibility · eligibility requirements (compound) · eligible for / eligible to (the adjective, same split)
entries.takes the act: eligibility for parole and eligibility to be paroled say the same thing with different grammar, and ✗ eligibility for be paroled and ✗ eligibility to parole are both errors. The adjective behaves identically — eligible for the draft, eligible to enlist — and ✗ eligible on is never right. In American college sports eligibility stands alone as a mass noun: he has one year of eligibility left.
entries.contrast: For takes the thing, to
entries.see also: entitlement to, criterion for, threshold for, exemption from, qualify for, for

entries.meaning: An official ban on trade in something, or on publishing something before a set time.
examples: The embargo on Cuban goods outlasted every president who inherited it.
Congress imposed an embargo on arms sales to the region in March.
The study is under embargo until nine Eastern on Thursday.
An embargo on exporting the ore would close two mines in a week.
Three outlets broke the embargo and published early.
The 1973 oil embargo is why the speed limit was fifty-five.
entries.русский: эмбарго на — запрет торговли либо запрет публиковать раньше срока
entries.register: neutral to formal — trade policy, diplomacy, and journalism, where it also names an agreed hold on publishing a story
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (an embargo on selling spare parts) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an embargo to sell spare parts) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an embargo on [goods / trade / news] · an embargo against [a country] · impose / lift / defy / break an embargo · under embargo · an arms / oil / news embargo
entries.variants: an embargo on names what is blocked and an embargo against names whom it is aimed at; on is far commoner in American writing, and both appear in the same paragraph without objection. The plural adds -es: embargoes.
entries.contrast: Against sanction against/sanctions on: an embargo is a total ban on trade in something, sanctions are a package of measures that may include one. Against moratorium on: a moratorium is a pause, an embargo is a prohibition with a political point. ✗ an embargo of oil is an error for the ban, though an embargo of 1973 dates it. Note the newsroom sense, which surprises people: a press release under embargo until Tuesday may be read now and printed then.
entries.see also: sanction against/sanctions on, moratorium on, prohibition on/against, tariff on/duty on/levy on, limit to/on, on

entries.meaning: Special importance or attention given to something.
examples: The program puts heavy emphasis on early literacy.
There's new emphasis on documenting every call.
Her training placed unusual stress on footwork.
The syllabus is history with an emphasis on primary sources.
The emphasis on test scores has crowded out everything else.
Note the stress on the second syllable: com-PA-ra-ble is a variant.
entries.русский: акцент на чём-л., упор на — особая важность, придаваемая чему-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (emphasis on getting the paperwork right) — never a to-infinitive (✗ emphasis on get it right, ✗ emphasis to improve safety) and never a clause (✗ emphasis that safety comes first; write emphasis on the fact that...).
entries.pattern: emphasis / stress on [noun phrase / verb-ing] · place / put / lay emphasis on [noun phrase] · with (an) emphasis on [noun phrase] · the emphasis of [work / program]
entries.variants: emphasis on — the standard noun frame · stress on — identical in meaning, plainer, and also the phonetic term (the stress on the second syllable)
entries.contrast: Both nouns take on; neither related verb takes anything. Emphasize and stress are bare transitive verbs — she emphasized the deadline, he stressed the risk — so ✗ she emphasized on the deadline and ✗ he stressed on the risk are errors, and they are among the most persistent in academic writing by non-native speakers. The noun cannot go without the preposition: ✗ emphasis the deadline. Note the unrelated stressed about (anxious) and stressed out, which have nothing to do with this pattern.
entries.see also: attention to, focus on, importance of/to, emphasize something, emphasize, on

entries.meaning: A meeting, usually brief, unplanned, or unwelcome.
examples: Her first encounter with the county assessor did not go well.
We had a brief encounter with a black bear on the switchbacks.
The report documents six encounters with armed patrols.
A chance encounter with an old professor turned into a job.
His only encounter with the criminal justice system was a parking ticket in 1988.
The film opens with an encounter with a stranger on a train.
entries.русский: встреча, столкновение с — обычно краткая, случайная или неприятная
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming a person, animal, or force met (an encounter with a bear). No gerund, no infinitive, no clause — ✗ an encounter with being arrested; write an encounter with the police.
entries.pattern: an encounter with [person / animal / force] · a chance / brief / violent encounter with [noun phrase] · have an encounter with [noun phrase] · a close encounter
entries.contrast: With is the only preposition — ✗ an encounter to, ✗ an encounter of, ✗ an encounter against. The verb, by contrast, takes a direct object and no preposition at all: we encountered heavy traffic, never ✗ we encountered with heavy traffic. This is a textbook noun-versus-verb shift and worth pairing in memory with meeting with and contact with, both of which behave the same way. Note that the verb also covers abstract obstacles (encountered resistance) where the noun usually does not.
entries.see also: interview with, relationship with/between, contact someone, argument with/about, with

entries.meaning: An enforceable right to receive something.
examples: Nothing in the handbook creates an entitlement to severance.
The statute gives every applicant an entitlement to a written decision.
Her entitlement to the survivor benefit vested after ten years.
He has an entitlement to be heard before the license is pulled.
Half the federal budget goes to entitlement programs and the argument never ends.
The kid's sense of entitlement did not come from nowhere.
entries.русский: право на что-л. — юридически обеспеченное притязание на получение
entries.register: formal — benefits law, employment contracts, pensions; in American politics entitlements is also the standing name for Social Security, Medicare, and Medicaid, and the bare noun is an insult
entries.complement: to + noun phrase (an entitlement to severance) or to + bare infinitive (an entitlement to receive severance) — both occur in legal writing, and the two to's are again different words. Never a gerund (✗ an entitlement to receiving severance is not the edited form) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an entitlement to [a benefit / a hearing / notice] · an entitlement to [verb] · establish / deny / forfeit an entitlement · a statutory entitlement · entitlement programs (American policy usage) · a sense of entitlement
entries.contrast: Against eligibility for, which is the distinction that decides cases: eligibility means you may apply and might qualify; an entitlement means the thing is already yours and can be enforced. A benefit you are eligible for can be denied on the merits; a benefit you have an entitlement to can only be taken away with process. ✗ entitlement of and ✗ entitlement for are errors. The adjective is entitled to with the same two complements (entitled to a refund, entitled to know), and entitled alone, as a description of a person, is purely pejorative in American English.
entries.see also: eligibility for, right to/of/over, claim against/for/to, beneficiary of/under, obligation to/under, to

entries.meaning: A getting away from confinement, danger, or routine.
examples: The escape from the county jail was captured on four cameras.
Gardening is her escape from a job she can't talk about.
There's no escape from the paperwork, only from doing it yourself.
They had a narrow escape on the icy stretch outside Laramie.
The book is an escape to a version of Maine that never quite existed.
An escape of natural gas forced the block to be evacuated.
entries.русский: побег из, бегство от — из заточения, от опасности или от рутины
entries.complement: from: a place, condition, or pursuer (an escape from the county jail, an escape from routine). A gerund is possible (no escape from having to decide). to: a destination or refuge. Never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an escape from [place / condition] · an escape to [refuge] · a narrow escape · make one's escape · there is no escape from [noun phrase] · a fire escape
entries.contrast: From for what you got out of; to for where you went. ✗ an escape of the jail is an error; an escape of gas is a different noun entirely, meaning a leak. The verb takes both a prepositional and a bare-object frame with a real difference in meaning: escape from prison is getting out of the building, while escape prison means avoiding a sentence, and escape someone's notice, escape injury, escape punishment are all bare and cannot take from. So ✗ the detail escaped from my notice is wrong: it escaped my notice.
entries.see also: departure from, protection from/against, limit to/on, danger of/to, escape from, from

entries.meaning: Facts or signs that support a conclusion.
examples: There's clear evidence of water intrusion behind the drywall.
The evidence for an earlier eruption is mostly in the ash layers.
No evidence that the driver had been drinking was ever produced.
The strongest evidence against him was his own text messages.
We found no evidence of forced entry.
That's one piece of evidence, not a case.
entries.русский: свидетельство чего-л., доказательства в пользу — в англ. неисчисляемо
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (evidence of tampering, evidence of having been moved). for: a claim, theory, or proposition supported. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: evidence that the seal was broken. Never a to-infinitive (✗ evidence to prove is a purpose clause, a different structure).
entries.pattern: evidence of [thing shown to exist] · evidence for [claim / theory] · evidence that [clause] · evidence against [person / theory] · in evidence · give / present / suppress evidence
entries.the countability rule is the trap: evidence is uncountable in American English, so ✗ an evidence, ✗ evidences, ✗ many evidences. Say a piece of evidence, two pieces of evidence, some evidence, much evidence. Compare proof of, which is also uncountable in this sense but countable in mathematics (two proofs of the theorem).
entries.contrast: Of is a trace; for is support for an argument. Evidence of tampering means signs that tampering happened; evidence for the early date means material that argues for a conclusion; evidence against him is material that incriminates.
entries.see also: proof of, example of, reason for, grounds for, of

entries.meaning: An instance that illustrates a general point.
examples: This is a textbook example of how not to run a hearing.
Can you give me an example of what you mean?
The clock tower is a good example of Richardsonian Romanesque.
She set an example for every apprentice who came after her.
Some cities — Portland, for example — never adopted the rule.
It was an example of overreaching that the court declined to endorse.
entries.русский: пример чего-л. — рус. родительный, не «для»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (an example of overreaching) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an example to overreach) and never a that-clause. In set an example, the complement is a person introduced by for or to.
entries.pattern: an example of [category / behavior] · for example · set an example for / to [person] · make an example of [person] · give / cite an example of [noun phrase] · by way of example
entries.contrast: Of for the category, for/to for the audience, and the two must not be swapped. An example of good design is an instance; an example for the younger staff is a model to imitate. ✗ an example about is an error, and ✗ for example of is a doubling. Note make an example of someone, which means to punish them publicly — the opposite of set an example for someone, though the words are nearly identical. The Latin abbreviation e.g. means for example and takes a comma after it in American style; i.e. means that is and is not interchangeable.
entries.see also: evidence of/for, proof of, reference to, exception to, of

entries.meaning: A case that a rule or generalization does not cover.
examples: Every rule in this handbook has at least one exception to it.
With the exception of two holdouts, the block voted the same way.
The zoning board made an exception for the corner lot.
She took exception to being told to smile more.
The policy applies to all employees without exception.
Weekends are the one exception to the parking ban.
entries.русский: исключение из — рус. «из», не «к» (исключение из правила)
entries.complement: noun phrase naming a rule, generalization, or pattern (an exception to the rule). A gerund is possible in the take exception to frame (took exception to being interrupted) — and note that this proves the to is a preposition, so never a bare infinitive (✗ took exception to be interrupted).
entries.pattern: an exception to [rule] · with the exception of [noun phrase] · make an exception for [person] · take exception to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · without exception · the exception that proves the rule
entries.contrast: Three prepositions doing three jobs. An exception to the rule is a case the rule does not cover; with the exception of Tuesday means "except Tuesday" and is a fixed phrase, so ✗ with the exception to Tuesday is wrong; and make an exception for Maria means bending the rule in her favor, so ✗ make an exception to Maria misfires. The idiom take exception to means to object, not to exempt — she took exception to his tone is a complaint. ✗ an exception of the rule is an error.
entries.see also: rule against/for, limit to/on, objection to, alternative to, to
