entries.meaning: A reason offered to justify a fault, or a pretext for doing something.
examples: There's no excuse for leaving the gate open in bear country.
He gave the same excuse for missing three meetings in a row.
The rain was just an excuse to stay in and read.
Stop making excuses for him.
What's your excuse for not registering by the deadline?
That radio is a poor excuse for a public address system.
entries.русский: оправдание за что-л.; также предлог для того, чтобы сделать что-л.
entries.complement: for: noun phrase or gerund naming what is being excused (an excuse for being late) — never a bare infinitive after for (✗ an excuse for be late). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition, meaning a pretext: an excuse to leave early. Both are correct and mean different things.
entries.pattern: an excuse for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an excuse to [verb] · make excuses for [person / verb-ing] · there's no excuse for [verb-ing] · a poor excuse for a [noun]
entries.contrast: For + -ing looks backward; to + infinitive looks forward. An excuse for leaving early justifies a departure that happened; an excuse to leave early is a pretext for one you want. ✗ an excuse of being late and ✗ an excuse about being late are errors. Note the sarcastic frame a poor excuse for a lawyer, where for means "in the role of." The noun is /ɪkˈskjus/ with an s sound; the verb excuse is /ɪkˈskjuz/ with a z, and it takes a person as its object with for on the offense: excuse me for interrupting, ✗ excuse for me.
entries.see also: apology for, reason for, grounds for, responsibility for, for

entries.meaning: Official release from a duty, tax, or requirement that otherwise applies.
examples: The church claimed an exemption from the county's assembly permit.
Small carriers got a two-year exemption from the new logging rule.
She filed for a medical exemption from the requirement.
There's a homestead exemption for owner-occupied property in this state.
No exemption from filing quarterly is available once revenue crosses the line.
Losing the exemption cost the foundation about $80,000 a year.
entries.русский: освобождение от — от обязанности, налога или требования
entries.register: neutral to formal — tax, regulatory, and school paperwork; an American meets it on a W-4, a property-tax form, or a vaccination waiver
entries.complement: from: the requirement escaped, as a noun phrase or gerund (an exemption from filing quarterly) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an exemption to file quarterly) and never a clause. for: who or what gets the break (an exemption for veterans). of: whoever is exempted, in formal drafting (the exemption of nonprofits from the tax).
entries.pattern: an exemption from [a tax / a rule / a requirement] · an exemption for [a group / a category] · claim / grant / seek / lose an exemption · a personal / homestead / religious / medical exemption · exempt from [noun phrase] (the adjective)
entries.contrast: From is what you escape, for is who escapes it. An exemption from the noise ordinance is the relief; an exemption for houses of worship is the class that gets it; ✗ an exemption of the noise ordinance reverses the sense. ✗ exemption to is an error, and it is common because exception to does take to — but an exception is a case the rule does not cover and an exemption is a release granted to somebody, so the two nouns are not synonyms and do not share a preposition. The adjective is exempt from, never ✗ exempt of.
entries.see also: exception to, immunity from, waiver of, eligibility for, compliance with, from

entries.respell: ig-ZIB-it too, SKED-jool too, AN-eks too
entries.meaning: A document attached to and made part of an agreement.
examples: The form of promissory note is attached as Exhibit B to the loan agreement.
Every open lawsuit is listed on the disclosure Schedule to the merger agreement.
The Annex to the treaty runs longer than the treaty.
Counsel added a schedule to the lease listing the fixtures that stay.
Nothing in the exhibits to the agreement changes the closing date.
She marked the letter as plaintiff's Exhibit 14 and handed it to the witness.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ɪɡˈzɪbɪt tə/, /ˈskɛdʒul tə/, /ˈænɛks tə/ · the noun is AN-eks, the verb uh-NEKS /əˈnɛks/
entries.русский: юр. приложение к договору — документ, ставший его частью
entries.register: legal — contract drafting, SEC filings, treaties. An American meets these on the signature-page side of a purchase agreement, a commercial lease, or an employment contract with a schedule of stock options.
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming the instrument the document is attached to — never a gerund, never an infinitive, never a clause. In court, exhibit takes no preposition at all: Exhibit 14, plaintiff's Exhibit A.
entries.pattern: Exhibit A to [the Agreement] · Schedule 2 to [the Purchase Agreement] · the Annex to [the Treaty] · attached as Exhibit B · set forth on Schedule 3.1 · incorporated by reference
entries.variants: the three are drafting conventions, not synonyms with fixed meanings, and firms differ: an exhibit is usually a stand-alone document (a form of note, a bill of sale); a schedule is usually a list keyed to a representation (the Disclosure Schedules); an annex is commoner in treaties and in agreements drafted outside the United States. An appendix belongs to reports and books — see appendix to — and an addendum adds new terms.
entries.contrast: All three take to and none takes of: ✗ Exhibit A of the Agreement is a drafting error a partner will circle, though it is everywhere in email. Note the case convention: capitalized and unhyphenated when they name a specific attachment (as set forth in Schedule 4.2), lowercase when generic (the schedules to the agreement). In litigation the word switches meaning entirely — Exhibit 6 is a thing handed to a witness, and it hangs off nothing.
entries.see also: appendix to, amendment to, party to, signatory to, warranty as to, to

entries.meaning: Accumulated know-how, hands-on dealings, or something lived through.
examples: She has eight years' experience in pediatric nursing.
Do you have any experience with payroll software?
The whole experience of moving cross-country aged me a decade.
He lacks the experience to run a crew that size.
I know from experience that the second week is the hard one.
Two bad experiences with the same contractor were enough.
entries.русский: опыт в чём-л., опыт работы с чем-л.; также пережитое
entries.complement: in: a field or activity — noun phrase or gerund (experience in managing volunteers) — never a to-infinitive (✗ experience to manage volunteers). with: a tool, system, or population dealt with. of: something undergone. The noun also takes a bare to-infinitive in the frame the experience to handle it, meaning enough experience.
entries.pattern: experience in [field / verb-ing] · experience with [tool / people] · the experience of [thing undergone] · the experience to [verb] · have / gain / lack experience · from experience
entries.variants: experience in — a field or discipline · experience with — hands-on dealings, the American preference on résumés · experience of — undergoing something, commoner in British English and in academic prose about lived experience
entries.countability matters: experience is uncountable when it means accumulated know-how (she has ten years' experience, ✗ ten years' experiences) and countable when it means an episode (a strange experience, two bad experiences).
entries.contrast: Three prepositions, three relationships to the thing. Experience in nursing is a career; experience with ventilators is having handled them; the experience of being a patient is having lived through it. American job postings overwhelmingly want experience with a technology and experience in a field, so ✗ experience of Excel reads as British or as a translation.
entries.see also: knowledge of/about, expert on/in, understanding of, success in/at, with

entries.meaning: Someone with deep knowledge of a subject or skill.
examples: She's the state's leading expert on groundwater contamination.
We brought in an expert in forensic accounting.
He's an expert at getting extensions out of the county.
The defense called two experts on eyewitness reliability.
You don't have to be an expert in nutrition to read a label.
My uncle is an expert at losing car keys.
entries.русский: эксперт по чему-л., специалист в чём-л.
entries.complement: on: a subject known about — noun phrase only (✗ an expert on how engines fail; write an expert on engine failures). in: a field practiced. at: a skill, and here a gerund is normal (an expert at getting funding) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an expert at get funding).
entries.pattern: an expert on [subject] · an expert in [field] · an expert at [verb-ing / skill] · expert testimony on [subject] · consult an expert on [noun phrase]
entries.variants: expert on — knows about it · expert in — works in it · expert at — is good at doing it; all three are standard American English and the choice is real, not stylistic
entries.contrast: Choose by what kind of thing follows. An expert on wolves studies them; an expert in wildlife biology practices the discipline; an expert at tracking wolves is skilled at the activity. ✗ an expert of wolves is an error in all three senses. The parallel adjective expert takes the same at and in (expert at splicing rope, expert in tax law) but not on: ✗ she is expert on wolves wants the noun, she is an expert on wolves. Compare authority on/over, which shares the on frame but adds a power sense that expert does not have.
entries.see also: authority on/over, knowledge of/about, experience of/in/with, grasp of, expert at, on

entries.meaning: Contact with something that can affect you — a substance, a risk, an idea — or the act of revealing something hidden.
examples: Years of exposure to solvents in the shop finally showed up on a scan.
Early exposure to a second language does more than later drilling does.
The fund cut its exposure to commercial real estate by half.
Two hikers died of exposure on the ridge that November.
The paper's exposure of the billing scheme took eighteen months.
OSHA limits exposure to silica dust to fifty micrograms per cubic meter.
entries.русский: подверженность чему-л., контакт с чем-л.; также разоблачение скрытого
entries.register: neutral; technical in medicine, industrial hygiene, and finance
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (exposure to being outdoors all day) — never a to-infinitive (✗ exposure to breathe the fumes) and never a clause. The revealing sense takes of instead: the exposure of the scheme.
entries.pattern: exposure to [a substance / a risk / a language / the elements] · the exposure of [a secret / a fraud] · limit / reduce / document exposure to [noun phrase] · occupational exposure · exposure to [a currency / a sector] (finance) · die of exposure
entries.contrast: To for what reaches you, of for what gets revealed. Her exposure to asbestos is contact; the exposure of the cover-up is disclosure — and ✗ the exposure to the cover-up would mean the cover-up was reaching her. ✗ exposure with and ✗ exposure on are errors. Note the American senses that take no complement: die of exposure is hypothermia, an exposure in photography is one frame, and good exposure for a business is publicity. In finance, exposure to the euro is how much you stand to lose if it moves, which is the risk sense, not the contact sense.
entries.see also: risk of, danger of/to, protection from/against, immunity from, vulnerable to, to

entries.meaning: Complete trust in someone or something, held without proof.
examples: I've lost what faith I had in the appeals process.
She kept her faith in the students long after the district gave up.
His faith in the machine survived three breakdowns in one week.
They negotiated in good faith and got nothing for it.
The board's faith that enrollment would rebound was misplaced.
Faith in institutions is measurably lower than it was in 1975.
entries.русский: вера в кого-л./что-л. — полное доверие, не требующее доказательств
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (faith in doing things the slow way) — never a to-infinitive (✗ faith to do things the slow way). The noun does take a bare that-clause: faith that it would work out.
entries.pattern: faith in [person / thing] · faith that [clause] · have / lose / keep faith in [noun phrase] · in good faith · an article of faith · bad faith
entries.contrast: In is fixed — ✗ faith on, ✗ faith to, ✗ faith about. The distinction from confidence in is one of evidence: confidence implies grounds, faith implies going beyond them, which is why blind confidence is odd and blind faith is idiomatic. Note the fixed legal phrases in good faith and in bad faith, which take no complement at all, and keep faith with someone (honor a commitment to them), where the preposition changes with the sense.
entries.see also: confidence in, belief in, dependence on/reliance on, hope for/of, in

entries.meaning: Being afraid of something, or being afraid on someone's behalf.
examples: Her fear of flying kept her off airplanes for twenty years.
There's a real fear of losing the farm if the drought holds.
The family expressed fear for his safety in the county lockup.
He never reported it, for fear of being blamed.
A fear that the levee would fail emptied the whole subdivision.
Out of fear of the paperwork, she let the claim lapse.
entries.русский: страх перед чем-л., боязнь чего-л. — рус. родительный или «перед»
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (a fear of flying, fear of losing the house) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a fear to fly). for: a person or thing whose safety is at stake (fear for her safety). The noun also takes a bare that-clause: a fear that the levee would fail.
entries.pattern: a fear of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · fear for [someone / something at risk] · a fear that [clause] · for fear of [verb-ing] · for fear that [clause] · out of fear of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Of is what frightens you; for is who you are frightened about. Fear of her father means he frightens you; fear for her father means you are worried about him — a total reversal from one preposition. The fixed adverbial for fear of requires an -ing form (he said nothing for fear of making it worse, ✗ for fear to make it worse), while for fear that takes a clause. The verb allows the bare infinitive frame that the noun forbids — I fear to think what it cost is archaic but grammatical, whereas ✗ a fear to think is not.
entries.see also: risk of, danger of/to, worry about, concern about/for, afraid of, of

entries.meaning: Concentrated attention, or the thing it is directed at.
examples: The district's new focus on attendance has already moved the numbers.
The focus of the audit is the 2023 fiscal year.
There's too much focus on the logo and not enough on the product.
The whole slide was out of focus.
Her focus on reducing packaging waste started as a side project.
The committee shifted its focus from prevention to treatment.
entries.русский: сосредоточенность на чём-л., фокус на; главный предмет внимания
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a focus on reducing waste) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a focus to reduce waste) and never a clause (✗ a focus that we reduce waste).
entries.pattern: a focus on [noun phrase / verb-ing] · the focus of [study / attention] · place / put the focus on [noun phrase] · in focus · out of focus · shift focus from X to Y
entries.variants: focus in on — an informal American intensifier of the verb (let's focus in on page three); harmless in speech, redundant in writing
entries.contrast: On for the target, of for whose focus it is: the focus of the study is what the study concentrates on, and a focus on cost is the thing concentrated on — both can appear together, the focus of the study on cost. ✗ a focus to, ✗ a focus about, ✗ a focus in are errors. Unlike emphasis on/stress on, the verb here keeps the preposition: focus on the numbers, ✗ focus the numbers — except in the optical and transitive sense (focus the lens, focus your attention on it).
entries.see also: attention to, emphasis on/stress on, interest in, concern about/for, on

entries.meaning: A liking for something, usually mild and slightly indulgent.
examples: He has a well-known fondness for diner coffee.
Her fondness for nineteenth-century sermons is hard to explain.
The judge showed no particular fondness for long opening statements.
I've developed a fondness for taking the long way home.
A fondness for the underdog runs in that family.
His fondness for the sound of his own voice was the whole problem.
entries.русский: любовь, слабость к чему-л. — мягкая, чуть снисходительная симпатия
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a fondness for taking the long way home) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a fondness to take the long way) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a fondness for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · develop / have a fondness for [noun phrase] · look back with fondness on [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: For is fixed — ✗ fondness of, ✗ fondness to, ✗ fondness toward. Do not carry over the adjective's preposition: the adjective is fond of (fond of jazz, ✗ fond for jazz), and the noun is fondness for, so the pair is a small but reliable trap. Note the gentle irony the word usually carries in American prose: a fondness for expensive shoes is nearly always a mild accusation. Compare taste for/in, which is close in meaning but splits by preposition, and preference for, which is neutral.
entries.see also: taste for/in, preference for, love for/of, interest in, fond of, for

entries.meaning: An understanding of a subject or situation.
examples: She has a firm grasp of the underlying statistics.
His grasp of what the job actually involves is shaky at best.
You can't teach this without a solid grasp of the chemistry.
A tenure-track job seemed, for one week, within her grasp.
The report shows almost no grasp of how the permitting process works.
The concept is not beyond the grasp of a bright ninth grader.
entries.русский: понимание чего-л., владение предметом — книжнее, чем handle on
entries.complement: noun phrase or a wh-clause (a firm grasp of what the job involves) — never a to-infinitive and never a that-clause. A gerund is possible but unusual (a grasp of doing the math in your head reads oddly; prefer a grasp of the arithmetic).
entries.pattern: a grasp of [subject / situation] · have / get / lose one's grasp of [noun phrase] · beyond / within someone's grasp · a firm / shaky / tenuous grasp of [noun phrase]
entries.variants: a grasp on — heard in American speech (a good grasp on the material), but of is the edited form; a grip on is the idiomatic alternative with on
entries.contrast: Of for understanding, within/beyond for the physical or figurative reach. A grasp of the material is comprehension; within his grasp is attainability — ✗ a grasp to the material is an error. The near-synonym grip prefers on (a grip on reality, get a grip on the situation), which is where grasp on comes from; both are acceptable in speech, but grasp of is what edited prose uses. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition: he grasped the point, ✗ he grasped at the point (which means something else — a desperate attempt, as in grasping at straws).
entries.see also: understanding of, knowledge of/about, insight into, awareness of, of

entries.meaning: A legally or logically sufficient reason for doing something.
examples: Repeated absence is grounds for dismissal under the contract.
The tenant has grounds for withholding rent until the heat is fixed.
We have grounds to believe the meter was misread.
The appeal was denied on the grounds that it was filed nine days late.
There are no grounds for reopening the investigation.
The permit was refused on the grounds of inadequate parking.
entries.русский: основания для — достаточная юридически или логически причина; обычно мн. ч.
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (grounds for firing him) — and separately a to-infinitive with no preposition (grounds to believe he lied). Also a that-clause in the fixed frame on the grounds that. ✗ grounds for to fire him mixes the two.
entries.pattern: grounds for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · grounds to [verb] · on the grounds that [clause] · on the grounds of [noun phrase] · have grounds for [noun phrase] · no grounds whatsoever
entries.variants: grounds (plural) — the normal form in this sense, even with a singular determiner (a single ground for appeal is possible but stiff) · ground for — occurs in legal writing (ground for reversal)
entries.two fixed phrases that get blended: on the grounds that the notice was late takes a clause, and on the grounds of procedural error takes a noun — ✗ on the grounds of that the notice was late is the blend. ✗ grounds of appeal is British legal usage; American practice says grounds for appeal. The unrelated singular ground meaning earth, and the plural grounds meaning the land around a building or the sediment in coffee, take no preposition at all.
entries.see also: reason for, evidence of/for, excuse for, cause of, for

entries.meaning: A firm promise that something will happen or hold up.
examples: A high LSAT score is no guarantee of admission anywhere.
The dealer offers a three-year guarantee on the transmission.
There's a written guarantee against corrosion for the first decade.
We got a guarantee that the crew would be out by the fifteenth.
The compressor is still under guarantee.
Paying early is no guarantee of getting your deposit back.
entries.русский: гарантия чего-л. — твёрдое обещание, что нечто произойдёт или выдержит
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (no guarantee of getting a refund) — never a to-infinitive after of (✗ a guarantee of to get a refund). The noun separately takes a that-clause (a guarantee that the work will hold) and, in commercial use, against (a guarantee against defects).
entries.pattern: a guarantee of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a guarantee that [clause] · a guarantee against [defect / loss] · a guarantee on [product] · under guarantee · no guarantee
entries.variants: guaranty — the same word in the narrow financial sense of a surety obligation; in ordinary American writing use guarantee for everything
entries.contrast: Of for the outcome promised, against for the risk covered, on for the product. A guarantee of delivery by Friday, a guarantee against rust, a two-year guarantee on the compressor — swapping these produces ✗ a guarantee for rust, which reads as though rust were promised. ✗ a guarantee to the buyer is wrong in the promise sense, though a guarantee can of course be given to a buyer. The verb takes a direct object, an indirect object, or a that-clause and no preposition: we guarantee the work, I guarantee you it will hold, ✗ we guarantee for the work.
entries.see also: proof of, responsibility for, protection from/against, confidence in, of

entries.meaning: A settled, repeated behavior.
examples: She has the habit of rereading every email before sending it.
I'm not in the habit of lending tools to people I just met.
He got into the habit of leaving the radio on all night.
Don't make a habit of parking there.
I checked the mailbox out of habit, though nothing comes on Sundays.
Breaking the habit of checking his phone at dinner took a year.
entries.русский: привычка делать что-л. — устойчивое повторяющееся поведение
entries.complement: of + gerund, almost always (the habit of checking twice) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the habit to check twice). A plain noun after of is rare and reads as a compound instead (a coffee habit, not ✗ a habit of coffee).
entries.pattern: the habit of [verb-ing] · in the habit of [verb-ing] · get into / out of the habit of [verb-ing] · make a habit of [verb-ing] · break the habit · out of habit · a habit of mind
entries.the infinitive is the error and it is ne: ✗ he has the habit to interrupt, ✗ I'm in the habit to walk after dinner. Every frame here requires -ing — the habit of interrupting, in the habit of walking. ✗ a habit to has no standing in American English. Compare the adjectives, which do take the infinitive and thereby reinforce the confusion: he is accustomed to walking (preposition, -ing) but he tends to walk (infinitive). Note out of habit (mechanically) against out of the habit of (no longer doing it) — one word apart, opposite meanings.
entries.see also: tendency to/toward, taste for/in, fondness for, difficulty with/in, of

entries.meaning: An informal grip on a problem — enough understanding to manage it.
examples: Nobody has a handle on how much the repairs will actually run.
Give me a week and I'll have a handle on the backlog.
She's got a good handle on the county's permitting mess.
We have no handle on why the returns spiked in March.
He's finally getting a handle on managing three sites at once.
His Twitter handle is the same one he used on CB radio in 1979.
entries.русский: разг. представление о проблеме — «ухватить суть» настолько, чтобы справиться
entries.register: informal American English — spoken, and fine in email and reporting, out of place in a brief or a scientific paper
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (a handle on managing the backlog) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a handle to manage the backlog) and never a clause. The noun is nearly always inside get or have a handle on; a bare the handle on the problem is not idiomatic in this sense.
entries.pattern: get / have a handle on [a problem / the numbers / a situation] · no handle on [noun phrase] · a good / firm / rough handle on [noun phrase] · a handle (a nickname or a screen name) · the handle on [a door] (the literal object)
entries.for the physical grip's owner: a handle on the budget is comprehension, the handle of the pitcher is the part you hold, and the handle on the door is also literal — context, not the preposition, separates the last two. Against grasp of, which is the same idea one register up: a grasp of the material is what you write in a recommendation letter, a handle on the material is what you say out loud. Compare understanding of, the neutral form. In American slang a handle with no complement is a name (what's your handle?) or, in basketball, ball-handling ability.
entries.contrast: On for understanding, of
entries.see also: grasp of, understanding of, insight into, knowledge of/about, control over/of, on

entries.meaning: A wish for a good outcome, and the expectation that it might come.
examples: There's still hope for a negotiated settlement.
Crews gave up hope of finding anyone alive on the fourth day.
She applied in the hope of getting in-state tuition.
The hope that the market would recover by spring did not survive February.
My hopes for the season died in the first quarter.
He has no realistic hope of making the payments.
entries.русский: надежда на что-л. — рус. «на», не «для»
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase naming what is wanted (hope for peace). of + gerund: the outcome hoped for (hope of finding survivors) — never a to-infinitive after either preposition (✗ no hope to survive, ✗ hope of to survive). The noun also takes a bare that-clause: the hope that it would blow over.
entries.pattern: hope for [noun phrase] · hope of [verb-ing] · the hope that [clause] · in the hope of [verb-ing] · in the hope that [clause] · give up hope of [verb-ing] · hopes for [the future]
entries.contrast: For takes a thing; of takes an outcome, always in the -ing form. ✗ no hope to find survivors is the classic error; write no hope of finding survivors. The verb behaves in the opposite direction and that is precisely why the noun trips people: hope to find survivors is perfectly good English with an infinitive, as are hope for the best and hope that it holds. So the same idea splits by word class — verb hope to do, noun hope of doing. ✗ hope in survives only in religious registers (hope in the Lord).
entries.see also: desire for, wish for, chance of, chance of, hope for, for

entries.meaning: A concept, a proposal, or an opinion.
examples: The idea of selling the house had never occurred to either of them.
She had a good idea for a documentary about the last drive-in.
The idea that the deed was lost in the 1911 fire is family legend.
I have no idea what the second key opens.
His ideas about discipline are twenty years out of date.
The whole idea behind the redesign was to cut one page from the form.
entries.русский: of — представление о чём-л.; for — идея, замысел чего-л.
entries.complement: of: a concept — noun phrase or gerund (the idea of moving) — never a to-infinitive after of (✗ the idea of to move). for: a proposal (an idea for a documentary). The noun also takes a bare that-clause (the idea that markets self-correct) and a wh-clause after no idea (no idea what he meant).
entries.pattern: the idea of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · an idea for [project] · the idea that [clause] · have no idea [wh-clause] · get the idea · ideas about [topic] · the idea behind [thing]
entries.variants: ideas about — opinions on a topic (ideas about parenting), distinct from both of and for
entries.contrast: Of is the concept, for is the proposal, and the two are not close. The idea of a second bridge is the notion itself; an idea for a second bridge is somebody's plan. ✗ the idea to move is an error in careful writing, though it is common in speech; write the idea of moving. The clause frame drops the preposition entirely — the idea that markets self-correct, ✗ the idea of that markets self-correct — and no idea takes a wh-clause with nothing in between: I have no idea what he meant, where no idea of what he meant is heavier but not wrong.
entries.see also: plan for, opinion on/of/about, view on/of, insight into, of

entries.meaning: Protection from legal consequences, or the body's resistance to a disease.
examples: He testified only after the U.S. Attorney granted him immunity from prosecution.
Most adults have lifelong immunity to chickenpox after one infection.
Qualified immunity shielded both officers from the civil suit.
The statute gives volunteers immunity from liability for ordinary negligence.
Immunity against the newer variant faded within about five months.
Diplomatic immunity covers the parking tickets, which is why there are so many.
entries.русский: юр. иммунитет от ответственности; мед. невосприимчивость к болезни
entries.register: from is legal and formal — prosecutors' letters, diplomatic notes, civil-rights suits; to is medical and everyday
entries.complement: from: the legal process or consequence escaped, as a noun phrase or gerund (immunity from being sued) — never an infinitive. to: a disease or agent (immunity to measles). against: an agent, in immunology (immunity against the variant). Never a clause after any of them.
entries.pattern: immunity from [prosecution / suit / liability] · immunity to [a disease] · immunity against [a pathogen] · grant / claim / waive immunity · diplomatic / sovereign / qualified / transactional immunity · herd immunity (no complement)
entries.contrast: From for the law, to for the body, and swapping them is the error: ✗ immunity to prosecution and ✗ immunity from measles both sound wrong to an American ear, though the second is heard. Immunity against is immunology's own variant and is normal in a virology paper, odd in a newspaper. Against exemption from: an exemption releases you from a requirement, immunity shields you from a consequence. American terms to keep straight: qualified immunity protects officials from suit, sovereign immunity protects governments, transactional immunity protects a witness from prosecution for whatever he testifies about.
entries.see also: exemption from, protection from/against, waiver of, liability for/to, right to/of/over, from

entries.meaning: A strong effect on something.
examples: The closure had an immediate impact on enrollment at both schools.
Nobody has measured the impact of the ordinance on small landlords.
Her testimony made a real impact on the committee.
The new rules will have almost no impact on rural carriers.
The environmental impact of the pipeline is still under review.
The airbag deployed on impact.
entries.русский: сильное воздействие на, влияние на — рус. «на», не «для»
entries.complement: noun phrase naming what is affected (an impact on enrollment). Gerunds are possible but heavy; never a to-infinitive (✗ an impact to reduce costs) and never a clause. The full frame names both sides: the impact of X on Y.
entries.pattern: an impact on [thing affected] · the impact of X on Y · have / make an impact on [noun phrase] · the impact of [event] · high-impact · on impact
entries.variants: an impact upon — formal, identical in meaning · an effect on — the plainer synonym; see effect on
entries.contrast: On is the preposition and to is corporate noise. ✗ the impact to the schedule has spread through American business writing since about 2000; it is not standard, and editors change it to the impact on the schedule. ✗ an impact for is likewise wrong. Of names the cause, on names the target, exactly as with effect on. Note that impact as a verb in the figurative sense (the tariff impacted sales) is disliked by many American editors, who prefer affected; the literal transitive verb (an impacted tooth, the bullet impacted the wall) is unobjectionable.
entries.see also: effect on, influence on/over, result of, consequence of, on

entries.meaning: A consequence for someone, an unstated suggestion, or involvement in something.
examples: The ruling has real implications for every month-to-month tenant in the state.
Nobody has thought through the implications for the pension fund.
The implication that she approved the transfer is not supported by a single email.
His implication in the bid-rigging came out three years later.
By implication, the memo concedes the deadline was missed.
A four-cent change has implications for margins nobody wants to discuss.
entries.русский: последствие для кого-л.; скрытый намёк; причастность к чему-л. (in)
entries.complement: for: who or what is affected, as a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ implications for raising rates; write implications for the rate decision) and never an infinitive. that: a bare that-clause, in the "unstated suggestion" sense (the implication that he knew). in: involvement in wrongdoing (his implication in the scheme).
entries.pattern: implications for [a group / a policy / a field] · the implication that [clause] · implication in [wrongdoing] · by implication · far-reaching / troubling / practical implications · the implications of [an event] for [a group]
entries.contrast: Three frames, three meanings. Implications for small landlords are consequences; the implication that he knew is a hint; his implication in the fraud is involvement. The full consequence frame stacks both prepositions: the implications of the ruling for small landlords — and dropping the of leaves the sentence hanging. Note the pair every editor watches: a writer or a fact implies, a reader infers, so the implication is in the text and the inference is in the reader's head. ✗ implications to the industry is an error.
entries.see also: consequence of, effect on, impact on, bearing on, relevance to, for

entries.meaning: The quality of mattering, and to whom.
examples: The report stresses the importance of early screening.
She never grasped the importance of showing up on time to a union meeting.
Water rights are of enormous importance to every rancher in the basin.
The board attaches great importance to the auditor's independence.
The importance of the find was not appreciated until the 1960s.
That distinction is of no importance here.
entries.русский: важность чего-л. для кого-л., значимость
entries.complement: of: what is important — noun phrase or gerund (the importance of showing up) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the importance to show up). to: the person or thing it matters to. Both frequently appear at once: the importance of sleep to recovery.
entries.pattern: the importance of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · of importance to [person] · attach importance to [noun phrase] · of little / no importance · stress the importance of [verb-ing]
entries.contrast: Of names what matters; to names whom it matters to. ✗ the importance to sleep is the classic slip, produced by reaching for an infinitive where a gerund belongs. Note the separate frame attach importance to something, where to introduces the thing valued rather than the person — so he attaches great importance to punctuality is correct and does not contradict the rule. The adjective is important to someone and important for something (important for growth), and there ✗ important of is wrong.
entries.see also: emphasis on/stress on, attention to, benefit of/to, point in/of, of

entries.meaning: A change for the better, or a version that beats an earlier one.
examples: There's been a measurable improvement in air quality since the plant closed.
The second edition is a real improvement on the first.
Her handwriting shows some improvement, mostly in the numerals.
The lease requires the tenant to pay for any improvements to the storefront.
This engine is a clear improvement over the one it replaced.
There's still room for improvement in how we handle refunds.
entries.русский: in — улучшение в чём-л.; on — усовершенствование по сравнению с прежним
entries.complement: in: what is getting better — noun phrase or gerund (an improvement in reporting) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an improvement to report faster). on / over: the earlier version being beaten. to: a physical alteration made to a property (improvements to the building).
entries.pattern: an improvement in [thing improving] · an improvement on / over [earlier version] · improvements to [property] · show / see an improvement in [noun phrase] · room for improvement
entries.variants: an improvement on — the standard comparative form · an improvement over — equally American and slightly commoner in technical writing
entries.contrast: Three prepositions and three claims. An improvement in air quality says the air is better than it was; an improvement on the 2019 model says this one beats that one; improvements to the building are renovations. ✗ an improvement of air quality is not idiomatic in the change sense, though the improvement of public health is fine as a formal abstract noun. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition (improve the design) or stands alone (she's improving), and improve on the design is not an error but a different claim: it means "do better than it," not "make it better" — a real and easily missed difference.
entries.see also: increase in/decrease in, progress in/on, change in/of, advantage of/over, in

entries.meaning: How often a condition occurs — either newly, over a period, or in total, at a moment.
examples: The incidence of Lyme disease in the county has tripled since 2010.
Prevalence of untreated hypertension is highest in the two rural districts.
Researchers compared the incidence of infection in vaccinated and unvaccinated groups.
The prevalence of asthma among children near the interstate is the study's finding.
A rising incidence of fraud complaints prompted the audit.
Note that incidence is a rate and incidents are the things that happened.
entries.русский: заболеваемость (новые случаи) и распространённость (все случаи разом)
entries.register: technical — epidemiology, public health, criminology — and their reporting; both words are singular mass nouns
entries.complement: of: the condition or event counted, as a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ the incidence of smoking cigarettes is odd; write the incidence of smoking), never an infinitive, and never a clause. in / among: the population (prevalence among adolescents, incidence in the exposed group).
entries.pattern: the incidence of [a disease / an event] · the prevalence of [a condition] · incidence in / among [a population] · a high / low / rising incidence · per 100,000 · incidence rate
entries.the technical split is the point: incidence counts new cases over a period, prevalence counts existing cases at a moment. A long-lasting disease has low incidence and high prevalence; a short one, the reverse — so ✗ the incidence of diabetes in the county is nine percent misuses the word, since a percentage of the living population is prevalence. And the spelling trap: incidence is a rate, incidents are events. ✗ the incidents of theft rose means individual thefts rose, which may be what you meant, but the incidence of theft rose is the statistic. Both words are uncountable in this sense: ✗ two incidences.
entries.see also: probability of/likelihood of, ratio of ... to, rise in/fall in, correlation with/between, exposure to, of

entries.meaning: A rise or fall in an amount, and the size of it.
examples: There's been a sharp increase in emergency room visits since June.
The board approved an increase of four percent for all classified staff.
We saw a steady decrease in complaints after the new signage went up.
The fee goes up by an increase to $45 effective in March.
Enrollment showed an increase from 812 to 940 in two years.
Bicycle theft is on the increase downtown.
entries.русский: рост чего-л. / снижение чего-л. — рус. родительный, не «в»
entries.complement: in: the thing that grew or shrank (an increase in premiums). of: the size of the change (an increase of nine percent). to: the endpoint reached (an increase to $18 an hour). Gerunds follow in (a decrease in reporting); never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: an increase / decrease in [thing measured] · an increase of [amount] · an increase to [new level] · an increase from X to Y · on the increase · a [percentage] increase in [noun phrase]
entries.variants: a rise in and a fall in behave identically; see rise in/fall in · a decline in is the formal synonym of a decrease in · a raise in American English is a pay increase, where British English says a rise
entries.contrast: In for what changed, of for how much, and this is the error people actually make. ✗ an increase of premiums says the premiums themselves were increased in number; you want an increase in premiums. Conversely ✗ an increase in nine percent is wrong for the size. All four can stack: an increase in premiums of nine percent, from $200 to $218. ✗ an increase on premiums is an error, though a tax on premiums is fine — see tax on. The verb takes no preposition when transitive (they increased the fee) and by for the amount (increased by nine percent).
entries.see also: rise in/fall in, improvement in/on, change in/of, demand for, in

entries.meaning: Power to affect how something turns out, or the effect itself.
examples: Her thesis adviser had an enormous influence on the way she writes.
The family retains real influence over the endowment's investments.
The influence of Dutch settlement on local place names is still visible.
He was arrested for driving under the influence.
That neighbor has been a bad influence on both of my kids.
She has some influence with the county commissioners.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈɪnfluəns ən/; over has no weak form
entries.русский: влияние на что-л., власть над кем-л.
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun; a wh-clause follows on in the frame influence on what gets published. Never a to-infinitive (✗ influence to change the vote) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: an influence on [outcome / person] · influence over [person / process] · the influence of X on Y · under the influence of [noun phrase] · exert / have influence on [noun phrase] · a bad influence on [person]
entries.variants: influence on — the effect produced · influence over — the power held, always with a person or process as complement · influence with — standing that lets you get things done (she has influence with the zoning board)
entries.contrast: On is an effect; over is power; with is access. His influence on the design changed how it looks; his influence over the committee means he controls it; his influence with the committee means they listen to him. ✗ influence to and ✗ influence for are errors. Under the influence on its own is an American legal idiom for intoxication and takes no complement. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition: the weather influenced the decision, ✗ influenced on the decision.
entries.see also: effect on, impact on, control over/of, authority on/over, over

entries.meaning: Facts provided or learned about something.
examples: There's very little information about the site's earlier owners.
The website has information on how to appeal a denial.
I got that information from the county recorder's office.
This packet is information for new parents, not a legal document.
One useful piece of information came out of the whole meeting.
The agency withheld information about the second inspection.
entries.русский: информация о чём-л., сведения по — в англ. неисчисляемо (✗ informations)
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (information about applying for aid), or wh-clause (information on how to appeal) — never a to-infinitive (✗ information to apply for aid). It does take a bare that-clause in formal use: information that the shipment had been diverted.
entries.pattern: information about / on [topic] · information from [source] · information for [audience] · for your information · a piece of information · withhold / disclose information about [noun phrase]
entries.variants: information on — a subject formally treated (information on the vaccine) · information about — the neutral conversational form · information regarding — bureaucratic
entries.contrast: The countability rule is the whole trap. Information is uncountable in American English: ✗ an information, ✗ informations, ✗ many informations, ✗ these informations. Use a piece of information, some information, much information, a lot of information. Speakers of French, Spanish, Italian, and German all have a countable equivalent, which is why this error is so durable. On prepositions, ✗ information of the delay is an error (though notification of the delay is correct), and for names the audience rather than the subject.
entries.see also: knowledge of/about, advice on/about, report on/of, evidence of/for, about

entries.meaning: A court order forbidding or compelling a specific act.
examples: The union sought an injunction against the lockout and got it in a day.
A federal judge issued an injunction against enforcing the ordinance.
The injunction against publishing the documents lasted nine days.
She violated the injunction twice and was held in contempt.
The order is an injunction to restore service, not merely to stop cutting it.
Plaintiffs asked for a preliminary injunction against the merger closing.
entries.pronunciation note: weak against has no weak form; the noun keeps full stress on -JUNK-
entries.русский: юр. судебный запрет — предписание суда не делать чего-л.
entries.register: legal — motions, orders, and the news coverage of them; an American meets the word when a court blocks a law, a strike, or a merger
entries.complement: against: the person or act enjoined, as a noun phrase or gerund (an injunction against publishing the file). to: a bare infinitive naming what the order compels (an injunction to restore service), which is the mandatory rather than the prohibitory kind. Never a that-clause. The archaic non-legal sense ("a solemn instruction") also takes to + infinitive.
entries.pattern: an injunction against [a person / an act] · an injunction to [verb] · seek / obtain / dissolve / violate an injunction · a preliminary / permanent injunction · a temporary restraining order · enjoin [someone] from [verb-ing] (the verb)
entries.contrast: Against stops something; to plus a verb starts something. An injunction against the demolition forbids; an injunction to reconnect the water commands. ✗ an injunction to demolish would order the opposite of what the plaintiff wanted, so the slip is expensive. Note the verb, which takes a different preposition entirely: the court enjoined the county from demolishing the building — enjoin from + -ing, never ✗ enjoin to stop. Against prohibition on/against: a prohibition is a standing rule, an injunction is a court order aimed at named parties.
entries.see also: prohibition on/against, moratorium on, judgment against/for, remedy for/against, jurisdiction over, against

entries.meaning: A formal investigation, or a request for information.
examples: The board opened an inquiry into how the contract was awarded.
She had one inquiry about the apartment and it came from a bot.
A congressional inquiry into the outage is scheduled for June.
That line of inquiry went nowhere in the first two interviews.
The paper's inquiry into the county's overtime billing ran for a year.
All press inquiries go through the communications office.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈɪntə/ · both stress patterns are standard American; IN-kwuh-ree is commoner in academic speech
entries.русский: расследование чего-л.; также запрос, наведение справок о чём-л.
entries.complement: into: the subject investigated, as a noun phrase or gerund (an inquiry into how the money moved takes a wh-clause; an inquiry into hiring practices takes a gerund) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an inquiry to find the cause, unless to find is a purpose clause). about / regarding: the simple-question sense (an inquiry about the vacancy). from: who is asking.
entries.pattern: an inquiry into [a subject] · an inquiry about [a detail] · inquiries from [customers / reporters] · open / launch / conduct / close an inquiry · a line of inquiry · a congressional / internal inquiry
entries.variants: American English spells it inquiry in both senses; enquiry is British and, where the distinction is kept there, is reserved for the ordinary question. Do not import the split into American copy.
entries.contrast: Into for an investigation, about for a question. An inquiry into the crash is a formal proceeding; an inquiry about the flight is a phone call. ✗ an inquiry on the crash is an error. Against investigation into, which is nearly a synonym: an inquiry is the more neutral and more official-sounding word, which is why bodies that do not want to accuse anyone open an inquiry rather than an investigation. Note the American office phrase for further inquiries, contact — plural, and only in the question sense.
entries.see also: investigation into, research on/into, report on/of, information about/on, insight into, into

entries.meaning: A clear or penetrating understanding of something complicated.
examples: The diaries give real insight into how the shop was run.
Her time on the ward gave her insight into what the families actually need.
The audit offered no insight into where the money went.
That's a useful insight into the way the committee makes decisions.
Twenty years of teaching gave him insight into how children fake reading.
The book's insights into small-town politics are its best feature.
entries.русский: понимание сути чего-л., проникновение в суть сложного
entries.complement: noun phrase, gerund (insight into running a small hospital), or a wh-clause (insight into how the fund actually works) — never a to-infinitive (✗ insight to run a hospital) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: insight into [noun phrase / verb-ing / wh-clause] · gain / offer / provide insight into [noun phrase] · a valuable insight into [noun phrase] · with the insight of [experience]
entries.variants: insights into (plural) — the commoner form in business and academic writing; the singular is more often abstract (a person of great insight)
entries.contrast: Into is fixed — ✗ insight in, ✗ insight on, ✗ insight about, ✗ insight of. The last of these is the trap for anyone who has learned understanding of, grasp of, and awareness of, all of which take of: insight is the odd one in that set. Note the second, uncountable sense meaning perceptiveness (a woman of considerable insight), which takes no complement at all, and the clinical sense in psychiatry (the patient lacks insight), likewise bare.
entries.see also: understanding of, grasp of, awareness of, knowledge of/about, into

entries.meaning: Curiosity about something, a financial stake, or money paid for borrowing.
examples: She's had an interest in nineteenth-century glass since college.
The interest on the second mortgage is what's killing them.
He holds a twelve percent interest in the brewery.
In the interest of time, let's take the rest by email.
The recordings are of considerable interest to linguists.
Nobody on the board took the slightest interest in the audit.
entries.русский: интерес к чему-л.; доля, участие в чём-л.; ср. interest on — проценты по кредиту
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (an interest in restoring old radios) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an interest to restore old radios) and never a that-clause (✗ an interest that the radios be restored). A wh-clause is fine (an interest in what happens to the building). The financial sense takes on: interest on the loan.
entries.pattern: an interest in [subject / verb-ing] · interest on [a loan / a balance] · an interest in [a company] (a stake) · in the interest(s) of [noun phrase] · of interest to [person] · take an interest in [noun phrase] · a conflict of interest
entries.variants: in the interest of and in the interests of — both standard American English; the singular is commoner in in the interest of time · interest on is not a separate headword but the same noun in its financial frame: interest on the loan, interest on unpaid balances, accrue / pay / earn interest on [an amount] — and it is the one frame of the three where ✗ interest of is flatly wrong
entries.contrast: In for curiosity or a stake; on for money. Her interest in the bank is either her curiosity about it or her ownership share; the interest on the loan is what it costs to borrow — and ✗ the interest of the loan is an error. ✗ an interest for photography and ✗ an interest about photography are errors as well. Note that of interest to reverses the direction: the file is of interest to investigators means they are interested in it. The adjective pair is the notorious one — interested in something, but interesting to someone — and ✗ I am interested to buy should be interested in buying unless you mean curiosity about a result (interested to hear how it went).
entries.see also: fondness for, focus on, concern about/for, share in/of, interested in, in

entries.meaning: A formal conversation, for a story or for a job.
examples: In an interview with the local paper, she refused to rule it out.
I have an interview for the assistant curator position on Thursday.
The podcast is a two-hour interview with the man who built the bridge.
He gave one interview about the settlement and never spoke of it again.
The interview with the arresting officer was never recorded.
She interviewed with four firms and got three offers.
entries.русский: интервью с кем-л.; также собеседование с кандидатом
entries.complement: with: the other person, in either role (an interview with the mayor). for: the job or program sought. about / on: the subject. Never a gerund after with, never an infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: an interview with [person] · an interview for [job / program] · an interview about / on [topic] · give / grant / conduct an interview · in an interview with [outlet] · a job interview
entries.names the other party regardless of who: an interview with the mayor is the same event whether the mayor sat down with a reporter or with a hiring panel. ✗ an interview to the mayor is an error, as is ✗ an interview of the mayor in ordinary usage, though an interview of forty candidates is possible in formal survey writing. For names the position: an interview for the assistant director job, ✗ an interview of the job. The verb takes a direct object and no preposition — she interviewed the mayor, ✗ she interviewed with the mayor if she was the reporter — but American English does use interview with for the candidate's side: I interviewed with three firms.
entries.contrast: With
entries.see also: encounter with, discussion about/of, reference to, request for, with

entries.meaning: A first exposure to a subject or a person, or the act of bringing something in.
examples: The course is a gentle introduction to medieval Latin.
That summer was my introduction to commercial fishing.
She wrote him a letter of introduction to the archivist in Madrid.
The introduction of electronic filing cut the backlog in half.
This book is a decent introduction to keeping bees in a cold climate.
By way of introduction, I should say I have no legal training.
entries.русский: знакомство с чем-л., введение в предмет; также внедрение нового
entries.complement: to: a subject or a person — noun phrase, or a gerund in the subject sense (an introduction to keeping bees) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an introduction to keep bees). of: the thing or person being brought in (the introduction of the new system).
entries.pattern: an introduction to [subject / person] · the introduction of [thing brought in] · a letter of introduction · by way of introduction · give [someone] an introduction to [subject]
entries.contrast: To for what you are being introduced to; of for what is being introduced. An introduction to statistics is a first course; the introduction of statistics into the curriculum is the act of adding it. ✗ an introduction of statistics in the course sense is a common and confusing error. The -ing rule applies to the to frame because a noun fits the slot: an introduction to keeping bees, ✗ an introduction to keep bees. The verb takes both: introduce someone to someone, introduce a bill, and ✗ introduce someone with someone is an error.
entries.see also: access to, reference to, approach to, experience of/in/with, to

entries.meaning: An official effort to find out how something happened or who is responsible.
examples: The NTSB opened an investigation into the derailment within hours.
An internal investigation of the sergeant's conduct is still open.
He has been under investigation for wire fraud since last spring.
The investigation into how the ballots were stored took four months.
Two reporters spent a year on an investigation into county overtime.
She was told the investigation had been closed without findings.
entries.русский: расследование чего-л. — рус. родительный, не «в»
entries.complement: into / of: the subject or target, as a noun phrase, gerund, or wh-clause (an investigation into how the fire started) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an investigation to determine the cause as a complement, though that is fine as a purpose clause). for: the suspected offense, in under investigation for. by: the investigating body.
entries.pattern: an investigation into [an event / a practice] · an investigation of [a person / a matter] · under investigation for [an offense] · open / launch / drop / close an investigation · a criminal / internal / independent investigation · the subject of an investigation
entries.variants: investigation into and investigation of are both standard American English: into emphasizes the probing of a question, of the examination of an object or a person. An investigation of Senator Ruiz points at a person; an investigation into the contracts points at a question — and journalists prefer into precisely because it accuses no one.
entries.contrast: ✗ An investigation on is an error, and it is the commonest one from Spanish and Portuguese speakers. Against inquiry into: an investigation implies suspected wrongdoing, an inquiry need not. Against research on/into: research seeks knowledge, an investigation seeks a culprit or a cause — which is why research into the cause of a fire and an investigation into the same fire are done by different people.
entries.see also: inquiry into, research on/into, report on/of, evidence of/for, judgment against/for, into

entries.meaning: A request that someone attend or take part.
examples: The invitation to the wedding came six weeks late.
She turned down an invitation to testify before the subcommittee.
There's an invitation from the dean sitting in your inbox.
We got an invitation for the Saturday session instead.
He was there at the invitation of the tribal council.
The reception is by invitation only.
entries.русский: приглашение на (мероприятие) или к кому-л.
entries.complement: to + noun phrase: the event (an invitation to the wedding). to + bare infinitive: the act invited (an invitation to speak). Both are standard, and the to is a preposition in the first and an infinitive marker in the second. for: a date or an occasion (an invitation for Friday). ✗ an invitation to speaking.
entries.pattern: an invitation to [event] · an invitation to [verb] · an invitation from [host] · an invitation for [date] · accept / decline / extend an invitation · at the invitation of [person] · by invitation only
entries.contrast: This is the one noun in the file where to + noun and to + infinitive are both right, and the meanings differ. An invitation to the conference is a summons to attend; an invitation to speak at the conference is a request to perform. Neither takes -ing: ✗ an invitation to speaking. ✗ an invitation for the wedding is an error where an invitation for Friday is fine, because for takes a time, not an event. The verb keeps both frames: invite her to the wedding, invite her to speak, and ✗ invite her for speaking is wrong.
entries.see also: request for, demand for, order for, permission for, to

entries.meaning: A court's final decision in a case, or, in ordinary use, an opinion or the capacity to form one.
examples: The bank has a judgment against him for $18,000 and it follows him.
The court entered judgment for the plaintiff on the second count only.
The motion asks for judgment on the pleadings before discovery starts.
She has good judgment about people and terrible judgment about cars.
Against my better judgment, I co-signed the lease.
A default judgment against the tenant issued when nobody appeared.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈdʒʌdʒmənt fɚ/; against has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. решение суда против кого-л. / в чью-л. пользу; также суждение, рассудительность
entries.register: legal in the against/for frames; neutral in the everyday sense of an opinion
entries.complement: against / for: the losing and winning party, as a noun phrase. on: the motion or claim decided (judgment on the pleadings). of: the court that entered it. about / on: what an opinion is about, in the everyday sense, where a gerund works (a judgment about hiring him). Never a to-infinitive (✗ a judgment to hire him) and, in the legal frames, never a clause.
entries.pattern: a judgment against [a defendant] · judgment for [a plaintiff] · judgment on [the pleadings / the merits] · enter / vacate / satisfy / appeal a judgment · a default / summary / money judgment · in my judgment · against my better judgment
entries.variants: the American spelling is judgment, without the e, in both the legal and the everyday sense; judgement is British and, in an American brief, reads as a typo
entries.is who collects: a judgment against the contractor and judgment for the homeowner describe one piece of paper from two sides. ✗ a judgment to the plaintiff is an error. In the everyday sense the prepositions change completely — a judgment about his character, in my judgment — and judgment there is uncountable in some frames (poor judgment, ✗ a poor judgment). Note judgment call, an American fixed compound, and against my better judgment, which needs no complement at all.
entries.contrast: Against is who pays, for
entries.see also: damages for, claim against/for/to, injunction against, liability for/to, default on/under, against

entries.meaning: A court's or an agency's legal power to act, and the reach of that power.
examples: The federal court has no jurisdiction over a purely local zoning dispute.
Whether the sheriff has jurisdiction over the campus was the whole argument.
The agency asserted jurisdiction over wetlands connected to navigable water.
The panel lacks jurisdiction to hear an interlocutory appeal here.
Forty-two jurisdictions have adopted some version of the model act.
That building sits outside the jurisdiction of the city fire marshal.
entries.русский: юрисдикция над, подсудность — правомочие суда или ведомства и его пределы
entries.register: legal and governmental; also ordinary speech about which agency handles what
entries.complement: over: the person, place, subject, or dispute, as a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ jurisdiction over deciding the fee), never an infinitive, and never a clause. in: a place or a field (jurisdiction in admiralty, no jurisdiction in Ohio). to: a bare infinitive, in the "power to act" frame (jurisdiction to hear the appeal).
entries.pattern: jurisdiction over [a person / a case / a territory] · jurisdiction to [verb] · within / outside the jurisdiction of [a body] · have / lack / decline / assert jurisdiction · personal / subject-matter / original / appellate jurisdiction · concurrent jurisdiction
entries.contrast: ✗ Jurisdiction on is an error and a frequent one; the noun takes over, matching authority on/over in its over sense and control over/of. Note the two to's again: jurisdiction to hear the case takes a bare verb, and there is no noun-phrase version of it — ✗ jurisdiction to the case. The word is also a countable noun meaning a place (forty-two jurisdictions have adopted the rule), and in that sense it takes no preposition at all.
entries.see also: authority on/over, control over/of, custody of, injunction against, applicability to, over

entries.meaning: An argument that something was right or necessary.
examples: There's no justification for charging tenants for a repair the landlord caused.
The memo offers three justifications for the reorganization and believes none of them.
What was the justification for holding the vote without notice?
He fired her without justification and the arbitrator said so.
The only justification for keeping the second office is the lease.
In justification of the decision, the chair cited a rule that does not exist.
entries.русский: оправдание чего-л., обоснование правильности или необходимости
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (no justification for raising the fee) — the edited frame. A to-infinitive occurs (no justification to raise the fee) and is common in speech and business writing, but for + -ing is the form that never draws a mark. A bare that-clause attaches to the noun as well: the justification that the roof was leaking.
entries.pattern: justification for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · no justification for [noun phrase] · offer / provide / demand a justification · in justification of [an act] (formal) · without justification
entries.the verb takes a gerund and refuses the: nothing justifies raising the fee, ✗ nothing justifies to raise the fee — a harder rule than the noun's, and the reason writers who get the verb right still stumble on the noun. Against reason for: a reason explains why something happened, a justification argues that it was right — which is why the reason for the delay is neutral and the justification for the delay implies somebody is being blamed. ✗ justification of the fee increase means the act of justifying it, not the argument.
entries.see also: reason for, grounds for, basis for, rationale for, excuse for, for

entries.meaning: The thing that makes something possible or explains it.
examples: The key to getting a permit here is starting in January.
Patience is the key to not ruining a brisket.
The county clerk holds the key to the whole dispute.
The key to the back gate is under the third flowerpot.
Consistent watering is the key to keeping tomatoes from splitting.
Nobody has found the key to why the ledgers stop in 1913.
entries.русский: ключ к — то, что даёт разгадку или делает что-л. возможным
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the key to solving it) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the key to solve it). This is one of the most frequently botched -ing patterns in American business and self-help writing.
entries.pattern: the key to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a key to [lock / door] · hold the key to [noun phrase] · the key to success · key [adjective] to [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Because a noun fits the slot — the key to the door, the key to success — the to is a preposition, and a verb after it must take -ing: the key to getting funded, ✗ the key to get funded. The adjective key uses the same preposition and is likewise fixed: a factor key to the outcome, ✗ key for the outcome in that sense, though key for our purposes is fine. ✗ the key of success is an error; the key of C is music, a different noun. Compare solution to and answer to, which share the preposition and the trap.
entries.see also: solution to, answer to, reason for, access to, to

entries.meaning: Facts, information, and skills a person has.
examples: She has a working knowledge of Portuguese and fluent Spanish.
His knowledge of the building's wiring saved us three days.
The lease was signed without my knowledge.
To the best of my knowledge, nobody has lived there since 2011.
Knowledge about the outbreak spread faster than the outbreak.
Knowledge that the tank was leaking would have changed the sale.
entries.русский: знание чего-л., знания о чём-л. — в англ. неисчисляемо
entries.complement: of: noun phrase, gerund (knowledge of having been passed over), or wh-clause (no knowledge of what the account was for) — never a to-infinitive. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: knowledge that the tank was leaking.
entries.pattern: knowledge of [subject] · knowledge about [subject] · knowledge that [clause] · a working knowledge of [skill] · to the best of my knowledge · without someone's knowledge · common knowledge
entries.variants: knowledge of — the edited default · knowledge about — conversational, and normal when the subject is a person or an event rather than a skill
entries.contrast: Of is the form to write. ✗ knowledge on the subject is an error; ✗ knowledges does not exist in American English, which treats the noun as uncountable — say a body of knowledge, a working knowledge of Spanish, ✗ he has good knowledges. The one indefinite article that is allowed is in the pattern a working / thorough / detailed knowledge of X, where the adjective licenses it. Distinguish from awareness of (perception that something exists) and understanding of (grasp of how it works); knowledge is the possession of facts.
entries.see also: awareness of, understanding of, grasp of, information about/on, of

entries.meaning: The absence or shortage of something needed.
examples: The whole project failed for lack of a single accountable owner.
There's a real lack of affordable rentals within walking distance of the plant.
Her lack of interest in the job showed in the first ten minutes.
The case was dismissed for lack of evidence.
A lack of sleep will do more damage than a bad diet.
The estate was large and the children lacked for nothing.
entries.русский: отсутствие, нехватка чего-л. — рус. родительный (глагол lack идёт без of)
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a lack of planning, a lack of anyone taking responsibility) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a lack of to plan) and never a that-clause. The complement is normally uncountable or plural — a lack of funding, a lack of options — and a singular count noun needs a modifier to sit comfortably: a lack of a clear plan is fine where bare a lack of a plan is stiff and no plan is the plainer fix.
entries.pattern: a lack of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · for lack of [noun phrase] · through lack of [noun phrase] · a lack of [interest / evidence / sleep] · lacking in [quality]
entries.contrast: A star noun-versus-verb shift. The verb lack is bare transitive — the report lacks detail — so ✗ the report lacks of detail and ✗ he lacks of experience are errors, and they are extremely common among speakers of Romance languages, where the equivalent verb is prepositional. The noun cannot go without of: ✗ a lack detail. A third form completes the set: the adjective is lacking in (the argument is lacking in evidence), so all three words in the family take a different construction — verb bare, noun of, adjective in. Lack for survives only in the fixed litotes he lacked for nothing (he had everything he needed); outside it, ✗ the report lacks for detail is an error.
entries.see also: need for, supply of, lack something, demand for, lack, of

entries.meaning: A written message, named by who sent it and who gets it.
examples: She wrote a blistering letter to the editor about the sidewalk plan.
There was a letter from the county assessor waiting on the porch.
He needs three letters of recommendation by the fifteenth.
The letter to shareholders never mentioned the write-down.
I got a letter about the easement two years after the sale.
Her letter of resignation ran to a single sentence.
entries.русский: письмо кому-л. / от кого-л.
entries.complement: to: the recipient. from: the sender. of: the letter's function, in fixed compounds (a letter of resignation, a letter of recommendation, a letter of credit). about: the subject. Never a gerund, an infinitive, or a clause after to.
entries.pattern: a letter to [recipient] · a letter from [sender] · a letter of [resignation / recommendation] · a letter about [subject] · write a letter to [person] · a letter to the editor
entries.contrast: To and from are unmissable; the trap is the verb. American English allows write me with no preposition — write me when you get in — where British English requires write to me. Both write to her and write her are correct in the United States, but only write to her travels. ✗ a letter for the editor is an error where a letter for you (meaning addressed to you and now in my hand) is fine. The of compounds are fixed: ✗ a letter for resignation, ✗ a recommendation letter of her — say a letter of recommendation for her.
entries.see also: reply to, response to, request for, report on/of, to

entries.meaning: Legal responsibility for something, or the person or body one is responsible to.
examples: The waiver does not eliminate liability for gross negligence.
The company's liability to bondholders comes ahead of anything owed to shareholders.
Liability for failing to inspect the boiler fell on the management company.
He set up an LLC to keep personal liability away from the rental property.
The audit moved $4 million from assets to liabilities.
Their liability under the indemnity clause is capped at the purchase price.
entries.русский: юр. ответственность за что-л. перед кем-л.; также обязательство, пассив баланса
entries.register: legal, financial, and insurance; the "burden" sense is neutral and informal
entries.complement: for: the harm, debt, or act you can be made to answer for, as a noun phrase or gerund (liability for failing to inspect) — never a to-infinitive (✗ liability to inspect, which would mean something else entirely). to: the person or body you owe it to (liability to third parties). under: the instrument or statute it arises beneath. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: liability for [damages / negligence / the debt] · liability to [a claimant / creditors] · liability under [a statute / the contract] · limit / assume / disclaim / insure against liability · joint and several liability · a limited liability company · liabilities (the balance-sheet plural)
entries.the person: liability for the collapse names what happened, liability to the tenants names who can sue — and a single sentence often needs both, its liability to the tenants for the collapse. The adjective is the classic trap: liable for means responsible (liable for the damage), but liable to plus a verb means likely (liable to fall), and liable to plus a person means answerable to them. Note the accounting plural, which takes no preposition: assets and liabilities. In everyday American speech a liability with no complement means a burden — the third baseman is a liability.
entries.contrast: For the harm, to
entries.see also: responsibility for, damages for, obligation to/under, duty to/of, immunity from, waiver of

entries.meaning: A legal claim attached to a piece of property as security for a debt.
examples: The roofer filed a mechanic's lien on the house eleven days after the last invoice.
There's a tax lien against the property that predates their purchase.
The title came back with two liens on it and one of them was thirty years old.
A judgment lien attaches to any real estate he owns in the county.
The bank released its lien on the truck the week the note was paid.
Buyers want the parcel delivered free and clear of liens.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /lin ən/ · American /lin/ rhymes with lean; the older two-syllable /ˈliən/ survives in some courtrooms
entries.русский: юр. право удержания, залоговое обременение имущества в обеспечение долга
entries.register: legal — real-estate closings, contractor disputes, tax collection. An American meets it when a title search turns up a mechanic's lien, or when the IRS files one.
entries.complement: on / against: the property or fund encumbered, as a noun phrase — never a gerund, never an infinitive, and never a clause. for: what is owed (a lien for unpaid taxes). in favor of: who holds it.
entries.pattern: a lien on [property] · a lien against [property / an estate] · a lien for [unpaid work / taxes] · file / perfect / release / foreclose a lien · a mechanic's / tax / judgment lien · free and clear of liens
entries.variants: lien on and lien against are interchangeable in American practice; on is commoner in statutes and title reports, against in collection letters and in loose speech about a person (a lien against him really means against his property)
entries.contrast: The object is the property, not the debtor: strictly, ✗ a lien on the contractor is imprecise, because the lien attaches to the building. Against claim against/for/to: a claim is a demand for payment, a lien is a security interest that rides on a specific thing until the debt clears. A mortgage is one kind of consensual lien; a mechanic's lien is imposed by statute whether the owner agrees or not. ✗ a lien of the property is an error.
entries.see also: title to, claim against/for/to, easement over/across, default on/under, judgment against/for, on

entries.meaning: A boundary, natural or imposed.
examples: There's a limit to how many times I'll explain the same form.
The city put a limit on short-term rentals in the historic district.
The speed limit drops to twenty-five past the school.
That whole floor is off limits to visitors.
We're at the limit of what the old wiring can carry.
There seems to be no limit to what she'll volunteer for.
entries.русский: предел чего-л., ограничение на что-л. — естественная или установленная граница
entries.complement: to: what has a natural boundary (a limit to my patience). on: what is being restricted by rule (a limit on spending). Gerunds follow both (no limit to what she'll try, a limit on borrowing). Never a to-infinitive (✗ a limit to spend) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a limit to [thing with a natural end] · a limit on [activity restricted] · the limit of [range / property] · within limits · off limits · set / impose / exceed a limit
entries.contrast: To is a natural ceiling; on is an imposed rule. There's a limit to how much I'll take describes reality; a limit on how much you may withdraw describes policy. ✗ a limit to withdrawals in the policy sense is the usual slip. A third form, the limit of, names the extent of a thing (the limits of the property, the limits of my knowledge).
