Note off limits, an American military idiom that takes no complement, and the plural in the fixed within limits. The verb takes a direct object and to for the ceiling: limit contributions to $500, ✗ limit contributions on $500.
entries.see also: control over/of, exception to, rule against/for, room for, on

entries.meaning: A connection or association between two things.
examples: Researchers found no link between the additive and the tumors.
There's a documented link between childhood lead exposure and later reading scores.
The company denies any link to the offshore accounts.
The archive page has a link to the original filing.
He was the last link to the generation that built the place.
The report suggests a link with two earlier cases in Ohio.
entries.русский: связь между чем-л. / с чем-л.
entries.complement: between: two or more items joined by and (a link between diet and blood pressure). to / with: a single item. Gerunds follow both. Never a to-infinitive (✗ a link to reduce risk) and never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: a link between X and Y · a link to / with [noun phrase] · a link in the chain · establish / find / deny a link between X and Y · a link to [a web page]
entries.variants: link with — an association or partnership, slightly more British in feel · link to — the American default and the only form for hyperlinks
entries.requires two things and the others requi: ✗ a link between smoking is incomplete; ✗ a link to smoking and cancer should be between. In epidemiology and reporting, a link between X and Y is deliberately weaker than a cause of — see cause of — and confusing the two is the standard failure of science journalism. The verb takes both frames: link X to Y, link X with Y, and ✗ link between X and Y is not available to the verb.
entries.contrast: Between
entries.see also: connection with/to/between, relationship with/between, cause of, similarity to/between, between

entries.meaning: Deep affection for a person, or strong enthusiasm for a pursuit.
examples: Her love for her students outlasted three principals.
A love of early jazz recordings runs through everything he wrote.
He married her for love, whatever the family said.
It was a labor of love and it took eleven years.
For the love of God, close the gate.
She fell in love with the house before she saw the roof.
entries.русский: любовь к — к человеку или к своему делу; рус. «к», не «для»
entries.complement: for: a person, or a thing regarded with warmth (her love for her students). of: an activity, art, or abstraction (a love of music, a love of arguing) — gerunds go here, never after for in edited prose. Never a to-infinitive (✗ a love to sing). In love with takes a person.
entries.pattern: love for [person] · love of [activity / art] · in love with [person] · for the love of [noun phrase] · a labor of love · fall in love with [person]
entries.variants: love for and love of overlap heavily with things (a love for jazz and a love of jazz are both fine); the split holds firmly only with people, where for is required
entries.contrast: For points at a person, of at a pursuit — his love for his sister is affection, while his love of his sister reads as connoisseurship, which is why the swap misfires. With activities, of is the safer choice, and it is close to obligatory before a gerund: a love of cooking, where a love for cooking is heard but marked. ✗ love to as a noun is an error, although the verb takes it freely (I'd love to). The adjective phrase is in love with, never ✗ in love to or ✗ in love of, and fall in love with is fixed.
entries.see also: fondness for, taste for/in, respect for, desire for, for

entries.meaning: The union of two people, named by who married whom.
examples: Her marriage to Tom lasted longer than either family expected.
This is his second marriage, and her first.
The marriage between the two families ended a forty-year feud over water.
He's my uncle by marriage, not by blood.
It was a marriage of convenience that turned out surprisingly well.
The book's subject is the marriage of engineering and design at Bell Labs.
entries.русский: брак с кем-л., женитьба на — рус. «с/на», англ. to (✗ marriage with)
entries.complement: to: the spouse (her marriage to Tom). between: both parties from outside (a marriage between cousins). Never a gerund, never an infinitive, never a clause. ✗ marriage with is not standard American English in the personal sense, though it survives in figurative use (a marriage of convenience, a marriage with industry).
entries.pattern: a marriage to [spouse] · a marriage between X and Y · by marriage · a marriage of convenience · the marriage of X and Y (figurative)
entries.contrast: One of the sharpest verb-to-noun shifts in English, and the source of a famous error. The verb marry is bare transitive — she married Tom, ✗ she married with Tom, ✗ she married to Tom — while the past-participial adjective takes to: she is married to Tom, ✗ married with Tom. The noun takes to as well: her marriage to Tom. So the sequence is: marry Ø, married to, marriage to. ✗ married with is the single most recognizable Spanish, Italian, and Portuguese transfer error in English, and married with children is correct only because with there means "having."
entries.see also: relationship with/between, marry someone, connection with/to/between, love for/of, married to, to

entries.meaning: Whatever is wrong with something, and other fixed uses of the word.
examples: What's the matter with the printer this time?
There's something the matter with the left rear tire.
Getting the permit is just a matter of waiting out the clerk.
Whether to prosecute is a matter for the district attorney.
As a matter of fact, I have the receipt right here.
We're going, no matter what the forecast says.
entries.русский: что не так с чем-л. — только в вопросах и отрицаниях: What's the matter with the car?
entries.complement: with + noun phrase, in the fixed interrogative frame what's the matter with X? — never a gerund, an infinitive, or a clause. The unrelated a matter of takes a noun or a gerund (a matter of waiting), and a matter for takes the party responsible (a matter for the police).
entries.pattern: what's the matter with [noun phrase] · there's something the matter with [noun phrase] · a matter of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a matter for [party] · as a matter of fact · no matter what / who / how
entries.contrast: With belongs only to the "what's wrong" frame. What's the matter with the car? asks what is broken; a matter of money means an issue of money; a matter for the courts means the courts' business — and ✗ what's the matter of the car mixes two idioms. The word takes no article in no matter what, and the fixed as a matter of fact has no complement. Note that in the "trouble" sense matter is almost always preceded by the and appears in questions and negatives, not in plain assertions: ✗ there is a matter with the car is not idiomatic; say there's something wrong with the car.
entries.see also: problem with, trouble with, difficulty with/in, point in/of, with

entries.meaning: A recollection, or the faculty that produces one.
examples: My clearest memory of that summer is the smell of creosote.
She has an uncanny memory for names and none at all for faces.
The bench was placed there in memory of a teacher who drowned in 1962.
He recited all forty lines from memory.
The flood of '72 is still within living memory in this town.
A memory of standing in the driveway waiting for headlights is all he has left.
entries.русский: память о, воспоминание о чём-л.; также память как способность
entries.complement: of: what is remembered — noun phrase or gerund (a memory of standing in the driveway) — never a to-infinitive. for: the faculty, what a person is good at remembering (a memory for names). The noun also takes a bare that-clause in formal use: a clear memory that the door was locked.
entries.pattern: a memory of [thing remembered / verb-ing] · a memory for [names / faces / dates] · in memory of [person] · from memory · within living memory · jog someone's memory
entries.contrast: Of is what you remember; for is what you are good at remembering. A memory of faces is a recollection; a memory for faces is a talent — a total reversal from one preposition, and the pair is worth memorizing. ✗ a memory about is an error, and ✗ in memory to should be in memory of. Distinguish from memory (without notes) from in memory (as a memorial). The verb remember takes a direct object with no preposition (✗ remember of it, ✗ remember about it, though remind someone of it is correct).
entries.see also: awareness of, knowledge of/about, understanding of, idea of/for, of

entries.meaning: An official, temporary halt to an activity.
examples: The county put a six-month moratorium on new short-term rental permits.
Congress extended the moratorium on evictions twice and then let it lapse.
There's been a de facto moratorium on hiring since the freeze in March.
The board lifted the moratorium on drilling in the watershed last fall.
A moratorium on issuing bonds would strand three projects mid-build.
Nothing in the ordinance says when the moratorium ends.
entries.русский: мораторий на — временный официальный запрет на какую-л. деятельность
entries.register: formal to neutral — government, finance, and journalism
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (a moratorium on issuing new permits) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a moratorium to issue new permits) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a moratorium on [an activity] · impose / declare / extend / lift a moratorium · a temporary / one-year / de facto moratorium · under a moratorium
entries.variants: the plural is moratoriums in American English and moratoria in stiffer or older prose; both are correct, and moratoriums is the safer choice outside a law review
entries.contrast: ✗ A moratorium of and ✗ a moratorium against are errors: the noun takes on and nothing else. Against embargo on: a moratorium is a pause, expected to end; an embargo is a ban with a political purpose. Against prohibition on/against: a prohibition is permanent until repealed. Against injunction against: an injunction comes from a court and names parties, a moratorium comes from a legislature or an agency and applies to everyone.
entries.see also: embargo on, prohibition on/against, injunction against, limit to/on, delay in, on

entries.meaning: A requirement for something, and the act it calls for.
examples: There's a documented need for another elementary school on the north side.
No need to apologize — the mail does that to everybody.
The whole porch is in need of rebuilding.
The grant is meant to meet a need for rural broadband.
There's no need for alarm; the readings are within range.
I'll drive, if need be.
entries.русский: потребность в чём-л., нужда в — рус. «в», не «для»
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase naming what is needed (a need for more housing). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: no need to worry. ✗ a need of survives only in the fixed in need of. ✗ a need for to worry mixes the two.
entries.pattern: a need for [noun phrase] · no need to [verb] · in need of [noun phrase] · meet / address a need for [noun phrase] · if need be · there's no need for [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: For takes a thing; to takes an act; of appears only after in need. A need for an inspection names the thing wanted, a need to inspect names the act, and the house is in need of an inspection is the fixed adjectival phrase — ✗ the house is in need for an inspection. There is need of is stiff but not wrong; American writing prefers there is a need for. The verb takes an object or an infinitive and never a preposition: we need an inspection, we need to inspect it, ✗ we need for an inspection (except in the dialectal need for you to sign, common in the American South).
entries.see also: demand for, lack of, desire for, request for, for

entries.meaning: A formal communication of a fact, given to someone entitled to know it.
examples: The landlord served a notice of termination on the first of the month.
Notice to the guarantor has to be sent by certified mail.
She filed a notice of appeal one day inside the deadline.
The lease requires sixty days' notice before any rent increase.
The company put the vendor on notice that the account was under review.
The board gave notice of the special meeting by email, which the bylaws do not allow.
entries.русский: юр. уведомление о чём-л., направленное кому-л.; также предупреждение об увольнении
entries.register: legal in the of/to frames — pleadings, leases, employment letters; neutral in take notice of and give notice
entries.complement: of: the subject of the notice, as a noun phrase or gerund (notice of intending to appeal is stiff; notice of intent to appeal is the idiom). to: the recipient. that: a bare that-clause (notice that the lease will not be renewed). to + bare infinitive in fixed legal phrases: notice to quit, notice to appear. Never notice about in the legal sense.
entries.pattern: notice of [default / appeal / termination / a meeting] · notice to [a party] · notice that [clause] · give / serve / receive / waive notice · on notice · without notice · thirty days' notice · take notice of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Of names the subject and to names the recipient, and a single document carries both: notice to the tenant of default. ✗ notice about the default is an error in a legal document, though it is fine in conversation. Watch the possessive in periods of time: thirty days' notice takes an apostrophe, and ✗ thirty days notice is a common slip. Note on notice, which means warned, and the everyday verb notice, which takes a bare object and no preposition at all: she noticed the leak, ✗ she noticed of the leak.
entries.see also: amendment to, default on/under, obligation to/under, waiver of, attention to, of

entries.meaning: A stated reason for disapproving of something.
examples: Her only objection to the plan was the cost of the sidewalk.
I have no objection to working weekends if the schedule is posted in advance.
The neighbors raised an objection to rezoning the corner lot.
Objections to being recorded should be noted for the minutes.
The judge overruled the objection and let the answer stand.
There were three written objections to the easement.
entries.русский: возражение против — рус. «против», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (an objection to being recorded) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an objection to be recorded, ✗ no objection to sign). The noun also takes a bare that-clause in formal and legal use: an objection that the question assumes facts not in evidence.
entries.pattern: an objection to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · have no objection to [verb-ing] · raise / overrule / sustain an objection · an objection on the grounds that [clause] · objections from [party]
entries.contrast: A prime -ing trap, and the test is easy: a noun fits the slot (an objection to the fee), so the to is a preposition and any verb after it takes -ing. ✗ I have no objection to pay should be to paying; ✗ her objection to be filmed should be to being filmed. ✗ an objection against is an error, and an objection about is heard but marked. The verb keeps the same preposition and the same trap: object to being asked, ✗ object to be asked, and ✗ object something is not English.
entries.see also: opposition to, resistance to, complaint about, disagreement with/about, exception to, object to, to

entries.meaning: Something a person is bound to do, and the instrument or relationship that binds them.
examples: The company has no obligation to renew the contract and has said so.
Her obligations under the settlement end when the last payment clears.
He feels an obligation to the people who hired him in 1994.
There's a statutory obligation to report a spill within twenty-four hours.
You can cancel in thirty days with no obligation to buy anything.
Nothing in the letter creates an obligation under the master agreement.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌɑbləˈɡeɪʃən tə/; under has no weak form
entries.русский: обязательство перед кем-л. / по договору, обязанность
entries.register: neutral to formal; the under frame is legal drafting
entries.complement: to: either a person or body owed (an obligation to his creditors) or a bare infinitive naming the act required (an obligation to disclose). Never a gerund after to (✗ an obligation to disclosing). under: the agreement, statute, or section the duty arises beneath. of: whose obligation it is. Never a that-clause.
entries.pattern: an obligation to [person] · an obligation to [verb] · obligations under [a contract / the statute] · meet / discharge / breach an obligation · be under an obligation to [verb] · without obligation
entries.contrast: The two to's, again, and the noun-slot test settles them: an obligation to the bank takes a noun, an obligation to repay takes a bare verb. Against duty to/of: obligations are typically created by agreement and duties by role, which is why a contract lists obligations and a fiduciary owes duties — but the grammar is identical and the two words are swapped freely in ordinary writing. ✗ an obligation for paying is an error; the obligation of paying is possible but stilted. Note the American sales phrase with no obligation to buy, where the infinitive frame is doing the work.
entries.see also: duty to/of, responsibility for, liability for/to, commitment to, entitlement to, hereunder

entries.meaning: Something that stands in the way of progress.
examples: The biggest obstacle to getting the permit is the parking study.
Financing turned out to be the only real obstacle to the sale.
Her age was treated as an obstacle to promotion, which was the whole problem.
Striking that one clause removed every obstacle to signing.
The court called the waiting period a substantial obstacle to access.
Language was never an obstacle between the two of them.
entries.русский: препятствие для чего-л., помеха чему-л. — рус. «для», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (an obstacle to finishing on time) — never a to-infinitive (✗ an obstacle to finish on time) and never a that-clause; a wh-clause is fine after the preposition (an obstacle to what the district is trying to do). A noun fits the slot (an obstacle to peace), which is what makes the to a preposition and forces the -ing.
entries.pattern: an obstacle to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · the main / chief / biggest obstacle to · pose / present / remove / clear an obstacle · an obstacle in [someone's] path
entries.variants: a barrier to · an impediment to · a hurdle to — all three take the same preposition and the same -ing rule
entries.contrast: To is the only preposition here — ✗ an obstacle of finishing, ✗ an obstacle against the deal, ✗ an obstacle for finishing. The near-synonyms behave identically, so the rule generalizes: a barrier to entry, an impediment to recovery, and ✗ a barrier to enter the market is the same mistake one word over. The one legitimate for frame takes a person and names who is blocked rather than what is blocked: an obstacle for first-time buyers. Compare difficulty with/in, where American English drops the preposition before the gerund altogether (difficulty finishing), and limit to/on, which marks a ceiling rather than a blockage.
entries.see also: difficulty with/in, problem with, limit to/on, solution to, to

entries.meaning: The burden of doing or proving something, and who carries it.
examples: The onus is on the state to prove every element beyond a reasonable doubt.
Putting the onus on tenants to document mold is how the ordinance fails.
After the fumble the onus was on the defense.
The onus of proof shifts once the plaintiff makes out a prima facie case.
The onus is on the seller to disclose a known defect in this state.
Nobody wants the onus and everybody has an opinion.
entries.русский: бремя доказывания на ком-л. — the onus is on you: доказывать придётся тебе
entries.register: formal to neutral; common in editorials, court opinions, and sports commentary, rare in casual speech
entries.complement: on: the person or body who bears the burden, as a noun phrase, usually followed by a to-infinitive saying what they must do (the onus is on the state to prove it). of: the burden itself (the onus of proof). Never a gerund (✗ the onus on proving it) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: the onus is on [someone] · the onus is on [someone] to [verb] · put / place / shift the onus on [someone] · the onus of [proof / responsibility] · the onus falls on [someone]
entries.contrast: The noun is nearly frozen in one frame. The onus is on you is idiomatic; ✗ you have the onus and ✗ the onus to you are not. Onus of names the burden (the onus of proof) and onus on names the bearer, and mixing them gives ✗ the onus on proof. The word is a mass noun with no plural: ✗ two onuses. It is Latin for "burden," and it lives in English only in this frame, alongside the fuller legal phrase burden of proof — see responsibility for for the ordinary word.
entries.see also: responsibility for, duty to/of, obligation to/under, liability for/to, presumption of/against, on

entries.meaning: A view held about an issue, or an estimate of someone's worth.
examples: What's your opinion on the proposed levy?
He has an unaccountably high opinion of his own singing.
In my opinion, the second draft was the better one.
The county attorney issued a formal opinion on the setback rule.
Public opinion about the closure shifted after the first winter.
Whether it counts as art is a matter of opinion.
entries.русский: мнение о чём-л.; of — ещё и оценка чьих-л. качеств
entries.complement: on / about: an issue — noun phrase, gerund (an opinion on raising the levy), or wh-clause (an opinion on what to do). of: a person or thing being evaluated (a low opinion of him). The noun also takes a bare that-clause: the opinion that the levy is regressive. Never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: an opinion on / about [issue] · an opinion of [person / thing] · the opinion that [clause] · in my opinion · a matter of opinion · a second opinion · public opinion on [issue]
entries.variants: opinion on — an issue formally at stake, and the form in a legal opinion on · opinion about — the conversational default · opinion of — an estimate of worth, not a position
entries.contrast: On is a position; of is a verdict on someone's quality. Her opinion on the mayor's budget is what she thinks should happen; her opinion of the mayor is what she thinks of him as a person — and they can be opposite. ✗ my opinion for the plan is an error. The fixed hedge is in my opinion, never ✗ according to my opinion, ✗ by my opinion, or ✗ to my opinion — all three are frequent transfer errors. According to takes a source other than yourself (according to the auditor), which is why according to me sounds absurd.
entries.see also: view on/of, attitude to/toward, comment on, advice on/about, on

entries.meaning: Resistance to a plan, policy, or person.
examples: Opposition to the pipeline came from both ends of the county.
There was surprisingly little opposition to closing the pool.
She resigned in opposition to the new testing policy.
The bill faces organized opposition to raising the assessment cap.
Opposition to the war cost him his seat in 1968.
The measure passed with only token opposition.
entries.русский: сопротивление чему-л., противодействие; несогласие с планом или человеком
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (opposition to raising taxes) — never a to-infinitive (✗ opposition to raise taxes) and never a clause. In the political sense the noun stands alone with the definite article: the opposition.
entries.pattern: opposition to [noun phrase / verb-ing] · in opposition to [noun phrase] · face / meet / drop opposition to [noun phrase] · organized opposition to [noun phrase] · the opposition (a party)
entries.contrast: The -ing rule is the entire difficulty: ✗ opposition to raise the levy is the error, opposition to raising the levy the fix, and the noun test settles it (opposition to the levy). ✗ opposition against is a redundancy, though it appears in translated prose. In opposition to is a fixed connector meaning "contrary to" and behaves like a complex preposition — see as opposed to for its close relative. The verb takes a direct object with no preposition: they opposed the levy, ✗ they opposed to the levy — an error made especially often by people who know the noun well.
entries.see also: objection to, resistance to, argument with/about, disagreement with/about, contrast to/with, opposed to, to

entries.meaning: A request for goods, a command, or a sequence.
examples: We placed an order for two hundred replacement filters in March.
The crew received orders to evacuate the platform by dawn.
That's the third order from the same address this week.
He put in an order of onion rings for the table.
The names are listed in order of seniority.
The second elevator has been out of order since Thanksgiving.
entries.русский: заказ на что-л.; отдельно — приказ (order to) и порядок, последовательность
entries.complement: for: goods or services requested (an order for fifty units). to + bare infinitive: a command (orders to evacuate). from: the customer or the source. of: a quantity or a sequence (an order of magnitude, the order of the names). ✗ an order for to evacuate.
entries.pattern: an order for [goods] · an order to [verb] · an order from [customer / authority] · place / fill / cancel an order for [noun phrase] · in order to [verb] · out of order · an order of [food]
entries.contrast: Commercial for, military to, and a pile of fixed phrases. An order for ammunition is a purchase; an order to withdraw is a command; ✗ an order for withdrawing mixes them. In order to is a purpose connector, not this noun at all (see in order to), and out of order means broken or procedurally improper. Note the American restaurant use: an order of fries is a portion, where British English says a portion of chips. The verb takes a person plus an infinitive (ordered him to leave, ✗ ordered that he leaves — the subjunctive is ordered that he leave) and a bare object for goods (ordered fifty units).
entries.see also: request for, demand for, permission for, rule against/for, for

entries.meaning: Someone who takes part in an agreement, a lawsuit, or a scheme.
examples: Both parties to the lease have to initial every change.
The United States is not a party to that convention.
She was never a party to the suit and was deposed anyway.
He refuses to be a party to anything that ends up in front of a grand jury.
The parties to the settlement agreed to keep the amount confidential.
A third party to the negotiation leaked the draft on Friday.
entries.русский: юр. сторона договора, участник разбирательства или сговора
entries.register: legal — contracts, pleadings, treaties; also ordinary formal English in be a party to something disreputable
entries.complement: a noun phrase naming an agreement, a proceeding, or a scheme — never a gerund (✗ a party to concealing it is heard but ✗ in edited prose; write a party to the concealment), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a party to [a contract / a suit / a treaty] · the parties to [an agreement] · be / become / remain a party to [noun phrase] · a third party · an interested party · a party of six (the restaurant sense)
entries.contrast: ✗ A party of the contract is the error; the noun takes to and only to, and it appears in the opening line of nearly every American agreement (the parties to this Agreement). Keep the other nouns separate: a party of six is a table at a restaurant, a party is the event, and the party is a political organization — none of them takes to. Note the moral use, which is common in journalism: he was a party to the cover-up means he took part in it, and it does not require a signature. Against signatory to: every signatory is a party, but a party may be bound without signing.
entries.see also: signatory to, beneficiary of/under, claim against/for/to, exhibit to/schedule to/annex to, agreement with/on, to

entries.meaning: The punishment attached to an offense, and the offense that draws it.
examples: The penalty for filing after April 15 compounds monthly.
There's a stiff penalty for early withdrawal from that certificate.
The court imposed a penalty of $2,500 and a year of probation.
I declare under penalty of perjury that the foregoing is true.
A holding penalty against the left tackle wiped out the touchdown.
The loan has no prepayment penalty, which is worth reading the note for.
entries.русский: наказание, штраф за что-л. — рус. «за», не «для»
entries.register: neutral; legal in under penalty of, and a fixed term in American sports
entries.complement: for: the offense, as a noun phrase or gerund (a penalty for filing late) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a penalty to file late) and never a clause. of: the punishment itself (a penalty of $500, the penalty of death). against / on: the team or player, in sports.
entries.pattern: a penalty for [an offense / verb-ing] · a penalty of [an amount] · under penalty of perjury · impose / assess / waive / pay a penalty · a penalty against [a team] · the death penalty · a prepayment penalty
entries.contrast: For the offense, of the punishment, and they stack: a penalty of $500 for filing late. ✗ a penalty for $500 reverses them and is a common slip in letters to the IRS. Against damages for: a penalty punishes, damages compensate — a contract clause that sets a number too high to be compensation is void as a penalty and enforceable as liquidated damages, which is the whole fight. In American football the penalty is against a team and on a player, and the penalty for the foul is the yardage. Note under penalty of perjury, the fixed formula at the bottom of a federal form.
entries.see also: damages for, tax on, sanction against/sanctions on, prohibition on/against, liability for/to, for

entries.meaning: Consent to do something.
examples: We never got permission for the second dumpster.
She has permission to leave early on Thursdays.
You'll need written permission from the property owner.
The photograph is reproduced with the permission of the estate.
He took the truck without permission.
Permission for the field trip has to be back by Friday.
entries.русский: разрешение на что-л. — рус. «на»; ср. permission to + инф. — разрешение сделать
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase naming the thing permitted (permission for the field trip). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: permission to leave early. ✗ permission of doing and ✗ permission for to leave are errors. from names the person granting it.
entries.pattern: permission for [noun phrase] · permission to [verb] · permission from [authority] · with the permission of [person] · ask for / grant / deny permission · without permission
entries.contrast: For takes a thing; to takes an act; of appears only in with the permission of. Permission for the recording is consent for a thing; permission to record is consent for an act — and ✗ permission of recording is wrong in both senses. ✗ permission of the teacher is an error where permission from the teacher is correct, though with the permission of the teacher is the fixed formal frame. The noun is uncountable: ✗ a permission, ✗ permissions in the general sense, although the plural is standard in computing (file permissions).
entries.see also: access to, invitation to, request for, authority on/over, for

entries.meaning: An intended course of action, and what it concerns.
examples: Do you have any plans for the long weekend?
The county has a plan for the old rail corridor that nobody likes.
There's a plan to sell the building and lease back two floors.
We need a plan of action before Tuesday's hearing.
Everything went according to plan until the fourth inning.
Her plans for retirement changed twice in one year.
entries.русский: план чего-л., планы на что-л. — намеченный курс действий
entries.complement: for: a noun phrase naming the occasion or object (a plan for the weekend, plans for the building). The same noun takes a to-infinitive with no preposition: a plan to sell the building. of appears in the fixed a plan of action, a plan of attack. ✗ a plan for to sell and ✗ a plan about are errors.
entries.pattern: a plan for [occasion / object] · a plan to [verb] · plans for [the future] · a plan of action · make plans for [noun phrase] · according to plan · a floor plan of [building]
entries.contrast: For takes a thing or a time; to takes an act. A plan for the renovation names what the plan concerns; a plan to renovate names what will be done — and ✗ a plan for renovate mixes them. Note that plans for the weekend means arrangements, while a plan of the weekend would be a diagram. The verb takes both an infinitive and on + -ing, and the on frame is the one that trips people: we plan to leave at six and we're planning on leaving at six are both American, but ✗ we plan on leave and ✗ we plan to leaving are not.
entries.see also: idea of/for, reason for, solution to, approach to, for

entries.meaning: Enjoyment, and the thing enjoyed.
examples: He takes obvious pleasure in telling people the office is closed.
The pleasure of your company is requested at seven o'clock.
It's a pleasure to finally put a face to the emails.
She reads maps for pleasure, which explains a lot about our vacations.
There's real pleasure in watching somebody who is very good at a small job.
I'd help you with pleasure, but I'll be in Denver.
entries.русский: удовольствие от чего-л., радость от — рус. «от», не «в»
entries.complement: in + gerund: what someone enjoys doing (takes pleasure in correcting people) — never a to-infinitive after in (✗ pleasure in to correct). of + noun phrase: the thing enjoyed, in fixed formal frames (the pleasure of your company). The noun separately takes a to-infinitive with no preposition in the greeting formula it's a pleasure to meet you.
entries.pattern: take pleasure in [verb-ing] · the pleasure of [noun phrase] · it is a pleasure to [verb] · with pleasure · at [someone's] pleasure · for pleasure
entries.contrast: Three frames that cannot be swapped. Pleasure in doing it is the enjoyment taken from an activity; the pleasure of your company is a formal noun frame from invitations; a pleasure to meet you is the greeting formula. ✗ the pleasure to your company and ✗ I take pleasure of correcting you are both errors. Note the register: take pleasure in usually carries a faint disapproval in American English (he takes pleasure in saying no), while it's a pleasure to is warm. The archaic at your pleasure (whenever you like) survives in legal and ceremonial writing.
entries.see also: interest in, fondness for, point in/of, taste for/in, in

entries.meaning: The purpose or use of doing something, or an item in an argument.
examples: There's no point in arguing with the parking division.
What's the point of a smoke detector nobody replaces the battery in?
No point waiting — the last bus left at nine.
She made a good point about the cost of the surveys.
The whole point of the exercise was to see who would speak up.
That he showed up at all is a point in his favor.
entries.русский: смысл делать что-л. (no point in waiting); также пункт, тезис в рассуждении
entries.complement: in / of + gerund: the purpose or use of an activity (no point in arguing, what's the point of arguing) — never a to-infinitive (✗ no point to argue). In American English the preposition can be dropped entirely: no point arguing. about: the topic of a remark (a point about the deadline).
entries.pattern: there's no point in [verb-ing] · what's the point of [verb-ing] · no point [verb-ing] · a point about [topic] · the point of [thing] · make / take / miss the point · a point in someone's favor
entries.variants: no point in doing, no point of doing, and bare no point doing — all three are current American English; in is the most usual in writing, and dropping the preposition is the most usual in speech
entries.and never an infinitive: ✗ there's no point to complain, ✗ what's the point to wait. Write no point in complaining, what's the point of waiting. The separate frame the point of the exercise takes a noun and is fine. Do not confuse this with the verb point to (indicate: the evidence points to arson) or point at (gesture toward), which are unrelated. A point about introduces the subject of a remark, and a point in her favor is a fixed idiom of credit.
entries.contrast: In or of plus -ing,
entries.see also: reason for, importance of/to, pleasure in/of, matter with, in

entries.meaning: Physical control of a thing, whether or not you own it.
examples: He was arrested for possession of a firearm by a convicted felon.
The buyer takes possession of the house on the fifteenth.
The originals are in the possession of the county recorder.
She was in possession of a key she was not supposed to have.
The team lost possession three times in the fourth quarter.
Possession of the deed is not the same thing as title to the land.
entries.русский: обладание чем-л., фактическое владение — независимо от права собственности
entries.register: neutral; a term of art in criminal law and property law, and a fixed term in American sports
entries.complement: a noun phrase — never a gerund (✗ possession of holding the deed), never an infinitive, and never a clause.
entries.pattern: possession of [a thing] · in possession of [a thing] · take / gain / lose possession of [a thing] · in the possession of [a person] · vacant possession · possession of a controlled substance · possession is nine-tenths of the law
entries.run in opposite directions: she was in possession of the file says she had it; the file was in the possession of her lawyer says who had it — the article flips the perspective, and getting it backward produces a sentence that means the file owned the lawyer. ✗ possession over is an error, though control over/of does take over. Note the criminal-law senses that stack with no extra preposition: constructive possession, possession with intent to distribute. In basketball and football, possession takes of the ball and stands alone in first possession.
entries.contrast: In possession of and in the possession of
entries.see also: custody of, title to, control over/of, claim against/for/to, access to, of

entries.meaning: Something that might happen or might be done.
examples: We can't rule out the possibility of a second recall.
There's a real possibility of frost before the end of the month.
She raised the possibility that the invoice had been paid twice.
The possibility of working four ten-hour days is being studied.
No one considered the possibility of the pump simply being unplugged.
The possibility that the seal had failed was dismissed too quickly.
entries.русский: возможность чего-л., вероятность того, что нечто случится
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (the possibility of rain, the possibility of losing the contract) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the possibility to rain, ✗ the possibility to lose the contract). The noun also takes a bare that-clause: the possibility that the seal failed.
entries.pattern: the possibility of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · the possibility that [clause] · raise / rule out / consider the possibility of [verb-ing] · there is a possibility of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: Of + -ing or that + clause, never an infinitive. ✗ the possibility to work from home is one of the most common errors in professional English written by Germans, Dutch speakers, and Scandinavians, whose languages allow it. Write the possibility of working from home — or, more naturally, the option to work from home or the chance to work from home, since chance of and option do take the infinitive. ✗ possibility for is likewise wrong. The adjective possible takes an infinitive freely (it is possible to work from home), which is exactly why the noun feels as though it should.
entries.see also: chance of, risk of, danger of/to, hope for/of, of

entries.meaning: An earlier case or act that justifies doing the same thing again.
examples: There's no precedent for letting a board member vote by proxy.
Approving this variance sets a precedent for every corner lot on the street.
The ruling breaks with forty years of precedent in the Ninth Circuit.
She found one precedent for reopening a closed claim after five years.
The appointment was without precedent and drew two lawsuits.
Lower courts are bound by precedent whether or not they like it.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈprɛsədənt fɚ/ · the noun is PRESS-, not pruh-SEED-; the adjective precedent /prɪˈsidənt/ is a different word
entries.русский: прецедент для — более ранний случай, оправдывающий повторение
entries.register: neutral to formal; a term of art in American law, where precedent is what binds a lower court
entries.complement: for: what the precedent would support, as a noun phrase or gerund (a precedent for reopening the case) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a precedent to reopen the case) and never a clause. in: the jurisdiction or body of law (no precedent in this circuit).
entries.pattern: a precedent for [an act / verb-ing] · precedent in [a court / a field] · set / establish / follow / overrule / break with precedent · without precedent · binding / persuasive precedent · legal precedent (uncountable)
entries.contrast: The countability rule is split by sense. A precedent is countable when it means one earlier case or act (that would set a bad precedent); precedent is uncountable when it means the whole body of decided law (there is no precedent for this in the circuit). Watch the near-homographs: precedent the noun is PRESS-uh-dunt, and president is PREZ-uh-dunt — a spelling error that survives spellcheck. ✗ a precedent of is an error in this frame, and the precedent of Marbury means the case itself rather than what it supports.
entries.see also: example of, basis for, grounds for, judgment against/for, citation to, for

entries.meaning: A liking for one thing over another.
examples: She has a marked preference for older buildings with bad wiring.
The survey found a clear preference for evening appointments.
He chose the county road in preference to the interstate.
The scholarship gives preference to applicants from the district.
My preference for working alone is not a comment on the team.
State your preference for morning or afternoon on the form.
entries.русский: предпочтение чего-л., склонность к одному в ущерб другому
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (a preference for working alone) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a preference to work alone). The fixed comparative frame is in preference to + noun phrase.
entries.pattern: a preference for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · in preference to [noun phrase] · have / show / express a preference for [noun phrase] · give preference to [group] · a stated preference
entries.contrast: For names what you like better; to appears only in in preference to and give preference to. ✗ a preference to the older model is an error where a preference for the older model and chose the older model in preference to the new one are both correct. ✗ a preference of is wrong. The related verb takes yet another construction and is the real trap: prefer X to Y (✗ prefer X than Y), prefer to do it (infinitive), and prefer doing X to doing Y — so the verb takes to where the noun takes for.
entries.see also: fondness for, taste for/in, desire for, alternative to, prefer to, for

entries.meaning: An amount paid above a baseline, the payment on an insurance policy, or unusual value placed on something.
examples: The offer is a thirty percent premium over Friday's closing price.
Buyers are paying a premium over asking on anything with a garage.
The premium on the flood policy doubled after the map was redrawn.
He let the premium lapse and found out in the worst possible week.
The new manager puts a premium on showing up prepared.
A hospital that places a premium on speed will lose something else.

senses.head: The extra above a baseline price
body: The complement is over, above, or to, and the baseline is a market price, a book value, or a previous offer. The percentage comes in with of: a premium of 34 percent over Friday's close.
examples: The offer is a thirty percent premium over Friday's closing price.
Buyers are paying a premium over asking on anything with a garage.

senses.head: The periodic payment on an insurance policy
body: The complement is on, and the noun is countable.
examples: The premium on the flood policy doubled after the map was redrawn.
He let the premium lapse and found out in the worst possible week.

senses.head: High value placed on a quality
body: Only in the frame place / put a premium on, which takes a noun phrase or a gerund.
examples: The new manager puts a premium on showing up prepared.
A hospital that places a premium on speed will lose something else.

entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈprimiəm ən/; over has no weak form
entries.русский: over — надбавка сверх базовой цены; on — страховой взнос либо особая ценность
entries.register: finance and insurance; the place a premium on frame is general formal English
entries.complement: over / above / to: the baseline the price exceeds, as a noun phrase. on: the policy or the thing valued, as a noun phrase or gerund (a premium on getting there first). for: what the extra buys. Never an infinitive (✗ a premium to arrive first) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a premium over [a price / the market] · a premium on [a policy] · place / put a premium on [noun phrase / verb-ing] · pay a premium for [something] · at a premium · a premium of [a percentage]
entries.contrast: Over measures an excess, on names either a policy or a prized quality, and the two never swap: ✗ a premium on the market price is an error for the takeover sense, and ✗ the premium over my policy is an error for the insurance sense. At a premium means scarce and expensive and takes no complement (parking is at a premium). Note that premium also works as an adjective with no preposition at all — premium gas, a premium account — which is where American advertising has taken the word.
entries.see also: price of/for, return on, interest in, tax on, importance of/to, over

entries.meaning: A starting position that holds until someone proves otherwise.
examples: The presumption of innocence is not a rule of evidence but the whole frame.
There's a strong presumption against reading a statute to apply retroactively.
Courts apply a presumption of regularity to what an agency says it did.
The presumption that a mailed notice was received can be rebutted by testimony.
A seven-year absence raises a presumption of death in most states.
The board acted on the presumption that the grant would be renewed.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /prɪˈzʌmpʃən əv/ → /prɪˈzʌmpʃən ə/; against has no weak form
entries.русский: юр. презумпция чего-л. / против чего-л. — исходное допущение до опровержения
entries.register: legal and formal — jury instructions, statutory interpretation, editorial writing
entries.complement: of: what is assumed true until disproved, as a noun phrase (a presumption of innocence, a presumption of validity). against: what the law starts out disfavoring (a presumption against retroactivity). in favor of: the mirror image. The noun also takes a bare that-clause (the presumption that the letter was received). Never a to-infinitive.
entries.pattern: a presumption of [innocence / regularity / death] · a presumption against [a result] · a presumption in favor of [a party] · the presumption that [clause] · rebut / overcome / raise a presumption · on the presumption that [clause] · a rebuttable presumption
entries.contrast: Of is what you start by believing, against is what you start by doubting — and the same statute can carry both (a presumption of validity for the agency's rule, a presumption against applying it retroactively). ✗ a presumption to is an error. Do not confuse the word with presumptuousness: the presumption of innocence is a legal default, but the presumption of the man means his gall — a second, older sense that takes of as well and has ruined more than one sentence. Against idea of/for: an assumption is anything taken for granted; a presumption is one the law or the argument requires until rebutted.
entries.see also: onus on, probability of/likelihood of, evidence of/for, doubt about, judgment against/for, against

entries.meaning: What something costs, in a market or in a particular deal.
examples: The price of diesel went up eleven cents in a week.
He got a decent price for the truck considering the mileage.
The price of being early to a bad idea is that everyone remembers.
The units sold at a price of $340,000 apiece.
You can't put a price on a Saturday morning with nothing scheduled.
The price for the same procedure varies by a factor of six across the state.
entries.русский: цена чего-л. (на рынке) / за что-л. (в конкретной сделке)
entries.complement: of: what the item costs in general (the price of gas). for: an amount named in a particular transaction (a fair price for the truck). A gerund follows of in the figurative sense (the price of being right). Never a to-infinitive and never a clause.
entries.pattern: the price of [commodity] · a price for [item in a deal] · at a price of [amount] · the price of [verb-ing] (figurative) · put a price on [noun phrase] · at any price · price per [unit]
entries.contrast: Of is the market; for is the deal. The price of the truck is what trucks like that cost; a good price for the truck is what you and I agreed on. Neither is ungrammatical, but the price for gas is up reads oddly in a market report and what's the price of your truck reads oddly in a negotiation. Put a price on is fixed — ✗ put a price to. The figurative sense takes of + -ing: the price of being right about this is what it costs you socially.
entries.see also: supply of, demand for, tax on, importance of/to, of

entries.meaning: How probable something is.
examples: The probability of a hundred-year flood in any given year is one percent.
The likelihood of being audited on a return like this is very small.
What's the probability that both machines fail in the same week?
Insulating the attic reduces the likelihood of ice dams.
In all likelihood the case settles before anyone sees a jury.
He put the probability of success at about one in three and was optimistic.
entries.русский: вероятность чего-л. — насколько правдоподобно, что нечто случится
entries.register: probability is technical in statistics and neutral elsewhere; likelihood is neutral
entries.complement: of: a noun phrase or gerund (the probability of rain, the likelihood of being audited) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the probability to rain, ✗ the likelihood to be audited). Both also take a bare that-clause: the probability that the well is dry. Never probability for.
entries.pattern: the probability of [an event / verb-ing] · the likelihood of [an event / verb-ing] · the probability that [clause] · in all likelihood · a high / low / vanishing probability · increase / reduce the likelihood of [noun phrase]
entries.contrast: The adjectives take the infinitive and the nouns refuse it — this is the single highest-yield fact in the entry. It is likely to rain is correct; ✗ the likelihood to rain is not. Convert with of + -ing or with that: the likelihood of rain, the likelihood that it will rain. Against chance of, which splits by meaning: a chance of winning is a probability and a chance to win is an opportunity, so chance is the one noun in this family that does take an infinitive — with a different sense. ✗ the probability for rain and ✗ likelihood on are errors.
entries.see also: chance of, possibility of, risk of, incidence of/prevalence of, presumption of/against, of

entries.meaning: A fault, difficulty, or matter needing a solution.
examples: There's a problem with the wiring in the back bedroom.
The problem of deferred maintenance is not going away on its own.
I have a problem with being told after the fact.
That's a classic problem in elementary probability.
The problem is that nobody kept the original survey.
Two coats and it's fine — no problem.
entries.русский: проблема с чем-л., неполадка, затруднение — рус. «с», не «в»
entries.complement: with: the thing or person that is causing trouble (a problem with the wiring). of: the nature of the problem, formal (the problem of homelessness). in: a domain (a problem in logic). Gerunds follow with (a problem with getting parts); never a to-infinitive (✗ a problem to get parts) and never a that-clause in ordinary use.
entries.pattern: a problem with [thing / person] · the problem of [social issue] · a problem in [field] · have a problem with [noun phrase / verb-ing] · no problem · the problem is that [clause] · solve / cause a problem
entries.contrast: With for a specific fault, of for a category. A problem with the wiring is a fault to fix; the problem of rural broadband is a policy area. ✗ a problem about is an error, and ✗ a problem for the wiring means something else (whom it inconveniences). Note that the problem is that... takes a clause with no preposition — ✗ the problem is because... — the same fault treated under reason for. I have a problem with that is American idiom for disagreement, not for a malfunction.
entries.see also: trouble with, difficulty with/in, solution to, matter with, with

entries.meaning: Forward movement toward a goal or through a task.
examples: There's been real progress in reducing emergency room wait times.
What's the progress on the Fillmore Street repaving?
The district has made almost no progress toward its literacy goals.
Renovation is still in progress on the second floor.
The progress of the negotiations was reported daily and inaccurately.
Two years in, we've made some progress and no money.
entries.русский: прогресс в чём-л., продвижение в работе над — в англ. неисчисляемо
entries.complement: in: a field or general area, and gerunds (progress in reducing waste). on: a specific project or task (progress on the report). toward: a goal. Never a to-infinitive (✗ progress to reduce waste) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: progress in [field / verb-ing] · progress on [project] · progress toward [goal] · make progress · in progress · the progress of [disease / negotiation]
entries.variants: progress toward — American, no -s; progress towards is British
entries.contrast: In for a domain, on for a task, toward for a goal, and of for something unfolding. Progress in cancer research is a field advancing; progress on the grant application is one job moving; progress toward accreditation is a target approached; the progress of the disease is its course. ✗ progress for is an error. The noun is uncountable in this sense: ✗ a progress, ✗ progresses, ✗ many progresses — say some progress, a lot of progress, real progress. Note that progress the verb (pro-GRESS) stresses differently from the noun (PROG-ress).
entries.see also: improvement in/on, increase in/decrease in, success in/at, delay in, in

entries.meaning: A rule forbidding something.
examples: The ordinance imposes a prohibition on overnight parking from November to April.
The constitutional prohibition against ex post facto laws settled the question.
There's a blanket prohibition on accepting gifts from vendors.
The lease has a prohibition against subletting that nobody enforces.
A prohibition on selling flavored products took effect in three cities at once.
Prohibition closed the brewery in 1920 and the family never reopened it.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌproʊəˈbɪʃən ən/ · note the silent h: proh-uh-, not pro-hib-
entries.русский: запрет на что-л. — правило, запрещающее какое-л. действие
entries.register: neutral to formal — statutes, ordinances, policy writing
entries.complement: on / against: the act forbidden, as a noun phrase or gerund (a prohibition on selling alcohol before noon) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a prohibition to sell alcohol) and never a clause. of is possible and formal (the prohibition of torture).
entries.pattern: a prohibition on / against [an act / verb-ing] · the prohibition of [a practice] (formal) · impose / lift / enforce a prohibition · Prohibition (capitalized: the American era, 1920–1933) · a blanket prohibition
entries.variants: prohibition on and prohibition against are both standard American English and freely interchangeable; on is slightly commoner in ordinances, against in constitutional writing (the prohibition against cruel and unusual punishment)
entries.contrast: ✗ A prohibition to is the error, and it is the direct translation from several European languages. Against moratorium on: a moratorium pauses, a prohibition forbids indefinitely. Against injunction against: an injunction is a court order against named parties, a prohibition is a rule against everyone. Capitalized and bare, Prohibition is the American constitutional experiment of 1920–1933, and it takes no complement at all.
entries.see also: moratorium on, embargo on, injunction against, rule against/for, limit to/on, against

entries.meaning: Something that establishes a fact beyond doubt.
examples: Bring proof of residence and a photo ID.
There's no proof of forced entry, only a broken latch.
The receipt is your proof of purchase.
He wanted proof that the check had actually cleared.
The burden of proof is on the party seeking the injunction.
The paper gives two independent proofs of the same result.
entries.русский: доказательство чего-л., подтверждение — то, что устраняет сомнения
entries.complement: of: noun phrase or gerund (proof of having paid) — never a to-infinitive. The noun also takes a bare that-clause: proof that the check cleared. ✗ proof for is not standard in the evidentiary sense; use evidence of/for.
entries.pattern: proof of [noun phrase / verb-ing] · proof that [clause] · proof of purchase / address / insurance · the burden of proof · beyond proof · a proof of [theorem]
entries.the countability rule is split by domain: in ordinary use proof is uncountable, so ✗ two proofs that he paid and ✗ he offered several proofs are errors — the fixed compounds a proof of purchase and a proof of address are the one place an article turns up. In mathematics and printing the noun is fully countable (two proofs of the theorem, the galley proofs). Note the fixed proof of purchase, proof of address, and proof of insurance, which take no article.
entries.contrast: Of is the only preposition here. ✗ proof for the theory should be evidence for the theory, because proof in American usage claims certainty where evidence claims support — a difference worth keeping.
entries.see also: evidence of/for, guarantee of, example of, grounds for, of

entries.meaning: A defense against a threat, and who or what it covers.
examples: The awning offers some protection from the afternoon sun.
The policy provides protection against flood damage up to $250,000.
There's almost no legal protection for tenants in month-to-month leases.
The statute concerns the protection of archaeological sites.
Witnesses were placed under the protection of the marshals.
Two coats of sealer give real protection against freeze-thaw cracking.
entries.русский: защита от чего-л. — рус. «от», не «против»
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (protection against being sued) — never a to-infinitive (✗ protection to be sued) and never a clause. Protection for names who is protected; protection of names what is being kept safe.
entries.pattern: protection from / against [threat] · protection for [person protected] · the protection of [thing kept safe] · under the protection of [authority] · offer / provide protection against [threat]
entries.variants: protection from and protection against — both standard American English; from is commoner with immediate physical threats (protection from the rain), against with risks and adversaries (protection against fraud)
entries.contrast: Four prepositions, and only two of them are interchangeable. Protection from/against the wind names the threat; protection for the seedlings names who benefits; the protection of the wetlands names what is being conserved — and ✗ protection of the wind would mean the wind is what you are safeguarding. ✗ protection to is an error. The verb takes both prepositions of threat and a bare object: protect the seedlings from frost, ✗ protect from the seedlings.
entries.see also: danger of/to, threat to, risk of, cure for, protect from, protect against, against

entries.meaning: A comparison of two quantities, expressed as one number against another.
examples: The ratio of applicants to seats was almost nine to one.
Mix it in a ratio of three parts sand to one part cement.
The county's ratio of nurses to residents is the lowest in the state.
Their debt-to-equity ratio got worse every quarter for two years.
The ratio of signal to noise in the recording is hopeless.
A student-teacher ratio of thirty-two to one is not a class, it is a crowd.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈreɪʃoʊ əv/ → /ˈreɪʃoʊ ə/, /ˈreɪʃoʊ tə/ · American RAY-shoh; the older RAY-shee-oh /ˈreɪʃioʊ/ is heard in mathematics classrooms
entries.русский: соотношение чего-л. к чему-л., пропорция двух величин
entries.register: neutral; technical in finance, statistics, and engineering
entries.complement: two noun phrases, the first after of and the second after to — never a gerund, never an infinitive, and never a clause. The numbers themselves may fill the of ... to frame directly (a ratio of three to one).
entries.pattern: the ratio of X to Y · a ratio of [number] to [number] · in a ratio of 2:1 · a high / low ratio · the student-teacher ratio (compound, no preposition) · the debt-to-equity ratio
entries.contrast: Both halves are obligatory in the full frame: ✗ the ratio of doctors and patients is an error — and cannot replace to — and ✗ the ratio between doctors to patients mixes two frames. A ratio between X and Y does exist and is looser; the edited form for a computed figure is of ... to. Note that the compound forms hyphenate and drop the prepositions entirely (the debt-to-equity ratio, a 3-to-1 ratio, the student-teacher ratio), which is why writers forget the prepositions when they need them. Against in proportion to: a proportion is a part of a whole, a ratio compares two quantities that need not belong to the same whole.
entries.see also: in proportion to, correlation with/between, incidence of/prevalence of, share in/of, disparity between/in, to

entries.meaning: The reasoning offered for a decision or a practice.
examples: Nobody has explained the rationale for moving the deadline twice.
The rationale behind the merger was cost savings that never showed up.
The memo gives a two-sentence rationale for closing the branch.
What's the rationale for charging residents and not commuters?
The stated rationale and the actual reason were not the same thing.
Her rationale for keeping the old system is that the new one has never been tested.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˌræʃəˈnæl fɚ/ · four syllables, final stress; not RASH-un-ul, which is the adjective rational
entries.русский: обоснование чего-л., логика решения или практики
entries.register: neutral to formal — memos, opinions, grant applications
entries.complement: noun phrase or gerund (the rationale for closing the branch) — never a to-infinitive (✗ the rationale to close the branch) and never a clause; a that-clause needs a verb between (the rationale was that the branch lost money).
entries.pattern: the rationale for [a decision / verb-ing] · the rationale behind [a decision] · offer / explain / question the rationale · the stated rationale · the underlying rationale
entries.variants: rationale for and rationale behind are both standard American English; behind suggests a reason that was not stated openly, for the reason given. Rationale of occurs in older and stiffer prose and is now uncommon.
entries.contrast: Rationale is a noun and rational is an adjective, and they are not pronounced alike: rash-uh-NAL against RASH-un-ul. ✗ the rational for the decision is a spelling error that spellcheck will not catch. Against reason for: a reason can be a bare fact, a rationale is a worked-out justification — which is why an agency publishes the rationale for a rule and a person gives a reason for being late. Against justification for: a justification argues that the act was right, a rationale only explains the thinking.
entries.see also: reason for, justification for, basis for, grounds for, excuse for, for

entries.meaning: A response to something that has happened.
examples: Her reaction to the news was to reread the letter twice.
The doctor thinks it's an allergic reaction to the new detergent.
The whole style was a reaction against the ornament of the previous decade.
Public reaction to the closure was louder than anyone at the district expected.
In reaction to the audit, three managers took early retirement.
His reaction to being corrected in public was predictably awful.
entries.русский: реакция на — рус. «на», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (her reaction to being passed over) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a reaction to be passed over) and never a clause. Reaction against names a movement in opposition to something.
entries.pattern: a reaction to [event / substance] · a reaction against [trend / movement] · an allergic reaction to [substance] · in reaction to [event] · provoke / gauge a reaction
entries.contrast: To for a response, against for a backlash. A reaction to modernism is what people thought of it; a reaction against modernism is a movement rejecting it. ✗ a reaction on the news and ✗ a reaction about the news are errors, produced by borrowing from comment on and opinion on/of/about. The -ing rule holds: a noun fits the slot (a reaction to the news), so ✗ a reaction to be told should be to being told. The verb keeps the preposition — react to the news, ✗ react the news — and the chemistry sense adds with (sodium reacts with water).
entries.see also: response to, reply to, attitude to/toward, opposition to, react to, to

entries.meaning: The explanation for something, or a justification for doing it.
examples: Nobody has given us a reason for the delay.
The reason for leaving early was that the last ferry is at six.
That's the reason why she never puts anything in writing.
The reason that the deed was never filed is buried in a 1948 probate file.
There's every reason to believe the numbers will be revised.
The reason the road floods is that the culvert was sized for 1962.
The reason is that the county never accepted the dedication.
entries.русский: причина чего-л., основание для — reason why и reason that тоже норма
entries.complement: for: noun phrase or gerund (the reason for the delay, the reason for leaving early) — never a to-infinitive after for (✗ the reason for to leave). The same noun takes a bare to-infinitive meaning a justification (a reason to leave), a bare why-clause (the reason why she left), a bare that-clause (the reason that she left), and a zero clause (the reason she left).
entries.pattern: the reason for [noun phrase / verb-ing] · a reason to [verb] · the reason why [clause] · the reason that [clause] · the reason ø [clause] · the reason is that [clause] · for some reason · by reason of [noun phrase] · within reason
entries.variants: the reason why, the reason that, and the bare the reason + clause are all standard American English; why is the most emphatic, the bare form the most conversational
entries.contrast: The four good frames and the one bad one. The reason for the delay takes a noun; the reason why / that / ø she left takes a clause; a reason to leave takes an infinitive and means a justification for a future act rather than an explanation of a past one. The error is the reason is because: because already means "for the reason that," so ✗ the reason is because he was sick says it twice — write the reason is that he was sick, or just he was sick. Two further notes: ✗ the reason of the delay is not American English, and the old objection to the reason why as redundant is a nineteenth-century invention with no basis in the record; it has been in continuous good use since Middle English.
entries.see also: cause of, grounds for, excuse for, point in/of, for

entries.meaning: A set of instructions for making a dish — or, figuratively, a reliable way of producing a result.
examples: She still uses her grandmother's recipe for cornbread and refuses to write it down.
Cutting the inspection budget is a recipe for disaster.
Do you have a good recipe for pickled okra?
Three managers with the same authority is a recipe for nobody deciding anything.
The recipe for the sauce calls for twice as much butter as anyone admits.
Borrowing against a house to pay a credit card is a recipe for losing both.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈrɛsəpi fɚ/ · three syllables, stress on the first; not /rɪˈsaɪp/
entries.русский: рецепт чего-л. — кулинарный и переносный («верный способ получить»)
entries.register: neutral; the figurative frame is idiomatic and very common in American speech and journalism
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (a recipe for getting yourself fired) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a recipe to get yourself fired) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: a recipe for [a dish] · a recipe for [disaster / trouble / success] · follow / double / ruin a recipe · a recipe calls for [an ingredient] · my grandmother's recipe
entries.contrast: ✗ A recipe of is an error in both the literal and the figurative sense. The figurative frame is nearly fixed and overwhelmingly negative: a recipe for disaster, for trouble, for failure — a recipe for success exists but sounds like a motivational poster. Note the recipe calls for, an idiom where the recipe itself does the asking, and note that receipt was once the same word and now means only a proof of purchase: ✗ a receipt for banana bread is a nineteenth-century usage that will read as a mistake.
entries.see also: cure for, solution to, way of/to, key to, plan for, for

entries.meaning: The option of turning to some remedy or authority, and whom a creditor may pursue.
examples: Tenants in that building have almost no recourse when the heat fails.
The clause forces recourse to arbitration before anyone files suit.
The lender has no recourse against her personally, only against the property.
He was left with no recourse but to sell at a loss.
Any recourse to the courts under this section waives the informal process.
She endorsed the note without recourse and slept better for it.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈrikɔrs tə/ · American stress varies: REE-korss and rih-KORSS are both current
entries.русский: юр. обращение к средству защиты; право регресса к должнику
entries.register: formal; legal and financial in the against and without frames
entries.complement: to: the remedy, authority, or means turned to, as a noun phrase or gerund (recourse to litigating every claim) — never a to-infinitive (✗ recourse to sue). against: the person or asset a creditor can proceed against. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: recourse to [the courts / force / an authority] · recourse against [a borrower / a guarantor] · have / seek / be left with no recourse · without recourse · a non-recourse loan · as a last recourse
entries.contrast: To is what you resort to, against is whom you can pursue. Recourse to arbitration is a path; recourse against the guarantor is a target — and the American mortgage term non-recourse means the lender may take the house and nothing else. ✗ recourse for is an error. The bare no recourse is the everyday form (the tenant has no recourse), and without recourse written above a signature on a negotiable instrument disclaims liability. The verb is resort to, not ✗ recourse to — recourse is a noun only in modern American usage.
entries.see also: remedy for/against, claim against/for/to, liability for/to, lien on/against, resort to, to

entries.meaning: A mention of something, or a person who vouches for you.
examples: The contract makes no reference to the easement at all.
There's a passing reference to the fire in the county history.
She listed two former supervisors as references.
I'm writing with reference to your letter of March 4.
The map was drawn without reference to the actual property lines.
Keep the confirmation number for future reference.
entries.русский: упоминание чего-л., ссылка на; также рекомендация или рекомендатель
entries.complement: noun phrase, pronoun, or gerund (a reference to having served overseas) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a reference to serve overseas) and never a that-clause. In the employment sense, a reference for takes the person recommended.
entries.pattern: a reference to [thing mentioned] · a reference for [job applicant] · with reference to [noun phrase] · in reference to [noun phrase] · make reference to [noun phrase] · a frame of reference · for future reference
entries.variants: with reference to and in reference to — both formal correspondence openers; American editors cut both to about or regarding wherever possible. See with reference to
entries.contrast: To for a mention, for for a recommendation. A reference to the 1996 agreement is a mention of it; a reference for the applicant is a letter vouching for her — ✗ a reference of the applicant is an error. The -ing rule holds because a noun fits the slot: a reference to being overseas, ✗ a reference to be overseas. Note that the phrasal opener with reference to is a preposition in its own right, treated in the topic and reference file, and that without reference to means "disregarding."
entries.see also: comment on, report on/of, connection with/to/between, example of, to

entries.meaning: A connection between people, or between variables.
examples: She has a complicated relationship with her father's second family.
The study found no relationship between the additive and the symptoms.
What is your relationship to the deceased?
The firm has had a relationship with that supplier since 1978.
The relationship between rainfall and yield is not linear.
They've been in a relationship for about two years.
entries.русский: отношения с кем-л.; связь, зависимость между величинами
entries.complement: with: the other party (a relationship with my father). between: both parties or variables named from outside (the relationship between diet and blood pressure). to: a formal or structural connection (her relationship to the deceased). Never a gerund after with, never an infinitive, never a clause.
entries.pattern: a relationship with [person / institution] · the relationship between X and Y · [someone's] relationship to [person / thing] · have / build / end a relationship with [person] · in a relationship
entries.contrast: With is personal, between is external, to is structural. Her relationship with the victim describes how they got along; her relationship to the victim asks how she is related — sister, employer, neighbor — and a police report that confuses the two produces a very different document. Between requires two named items: ✗ the relationship between diet is incomplete. ✗ a relationship of is an error except in formal compounds (a relationship of trust). In American speech in a relationship with no complement means romantically involved.
entries.see also: connection with/to/between, link between/to, marriage to, similarity to/between, between

entries.meaning: The quality of having a bearing on the matter under discussion.
examples: I don't see the relevance to anything we're deciding tonight.
Counsel objected to the relevance of the question to the charged conduct.
The 1974 study has real relevance to how the pipe was specified.
His military service is of no relevance to the permit application.
The committee questioned the survey's relevance to rural districts.
Half the exhibit was excluded for lack of relevance.
entries.русский: отношение к делу, значимость для рассматриваемого вопроса
entries.register: neutral to formal; a working term in courtrooms, where an objection is simply "Relevance."
entries.complement: a noun phrase or gerund (its relevance to choosing a site) — never a to-infinitive (✗ relevance to choose a site) and never a clause.
entries.pattern: relevance to [a question / a case / a decision] · the relevance of X to Y · have / lack / question the relevance of [noun phrase] · of no relevance · contemporary relevance
entries.variants: relevance and relevancy are both current in American English; relevance is the ordinary form and relevancy survives in evidence law (the relevancy of the exhibit)
entries.contrast: ✗ Relevance on and ✗ relevance for are errors — the noun takes to, matching the adjective relevant to. Against bearing on, which means the same thing with a different preposition: no relevance to the case and no bearing on the case are equivalent, and swapping the prepositions produces two errors at once. The full frame needs both halves when the source is named: the relevance of his tax returns to the zoning question.
entries.see also: bearing on, applicability to, importance of/to, connection with/to/between, relevant to, to

entries.meaning: Something that cures a problem, and, in law, the relief a court can give.
examples: There's no quick remedy for a foundation that has already shifted.
The statute gives homeowners a remedy against the original builder.
Repair or replacement is the buyer's sole and exclusive remedy under this warranty.
Her grandmother's remedy for a cough involved more whiskey than honey.
Plaintiffs must exhaust administrative remedies before filing.
Firing the vendor is not a remedy for a process that was broken to begin with.
entries.pronunciation note: weak /ˈrɛmədi fɚ/; against has no weak form
entries.русский: средство от чего-л.; юр. способ правовой защиты
entries.register: neutral in the everyday sense; legal in the against frame and in remedies at law
entries.complement: for: the problem or ailment cured, as a noun phrase or gerund (a remedy for overcharging customers) — never a to-infinitive (✗ a remedy to overcharge). against: the party a legal remedy runs against. Never a clause.
entries.pattern: a remedy for [a problem / an illness] · a remedy against [a defendant] · seek / have / exhaust a remedy · remedies at law and in equity · a home remedy · the exclusive remedy
entries.contrast: For the trouble, against the person. A remedy for the leak fixes the leak; a remedy against the seller is what you can make him do. ✗ a remedy to the problem is an error, and it is the commonest one here, borrowed from solution to — which does take to. Note the American contract phrase sole and exclusive remedy, which limits everything a party can ask for, and exhaust your remedies, which means using every available process before going to court. In everyday speech, a home remedy takes for an ailment.
entries.see also: cure for, solution to, recourse to/against, damages for, injunction against, for

entries.meaning: An answer to a message or a statement.
examples: I never got a reply to the second letter.
In reply to your inquiry, the fee schedule is attached.
His reply to the accusation was four words long.
There's been no reply from the county in six weeks.
She hit reply all by mistake and copied the whole board.
A prompt reply to the notice will keep the account open.
entries.русский: ответ на письмо или реплику — рус. «на», не «к»
entries.complement: noun phrase or pronoun naming the message answered (a reply to my email). Never a gerund, never an infinitive, never a that-clause in ordinary use. In reply to is the fixed formal opener.
